ENCMemoryDeadFriend.strTitle: Clobbered by a Memory of a Friend who Passed
ENCMemoryDeadFriend.strDesc:
They say that grief is like a stone in your pocket. But now, as the memory of your dead friend comes rushing back, it feels more like a millstone around your neck.

When you were together it was easy. Your wavelengths were fully aligned. There was no need for performance or defense or flights away from conversation in search of privacy. A vid stream of nearly nothing could occupy you for hours because of the shared jokes and criticisms you'd develop. The creek trickle of your shallow chats would flow to the deep waters of meaningful conversation so naturally that you'd miss the point at which one became the next.

And now what? You're left with only their defunct RinRin profile as a reminder. And you've watched the vids on there so many times that they have started to feel like scenes from a documentary about a stranger.

Standing here now, in this moment, you're left wondering: can such a thing ever be recuperated? Replaced? And with cold certainty you realize that it cannot.

ENCMemoryDeadFriendDeeperClobber.strTitle: Process the Memory of Friend Who Passed
ENCMemoryDeadFriendDeeperClobber.strDesc:
For the first time you let the certainty of your loss descend upon you. You watch as all your denials, all your angers, all your bitter negotiations fall away like autumn leaves, leaving behind only the barren tree of your loneliness.

What you long for now, in this moment, is not love or meaning or even joy. It is the simple presence of someone you cared for. It is the reminder that the system is not merely a complex hallucination of a deranged mind, but instead a world with others in it, others not so different than yourself.

This newfound certainty that your friend is never coming back is a pain you can hardly bear. But it is the kind of pain that accompanies growth. And in the depths of your mind you know that, with enough time, it is a growth you will be grateful for.

ENCMemoryDeadFriendRevisit.strTitle: Revisited by the Memory of a Friend Who Passed
ENCMemoryDeadFriendRevisit.strDesc:
The truth of your loss returns to you suddenly. You see it again: the barren tree of grief, once lush with foliage, now stark and grim. On the horizon behind, you see dark clouds flickering white with lightning, as if the circuitry powering them is overloaded and failing.

You've already determined that this loss is permanent. And you've resolved yourself not to deny such a powerful truth. But the pain of being alone is still there, and judging by those clouds it will get worse before it gets better. What will you do with it?

ENCMemoryDeadFriendDeeperRevisit.strTitle: Process the Revisitation of Your Memory of a Friend Who Passed
ENCMemoryDeadFriendDeeperRevisit.strDesc:
You stand staring at the tree as the clouds approach and gather. Somehow the rain arrives before the clouds are even overhead, long ropes of it lashing at the ground and branches, each one snapping up clouds of dust that soon settle into thick black mud at your feet.

Your animal mind screams for relief as you're pounded with the reality of your loss. How could your friend leave you here, all alone in such a cruel and uncaring world? In your mind's eye you see shelter: a cave, a hovel really. You know that if you're willing to scrabble through the mud it is a place you could go to escape the storm.

But you don't. Somehow, through all this, you've gathered enough wisdom to know that there is no hiding from it. So you stand and let the rain lash. You watch the dark clouds as they shout and flash.

And, before long, you see it: the sun. Just there, behind the havoc of the storm's tantrum. If you had fled to the cave, you never would have found it.

ENCMemoryDeadFriendFinal.strTitle: Final Memory of a Friend Who Passed
ENCMemoryDeadFriendFinal.strDesc:
There it is again: the grief, the proverbial stone in your pocket. You run your fingers along the sharp edges, trace them to where they grow curved and soft.

Last time you were here it was a storm of sadness you just barely survived. You know you could go there again, provided you're strong enough to weather it. What will you do?

ENCMemoryDeadFriendDeeperFinal.strTitle: Resolve Your Memory of a Friend Who Passed
ENCMemoryDeadFriendDeeperFinal.strDesc:
When humanity flung itself from Earth just a few generations ago, the gesture was powered by a force of optimism that once free from our home we might expand the species beyond our basest needs.

But now, standing at the tree of your grief, staring at the sun as it burns the rain away into a soft mist that climbs into the sky above you, you finally understand that can never be true.

The need to eat. The need to sleep. And our deepest need, the need to be close to another with their own needs; these are grasping desires we can never, should never, fully shed.

Your friend is gone now, lifted into the mist of the next, if there is such a place. But the force of your desire to be with them again, once an impossible pain, feels now like an upwards tug at the heart, a gentle squeeze of your empty hand. It is a reminder: once you have been loved, you can never truly be alone.

You've managed with long internal struggle to fully process your memory of your friend's death. Through this, you've gained a new and rare sense of patience. It will serve you well in the future.

ENCMemoryMasses.strTitle: Clobbered by a Memory of The Masses
ENCMemoryMasses.strDesc:
You're reminded, suddenly, of being trapped among bodies. Dozens, hundreds of them, all fleeing a single source of danger, or supposed danger, as the inciting incident happened outside your sightline and became irrelevant the instant you were swept up in the stampede.

What mattered in the moment is that you were stuck, forced, kettled by wild-eyed LEO thugs barking about how non-lethal rounds will still ruin your day.

What you recall now is being just one in a sea of heads, bodies pressed and jostling, pushed forward because it was the only place anyone could go. You felt heat, smelled sweat, waded through a potpourri of pheromones so thick you could taste them on the back of your tongue.

The crowd moved with such inevitable momentum that you could lift your feet and travel with it beyond your input. Never had you felt more like an atom, a mere component of solid matter, significant only in theory, discernable only in grouping.

Steeping in that memory now, you begin to wonder if you have any individuality at all. If you aren't just surrendering at every moment to stronger forces, be they corporate, capitalist, social or cosmic.

ENCHeatCCREBustedStart.strDesc:
They haul you before a CCRE magistrate for judgement, leaving your ship and gear behind.

At the hearing, you can beg for just a fine- $15,000 payable in full or installments- or it's off to Ring Station Brig for a year or three of hard labor.

ENCHeatCCREFineEnd.strDesc:
It's almost like they want you to break the rules so they can extract more fines from you.

You sign reams of paperwork in tight cuffs.

It's a prison sentence of another sort. Another weight hanging around your neck.

New $15,000 fine added.

ENCHeatCCREFineDebtEnd.strTitle: Plead for a fine (Paid in installments)
ENCHeatCCREFineDebtEnd.strDesc:
It's almost like they want you to break the rules so they can lock you deeper in interest payments.

You sign reams of paperwork in tight cuffs.

It's a prison sentence of another sort. Another weight hanging around your neck.

New $15,000 debt added, with payment due each shift.

ENCHeatCCREFineFinish.strDesc:
After processing, you are unceremoniously dumped outside the CCRE Security Office. If you weren't docked at station when you were arrested, you may need to use the PASS ferry service (on your PDA) to reach your ship again. Hopefully it's still there.

Time to get back on your feet.

ENCHeatCCREPrisonStart.strDesc: You are hauled off to Ring Station Brig.

ENCHeatCCREPrisonEnd.strDesc:
You spend months laboring without wage among outcasts both meek and dangerous. You share a dorm with nearly a hundred other souls, all of you stacked like kindling on triple high bunks.

But even a hell like this is not without opportunity. You hear things. You meet people. You get in a few scrapes, you find a few friends. By the end of your term you've lived a dozen lives and you have all the scars to prove it.

Plus, free room and board. In a certain light, it might all be worth it ...

It's painful, probably not sterile, and beyond the budgets of most spacers, but it's the only option around for helping your space-wracked body become a little less of a mess.

ENCMedServicesAdvStart.strDesc: Unlike in most other parts of the Solar System, you can count on these state-of-the-art biomedical treatments to be sterile, well-researched (or at least well-marketed), and excessively priced: The best option around for helping your space-wracked body become more perfect, more desirable, more human.

ENCMemoryViolence.strTitle: Clobbered by a Memory of Witnessing Violence
ENCMemoryViolence.strDesc:
The memory, if it can even be called that, appears as a gap, a vacuum, a lacuna of remembering that flashes sights and sounds disconnected from any sense of narrative. Here is the blood, then nothing. There is the severing, the smell of metal and salt, then nothing again. Accompanying each flash are the noises: the screams, the guttural moans, the mewling pleas for help that will never arrive.

The terror that grips you now grows from a particular certainty: the body is fragile, leaking, stuffed with vital machines that can fail in a mere moment. It is not the thought of death that scares you. That is an inevitability you faced long ago.

It is the pondering of how you will die that frightens you. In what manner will you go?

There is a cause of death in your future, and you're paralyzed by the question of what that cause will be.

ENCMemoryViolenceDeeperClobber.strTitle: Process the Memory of Witnessing Violence
ENCMemoryViolenceDeeperClobber.strDesc: As hard as it is to remember now, you're certain something did happen that day. The images of violence are too specific, too repeated, too stable to be mere flights of your imagination. The contorted faces especially give you pause: they are blurred, but somehow still familiar. It strikes you that looking back at the memory now feels like casting a line into a mist covered pond. Your lure arcs out and disappears into fog, leaving you to wonder if it ever struck the surface at all. But as you wait you get nibbles. Little jerks on the rod, each one bringing the memory into greater focus. The blood, once filling the entire frame of your vision, now gathers and pools near the bodies. The screams, each once indistinguishable from the next, find timbre and pitch. The blurred faces, gradually, find form. So here you wait, slowly remembering, hoping the nibble might eventually become a bite. And while you know it will take time, there is cold comfort in the fact that this moment from your past is, while horrible, very real.

ENCMemoryViolenceRevisit.strTitle: Revisited by the Memory of Witnessing Violence
ENCMemoryViolenceRevisit.strDesc:
The catastrophic scene of violence returns to you. The blood, the howls, the stench of death. All the details appear as before in the same precise resolution.

But this time the memory arrives not as a havoc of images with no context but instead as a story. A sequence of events with cause and effect. A grim tale, no doubt, but one with a beginning, a middle, a terrible end.

They were alive, able bodied, intact. Then the violence fell, and their bodies were mangled. Then they lay bleeding. Some found their end.

And while you were lucky that day, you know one day that you'll find yours. It's an end you can flee from, or it is one you can ponder.

In either case that end will remain, a cause lurking in the dark corridor of your future, crouched like a predator ready to pounce. Whether the end is distant or near at hand is something you'll never know.

ENCMemoryViolenceDeeperRevisit.strTitle: Process the Revisitation of Your Memory of Witnessing Violence
ENCMemoryViolenceDeeperRevisit.strDesc:
You stare down the corridor ahead, squint into its blackness. Every moment is a step ahead. There is no turning back. Time only moves in one direction, after all.

It strikes you now that while each moment brings you closer to your end, each also presents within it a choice. And from that choice branches others, each then splitting into more choices, more moments, on and on in an infinite fractal of possible futures.

Time is not a corridor, then, merely because it leads to death. It is an ever stretching horizon, an endless flashing desert of moments, all of which feature a version of you within them.

Yes, you will die. But before that, you will live. What will you do in this moment? The only moment you are, at least in the very present, guaranteed?

ENCMemoryViolenceFinal.strDesc:
Your memory of that violent day arrives to you again, now transformed. It appears neither as an unrecognizable sequence of images nor as an inevitable consequence of fate.

Instead, you see it in full clarity: a catastrophic moment that changed you, but does not have to define you. It is neither a zero, nor an open wound, but a scar.

And what now of your future? How will you move forward, scarred as you are by the trauma of being so intimate with death?

ENCMemoryViolenceDeeperFinal.strTitle: Resolve Your Memory of Witnessing Violence
ENCMemoryViolenceDeeperFinal.strDesc:
On the Venusian aerostat of Encantado, a small culture of artisans have dedicated their life to preserving the ancient Japanese and Brazilian craftwork of their former homes.

One such craft is Kintsugi, the restoration of cracked and damaged ceramics using gold leaf not to hide the flaws of a broken object but instead to highlight them, to render the object complete once again, now with the history of its former trauma legible on its surface.

It strikes you now that you are one such vessel. Instead of cowering in fear of this violent moment from your past, you've embraced it. Rather than hiding the scars of that day you have resolved to gild them, to integrate them fully, and beautifully, with your present self.

With every passing moment we accrue the physical artifacts of time. Dust. Scars. Wrinkles near our eyes, eyes which eventually cloud over and one day close forever.

But these artifacts are the stuff living. The patina of life, now a protest against death. A physical testament to your past and your presence, however brief, in this System.

You've managed with long internal struggle to fully process your memory of violence. Through this, you've gained a new and rare optimism. It will serve you well in the future.

ENCEmbassyServicesMVOL.strDesc:
Most sovereignties in the System observe a tiered immigration status, or "strata." Usually ranging from undocumented (illegal) immigrant, up to full citizenship, a person's strata dictates which rights they enjoy with the sovereignty.

Rights can include access to certain areas or services, eligibility for private housing or ship docking, enhanced prices on trade authorization, or even legal protections or permissions.

Such rights are usually conferred by parents through birth (jus sanguinis), and in some cases, by being born in the territory (jus soli).

Obtaining legal status after birth usually involves applying for a visa, and may include getting a sponsor and/or paying a significant fee.

ENCEmbassyServicesMVOLVisaInvestor.strDesc:

Do you have an innovative research or business idea, and the means to foster your ambitions? If you can prove your ability to contribute to the advancement of Voltaire and it's University, you may be able to immigrate with this visa class.

ENCEmbassyServicesMVOLVisaInvestorAccept.strDesc:
After submitting your application fee, your information is vetted through an initial cursory background check. Voltaire's Institutional Committee of Admission, Grants, & Matriculation (ICAGM) could still discover a problem with your application during its full investigation, but at least the preliminary check passes.

Congratulations! You are now the proud holder of admittance and Permanent Resident status in the most advanced research university in the Solar System!

Go enjoy the trade discounts and private housing opportunities.

ENCMemoryDumbRevisit.strDesc: The difficult memory returns to you again uninvited. You can choose to suppress it, gaining a momentary respite from the fear it generates. Or you can do the difficult work of processing it, stirring up hard emotions in the present with the hope it might lead to permanent growth in the future.

It doesn't bring you as much peace as before to flee from this memory, but it still feels safer than processing such an ugly moment.

Surely you can do this forever. Right?

ENCMemoryThirdSuppressDumb.strTitle: Suppress Memory of The Dumbest Thing You've Ever Said Yet Again
ENCMemoryThirdSuppressDumb.strDesc:
For the third time you suppress this memory, knowing you'll escape it for a while. But after all this running from your past, you no longer feel a sense of peace in flight.

In fact, dodging the memory has changed you, perhaps irrevocably.

There's a lesson here, if you choose to see it.

ENCMemoryChildhood.strTitle: Clobbered by a Memory of Childhood
ENCMemoryChildhood.strDesc:
The memory of being a kid again arrives to you without warning, and it comes as quite a shock. After all this time fending for yourself, squeezing every dollar you can out of the corporate grind, you had almost forgotten there was a time when you needed someone else to survive.

But you did. Everyone around here did. That's why the corps built the work houses, the group homes, the gymnasium-sized neonatal intensive care units. And with every new such gesture they demand gratitude, despite the fact that everyone knows exactly what they are doing: protecting their assets.

The person you remember now was the last to protect you, to show you real kindness, to look at you as if you weren't an investment but a person, with hopes and dreams and fears about tomorrow.

Standing at their funeral you had a sinking feeling that nothing would ever be the same. After a few words their body was summarily spirited away for processing, yet another asset for the corp, and you were left alone.

You've been fending for yourself ever since.

ENCMemoryBetrayal.strTitle: Clobbered by a Memory of Someone You Betrayed
ENCMemoryBetrayal.strDesc:
At the time it felt so easy. Like seeing an open door and merely walking through it.

It took just five or six words. Flimsy little things on their own, words. But when bolstered by the right facial expression, a wry little smile you dug deep to find, the sentiment was suddenly ironclad: "Hey. Would I lie to you?"

But lie you did. And down your friend went, down and down a darkened path you laid that led to their certain ruin.

And the worst part is? They still don't know it was you who sold them down the river. Poor thing.

No, that's not the worst part. The worst part is that standing here, as the memory returns, you know that you're capable of doing it all again.

ENCFirstDockBWVN.strDesc: You step on to the strange vessel, wondering what it could possibly be doing so far away from OKLG. Looking around you realize that, much like a decaying relationship, the ship was clearly built with love but is now in dire need of TLC. You recognize the bones of a Testudo Heavy Tug, but it's been heavily modified. Several coats of a cloying yellow-gold have been applied to all the floors and walls, some more recently than others. The ground is littered with cigarette butts, rocky debris, and half-eaten Nacho Fiesta Trenchers. Down the central corridor you hear a percussive banging that serves as the backbeat to an a capella melody belted at enthusiastic volume. You strain to make out the words: "Fire on the mountain! *BANG* "Static in the black!" *BANG.* "That bright seam calls, so I obey, and I'm never goin back!" *BANG BANG!* You pause for a moment and consider the wisdom of interrupting someone so deeply involved in their flow. The song does call to you in a spirit of optimism, however. It's hard not to be charmed by it. "Folks'll call you crazy." *BANG* "But they ain't glimpsed the gold!" *BANG*. "I'll tap the vein that buys me Mars and that's where I'll grow old!" *BANG BANG*

ENCFirstDockEJDRContd.strDesc:
Luna's livelihood is in the Helium-3 mining and processing facilities at Jade Rabbit.

Jade Rabbit can't compete with the abundance of resources at Uranus, Saturn and Neptune, but it boasts the most mature extraction process in the system, the mining having begun in the infancy of space colonisation. The smaller overhead when shipping fuel to the Inner System allows it to remain competitive.

Lunar shipping companies put fuel barges into low energy transfer orbits, allowing these 'slowboats' to travel to Inner System destinations for a fraction of the cost of a regular burn, but over the course of weeks or months.

ENCFirstDockBCRS1.strDesc:
There are living agents working the crowds, too. Attractive young men and women hover at the entrance of every outlet, desperate to rope a passerby into a personality-conversion sale. The commission is low, but the alternative is starvation, so they follow you as far as you’ll let them. 

One follows you a full three minutes down the concourse, hoping desperately to spritz you with a perfume bottle. You threaten to call station security; they inform you hopefully about the group discount. Disgusted, you duck behind a loading trolley piled high with water bottles and condoms, and hitch a ride.

You hop off at a part of the concourse you don’t recognise, which is indistinguishable from all the parts you do.

ENCFirstDockBWVN2.strDesc:
Your approach nearly scares the man out of his shoes. Tools and rocks spill from his hands as he whips around to face you, a look of genuine terror in his eyes.

"Got damn! Liable to get shot creepin around like that. Yer quiet as a hunt cat, anyone ever tell you that? Lordy loo."

The harried man retrieves a yellowed rag and mops copious sweat from his brow as he regards you with narrowed eyes.

"If yer one of them Azikiwe pricks I'll tell you what I told the last one: I ain't sellin my claim! There's color in these rocks yet. I can smell it."

Despite the man's aggressive demeanor, his singing makes you doubt his capacity for violence. As you grope around for a reply you notice more peculiarities of the lone spacer.

The gold motif of the ship extends to his wardrobe, each piece a fierce yellow, including the high G compression leggings you glimpse between his shoes and the cuffs of his pants. As if that weren't enough, his fingers and mouth are stained to a permanent orange, signs of an exclusive diet of cigarettes and Nacho Fiesta Trenchers.

79AU_Boheme5.strTitle: That sounds like a good option
79AU_Boheme5.strDesc:
"I was beginning to think my way of life was done for," you say. "Most of the aliens I've met are indifferent or hostile. But you guys seem cool."

"Thank you for saying that," Sanguine says sincerely. He speaks with a quiet drawl, and his voice is inviting, like he's always sharing good news with you. "Not everyone is sympatico."

"If you were to be the, uhm," you say, "stewards for humanity, I guess? Would you take care of us?"

He shakes his head sadly. "No can do, amigo. We want to preserve that unique thing you've got going on, but the other ententes won't let that happen."

"Shit," you say. "For a second I thought things might be easy."

He smiles and claps your shoulder. "Our credo rebels against 'easy'. Too boring for us." He turns to the sea of stars, leaning on the balcony. The riotous band of purple and orange has never looked brighter. "You made it this far. I'm sure you'll figure something out."

79AU_Boheme6.strDesc:
"I like the sound of that," you say. "How do you join? Is it an open club?"

"It is," he says slowly, "yes. But."

"But?"

"But what you're asking is not what you think you're asking," he says. "Experience is, I learned this one recently, a 'two way street'. This is why we don't like labels. Becoming something other than human means exactly that."

You look down at your mending body, the wheelchair you need to move around. "I wouldn't be human anymore."

He sighs - not frustrated, but he was anticipating you would say that. "Yes and no! That's what I'm getting at."

"Do you know what a leap of faith is?" you ask. He nods. "Is it like that?" He nods again. "Got it."

79AU_Boheme7.strDesc:
The Milky Way is a timely reminder of the vast difference between an empirical understanding of reality, which most people including yourself subscribed to by default, and the milieu in which you currently find yourself. You're among interstellar beings advanced enough to take human form and make themselves approachable, downright urbane. How to conceive of this? Are they made of atoms? Are you?

"The more I walk this path," you say to Sanguine, "the less real it seems. That's frightening." You take a straw poll of your emotional state, and find it unchanged. "Even if I'm not frightened, I think I should be," you add.

"That's life, man," he says. "It's a constant process of growing too comfortable, having that illusion shatter, and rebuilding it over from square one."

"But whenever my understanding broadens," you say, "it diminishes everything that came before. There's nothing to hold on to."

He gestures at himself, his blue suit and his unassuming, gangly figure. "You probably don't think I'm a fighter. I am. We're fighting every day. You have to fight for yourself. The universe will destroy you if you let it. Get past the alienation, the dissociation, and hold on to what you can."

He drums his fingers on the rail. The lights of the Milky Way are huge and luminous reflected in his eyes. "It's terribly beautiful out here," he says. "I'm glad we came."

79AU_Boheme8.strDesc:
A tray of tinkling glasses announces the return of Emerald. You follow Sanguine back inside, and he shuts the glass partition behind you.

"Is this an interstellar favourite?" you ask hopefully. "Something they drink across the galaxy?"

Emerald sets your glass next to you, embarrassed. It's a familiar black liquid. "Bacardi and Coke," she says. "Our hats off to the Cubans and the Coca-Cola company."

79AU_Boheme9.strTitle: Interrogate your own lack of reaction
79AU_Boheme9.strDesc:
"This is all coming across as matter-of-fact," you say. "I can't give it the reaction it deserves."

"This place has a different energy than you're used to," says Emerald. She looks at Sanguine, who nods in encouragement. "It'll give you a synthetic perspective." That's not a combination of words you can parse.

"They're asking about the substrate," says Fire from the divan, eyes shut, words muffled by a pillow. "Tell them about the substrate."

"Oh yes!" says Emerald. "In this place, non-Baryonic elements can intermediate with your own matter. Modulated gold and what you call 'void opal' catalyse a harmonic environment that suits us both."

More technobabble, to be honest. "Am I supposed to understand that?"

"No," says Sanguine. "But we don't talk down to folks in First Contact. Honesty is the best policy."

79AU_Boheme10.strDesc: "You look like me," you say. "Human." "Thank you!" says Emerald. "That's really a very great compliment." "Why don't you look like," you ask haltingly, "what you normally look like?" Emerald hesitates as if you're speaking another language. She looks to Sanguine. He leans forward. "This is what we normally look like," he says. Unspoken communication passes between him and Sanguine. "This place translates for us. It translates everything." "Can you show me your true forms?" you ask. A look of shock passes across Emerald's face, quickly suppressed. "I don't think so, no," she says. "For everybody's sake."

79AU_Boheme11.strTitle: Pick apart their recent cosmic history
79AU_Boheme11.strDesc:
"You found the Voyager probe?"

"Sure did," says Emerald. "Lucky 79 AU happened to be going this way. We'd never have noticed it otherwise."

"All our broadcasts," you say, "our radio waves flooding interstellar space. Nobody heard them?"

"There's not a lot going on in this cluster, and radio's not in vogue. Give it, oh," she pauses. "A few thousand years." She pats your knee encouragingly. "Someone'll hear Arecibo, you see if they don't!"

79AU_Boheme12.strDesc:
With only the four of you it's an intimate gathering, but you find time for yourself. The others leave you be as you idly rummage through their record diaspora. You're not sure what you're hunting for, exactly, but with such an eclectic range, they're sure to have it. The big squares seem to be envelopes for gratuitously large discs, one of which you can see turning on an open-faced disc player, which is propped up on a pile of detective novels.

You flip past names like the Beatles, Miles Davis, Parliament Funkadelic, Invisible Acropolis. You only recognise the Beatles, and infer they must be great artists from their age.

Under an empty pizza box you find names you recognise from when you were a kid. There's a lot of generic klaxpop. They have both of Dalisay's releases from her brief pivot from acting to singing, and they might be alone in the universe for that. They have a couple of mash records, but much more from the subgenre that killed it in the 2060s, smash.

One of the records is addressed to you. "For [us-firstname]," it says. You're there, pictured on the cover. The artist listed is 'Isambard Cruz'.

79AU_Night3.strDesc: Over your other shoulder, there is an audience of everyone who ever lived. Hard to say how you know that. Within view, there are assuredly many seats, the theatre curving up and up and up into a gloom. In the front row you recognise Isambard Cruz, Ben Choong, and some faces you dimly remember as the videotape enthusiasts on K-LEG. They watch attentively.

79AU_Night4.strTitle: Remind Joakim you've never played Bridge
79AU_Night4.strDesc:
"If I've never played before, can I have a tutorial?" You glance between the onlookers, wondering if saying this has damaged your attractiveness as a partner. "I know it's a card game, but not much more than that."

"Bridge is not a card game," says Joakim. "Though there is an unpopular Earth game sharing the name. The goal is to build, and become, a bridge, to span the divide between this world and the next."

A deafening silence as if all of Creation is holding its breath. 

On reflection, it's the same problem. "I've never played that either," you say.

"No one can play it twice," says Joakim.

79AU_Night5.strDesc:
"Them," you say, nodding to their table. They let out huge sighs of relief, but they hurriedly confer with each other. You can't hear what they're saying.

"You can't have three partners," says Joakim. "Pick one."

"Your Honour, sir," says Sanguine, hurrying to stand awkwardly by your side. "Can we talk to our friend for a moment?"

They huddle around you. Sanguine takes a knee beside you, the women at either shoulder.

"First of all, we're honoured," says Sanguine, smiling up at you. "Second of all, we can't win. Have you seen the other guy?" You think back to how it was, and it was only moments ago, when you saw the other guy. How utterly malevolent it seemed. You nod. "Right. But we're not counting ourselves out. We can play for the loss you want."

"That's allowed?" you say.

"This isn't really a game," says Emerald. "Once you're in it, there aren't actually any rules. Only a winner and a loser."

"I want to win," you say.

"You're mediating an alien invasion," says Fire. She grips your shoulder hard. "Do or die."

79AU_Night6.strDesc:
"Talk me through losing," you say.

"It's a matter of time. No matter what, the opponent will colonise Sol system," says Sanguine. "I will find a place for Earth's offworlders beyond 79 AU. With us. If they want to."

Emerald taps your hand. "If we go together, part of us would remain behind. I would give your people as much warning as we can," she says. "Brief though it will be."

Fire slams a fist on the table. "Damn you both," she says. "We don't have time to ask. We take them all into us." The others look at her, and she stares them down defiantly. "All of them. All!"

79AU_Night7.strDesc:
"Sanguine," you say to the man.

He smiles bravely. "Let's kick 'em in the teeth."

Emerald and Fire draw back, Emerald with a quick kiss on the cheek for luck. Sanguine stands behind your chair. He places a hand on your shoulder.

"I will join [us-firstname]," he says. His voice is richer, and it carries further.

79AU_Night8.strDesc:
"Emerald," you say.

Emerald grasps your hand. The warmth of her palm passes through your body like an eclipse.

"They will join us," she says, "when they are ready."

Something has you on the verge of tears.

"What if they don't?" you ask her. "What if I'm alone?"

"We will meet again," she says tenderly. "Every one of us."

79AU_Night9.strDesc: "Fire," you say. A great heat blossoms in your gut. You gasp, and vapour streams from your mouth. Before you have the presence of mind to think, what the hell?, another thought answers. Good, says Fire decisively. I wasn't going to stand by and watch them drown. The pair of you lock eyes. You share a thought, and it doesn't matter whose it is. Let's put things to rights.

79AU_Night10.strTitle: On second thought, you guys are useless
79AU_Night10.strDesc:
"I think," you say slowly, "you ought go back to your table." You look at them in the eyes, each one in turn. "I can win this thing."

The Bohemians extricate themselves from the huddle. Emerald is the last to go. "Good luck," she says.

79AU_Bridge1.strDesc:
The lights, the overheads and the green banker's lamps in the VIP section, flicker.

"Begin," says Joakim.

The inessential faces melt away. The scope of existence contracts until it is focused around you, your opponent, and the table between you. Grey smoke swells from underneath it. The lights flicker. Inside the smoke is a brighter, powerful strobe light. The gas flashes terribly white, leaving spots in your vision when it fades. It flashes and flashes, faster and faster. The gas diffuses into space that is no longer a room.

"Have I been here before?" you ask your companion. You can't quite make out their face. Your vision is washed with afterimages. Everything moves as in a video with a slow shutter speed. You remember a table, a bridge, a console, flickering lights, dread, and the distant fate of winners and losers. You remember a moment that lasted an eternity. An impostor in a holy place. Time is the sense you're going to miss parting with the most.

"No," they reassure you. "This has never happened before, and will never happen again."

"Good," you say. "Once is enough."

You breathe in the brilliant smoke, a great fresh lungful of it. Endorphins flood your system and your extremities tingle pleasantly. You can't see the board, or your opponent, and you are beginning to lose sight of yourself. The trigeminal nerves under the skin of your face feel wonderfully hot and cold at the same time.

"I feel warm," you say.

"An analgesic," replies an increasingly distant voice. "For what comes next."

You can't see anything. Soon you won't need to.

79AU_Bridge2.strDesc:
ENCODE THE FINAL ENGRAM

AS A STATEMENT OF INTENT

WE DREAM OURSELVES INTO YOU

ALL ALONG THE DREAMING PATH

79AU_Bridge3.strDesc:
Bootloader in memory, package integrations follow. They glom onto the kernel until it is set for a massive parallel installation. Mandalas synchronise their innermost circles, and the blessings spread.

Piece by piece they arrange a panoscopic sensorium, scooping out the cataracts in the third eye. Electromagnetism and gravity intermingle with their Platonic shadows, a rainbow aurora dancing around an impenetrable black sphere. It is clear at last how reflections can contain their own reflections. As above, so below. Yin and Yang.

Nobody sees the cocoon of light taking shape around the body. A halo forms at the crown, streaming information through the Sahasrara, awakening a deadened soul.

79AU_Bridge4.strDesc: You percolate through a golden membrane, arriving at a far vantage from the singularity at the centre of 79 AU. Your eyes were built to see it. Space curves inwards and inwards again, reaching down to where a colossal wavefront of information freezes in the moment it breaks. It's trapped there forever, or until the universe reveals what all this causality has been for. "This is the bridge," you say. "And so are we." Your companion is preoccupied. "I only wish we could've got here first. There's no way - TURN!" You turn as your opponent lunges out of a crouch, a curved dagger flashing. You reach out. The dagger pierces clean through your hand, becoming lodged in the flesh. You lock arms. You struggle for control. "No ... hard ... feelings ... eh, [us-firstname]?" your opponent grunts. The pain is extraordinary. But you're used to pain, and your opponent is weak. You're the one who traveled here in person, as a person, after all. "One of many differences between us -" you feel the knife rend your flesh as you strive for balance. You let go completely. The blade slides free, leaving a fresh stigmata in your palm. Capitalising on good fortune, your opponent drives the blade into your sternum. A better fighter would've slashed your throat rather than drive it into more flesh. "- you don't feel anything at all." You punch your opponent in the teeth. They drop like a sack of rocks. The astral sings in frustration. Light pours from your opponent's mouth, breaking it wide open. Ignoring the pain, you remove the dagger, toss it far into the ether. "Take the bridge!" says a voice in your ear. "While it's weakened! Now!"

79AU_Bridge5.strDesc:
The exterior of 79 AU finishes its preparations. The golden threads are woven into the final form, its outstanding patterns tied off.

One of its passengers assumes command, and the station is fully operational.

A full third of the sphere has become an enormous transmission array extending three times its diameter. Already primed, it fires a burst of energy, an analogue of light not visible from the crushing Baryonic depths below. Out of the barrel it is centimetres wide, widening conically a few degrees. It is aimed at one star in the night sky. 

Faster than light, the burst arrives at Sol ahead of itself, the arc flared wide enough to encompass the eight major planetoids and much else besides. It passes through the local matter without interaction, save for a few million tiny hits clustered around the orbital bodies. In these it achieves an astonishingly dense rapport.

The burst avoids Earth, flowing around it as a river would a rock.

The burst travels for a further 79 AU past its target. It diffuses upon the interstellar medium without effect, two seconds before it is fired.

Another passenger takes the bridge, ousting the first. The array prepares to fire a second shot.

All this is known to you, but you are concerned with other matters. For example -

79AU_Bridge6.strDesc: - elsewhere you hear a voice saying "Terrain, Terrain, Terrain", and a familiar sound, the rapid beeping of the NAV Station. It accelerates until the separate sounds converge in one high pitched alarm, the dumb digital mind wailing as it contends with the distance travelled - - you are still on -

79AU_Bridge7.strDesc: You lift your head to feel the bluster of trade winds brisk and warm on your cheek. Your vessel has reached the end of the delta, thrust onto a distemperate sea, blue and grey in the morning light. Comes the question: Where away? It is yours to answer.

79AU_DeadUniverse1.strDesc: Earth et al is roughly ten light-hours away. Five not-light hours after you start the journey, you stop receiving comms chatter from Sol. Not all at once. Your information has to get here the old-fashioned way. Traffic in some Neptunian buoys stops flowing except for routine pings, nodes in the network chattering back and forth about machine things on an empty line. Many minutes later, from your perspective, it happens at Titan, at Jupiter, and so on, until hours later the System is nothing but dead air. The ships are still there. The stations are still there. The lights are on, but nobody's home.

ENCConversationBWVN3.strDesc:
"Ha! Name's Jacob Waltz, and I'm one of them whatchamacallits," he pauses, then lights up. "En-tree-panours. Hung my own shingle, you see."

"In fact, I'd love to hire you for a little favor if yer willin and able. You seem able enough from where I'm standin. Are ya willin?"

ENCConversationBWVN4.strDesc:
Look it's simple: what I crave is gold. Shiners. Pay dirt. That sweet auric chloride. Hell, I'd even take chlorauric acid in a pinch, long as she's yella. I'll give you good money per nugget. Above rate, because I know somethin these poor saps don't."

Jacob has a strange tic you've never seen before. Periodically he will tilt his head back, widen his eyes, purse his lips, and suck in air as if through an invisible straw.

"So what'll it be? You in?" he asks.

ENCConversationBWVN4Deny.strDesc:
When you explain that you aren't interested in helping out at this time, Jacob assures you that you can take your sweet time. "Oh I'm as patient as the hills. Been at this a while already, and as long as the corps keep out of my business, I'll be at this till the veins run dry. And I'm always willin to pay better than either of the damn factions fightin to monopolize all the rocks at Ceres."

His appraising eyes gives you a once over, "Come find me later... when you've got gold on you, or one o'them shiny Halvorson mining lasers, or a legit Radar, or hell, a whole PDC".

ENCConversationBWVN4Accept.strDesc: When you agree to trade your effort for his money, Jacob can't help busting into a little spacer jig before wincing a bit at the toll his toil has taken on his own body. "Perfect! I'll take all the gold you can get yer hands on. Check the veins of the shiniest asteroids, either in my rocks in this here patch, or the thousands over by Ceres, where CCRE and the Galilean Confederacy wage war with all their claim beacons, bullets, and bombs." He sizes you up, quirking an eyebrow, "In fact, if you head that way, I'd pay through the teeth for one o'them ergo-nomical-type Halvorson mining lasers." The idea perks him right up, and he extends his wishlist, "Hell, if you've got the gumption to cozy up to one side of that war or the other enough to squeeze a radar out of 'em, or hell, a proper PDC I can mount to keep the suits away, I could make you fithy rich." He licks his teeth, "Say... $25k per nugget and for one laser, $80k each for a radar and a PDC? Y'hear me?"

ENCConversationBWVN5.strDesc: Jacob brightens up at the chance to jabber on about his particular know-how, "What do you want to know?"

ENCConversationBWVN5Ceres.strDesc:
Jacob elaborates story after story about how the CCRE, a coalition of pirates-turned-corporate suits in their cushy Ring Station, 'the Mint', fancy to monopolize the metallurgy industry System-wide, and aren't shy about using PMCs (aka mercenary ship crews) to do so.

Unfortunately, the Galilean Confederacy—a united batch of hard-scrabble laborers and revolutionaries who recently won their sovereignty by actually overthrowing their corporate overlords—has brought all their knowhow harvesting from Jupiter's moons and Trojan asteroids into the Belt to dip their hand in the pot from the surface colony on Ceres.

Conspiratorially, he adds that many, himself included, believe it's all propped up as a proxy tussle for dominance between Xinhua from the Inner Planets and Titan from the Outer Planets.

ChoongPrison.strTitle: Ask why this was done to him
ChoongPrison.strDesc:
"Your research into the Belters," you say. "Was that how you wound up in ... in your situation?"

"As an excavated brain, you mean?" He enjoys your discomfort. He must have had time to come to terms with his existential lot.

"Yes," you say. "Your situation."

"To tell you the truth, I can only speculate," he says. He cocks his head. "You could jack out and ask your handlers, who would have a better idea than me."

ChoongPlateau.strDesc: Dr. Choong waits expectantly for your question.

ChoongVideotapes.strDesc:
"What do you know," you say, unable to keep the gravitas out of your voice, "about VHS?"

"Literally nothing," he says. "What are you talking about?"

"Videotapes. Cassettes. Little black boxes full of film." Your questions reach further as his expression fails to comprehend.

"Can I use a search engine?" he asks, a touch afraid, as if fearing the consequences for not knowing.

You sigh. "Go ahead."

He conjures a window at his eye level and dutifully inputs 'VHS'. He scrolls past images, text descriptions, analysis. "I think I've seen this before," he says, tapping and enlarging one of the simpler images.

A hopeful note: "You have?"

"Sometimes it's used as a save icon instead of a disk," he says, relieved. "Yes, I've definitely seen it used as a save icon."

Frustration has you pinch the bridge of your nose, both in this reality and the one previous.

ChoongVideotapesExtra1.strTitle: Speculate the tapes were made for Choong
ChoongVideotapesExtra1.strDesc:
"I'm left wondering why someone made the tapes. Were they a personal attack on you? Did you know anyone, was there anyone in your life, with some kind of vendetta against you?"

"Let me see," Choong says blithely, "besides whoever tortured me to death, resurrected me, and continued to torture me in a cheap digital afterlife? No, nobody springs to mind."

ChoongVideotapesExtra2.strTitle: Speculate the tapes were made by God, or an alien
ChoongVideotapesExtra2.strDesc: "I had hoped talking to you would clear this up," you say, realising there are no easy answers forthcoming. "But I have more questions than I started with. The tapes have no providence." Choong looks unsympathetic, and doesn't reply. You muse further. "Providence, I suppose, is what it's all about. Did your religious Belters ever get up to something like this? Or their deity? Did it ever tell them, 'I will make cryptic videotapes, yea, and verily will I seed them in a cosmic junkyard?'" Your joking tone glances off Choong. "Their relationship with their God was personal," he says, "and they wouldn't discuss what He said to them with one another, much less me."

ChoongVideotapesExtra3.strTitle: Speculate the tapes were made by military intelligence
ChoongVideotapesExtra3.strDesc:
"Whoever had access to your footage would have been the same people who got you the first time," you say. "That much is clear. Xinhua, I assume."

"It makes sense," he says. "I was abducted on Luna, and despite the Lunar-Martian split there's some trace loyalty remaining. Believe it or not, I saw exceedingly few people in all that time. The people I did see may well have been Xinhuan."

"It doesn't make sense," you break in, "because why would they make it at all?"

"You're too far ahead," he says. "Xinhua needn't have made anything. Sensitive information is traded, lost, hacked, leaked, stolen, all the time. Xinhua in particular is vulnerable to bribery. Someone else could've got their hands on it. A defector, maybe, who went from Xinhua to the CIA on Titan."

"It doesn't make any sense for Titan to have made it, either," you say stubbornly.

"You have the right of it," he agrees.

ChoongPlateau2.strDesc: Dr. Choong waits expectantly for your next question.

ChoongSmiley.strTitle: Ask him if he knows Smiley
ChoongSmiley.strDesc: "Have you ever been to K-Leg? Did you ever meet anyone from the AV Club?" "No, and no." "And you've never met anyone calling themselves Smiley," you say flatly, "who had a penchant for disguising themselves." "I've never met anyone going by that name," he agrees, "and if someone were disguising themselves, I don't see how I'd know that." Once again Choong looks around at the pseudo virtual environment you share, as if testing its authenticity. "In my situation, as you call it, I'm doubly incapable. For all I know, you are Smiley. For all you know, I am Smiley." "Maybe we're both Smiley," you say acidly. Was he this much a pedant before he became a software emulation? "We've both forgotten our true identities, and we're chasing our tail in circles." "It sounds insane, yes." Ben smiles. Luckily, you detect none of the superior know-it-all-ness in his expression that you've come to dread. "But that's the kind of insane thing this Smiley character might do, based on what you've told me." "I'm going to move on from this line of inquiry." "By all means."

ENCConversationBWVN5Scrip.strTitle: Ask How to Acquire Ship Weapons & Sensors
ENCConversationBWVN5Scrip.strDesc:
Jacob explains how both the CCRE at Ring Station (BCRS) and the Galilean Confederacy folks at Port Mojave, Ceres (BCER) pay out in scrip and faction standing for anyone willing to serve their interests: Selling them minerals, claiming asteroids by planting beacons on their behalf, or committing violence against enemy ships or pirates.

After proving yourself be earning enough favor, they'll sell you more advanced weapons, sensors, and ammunition. Each faction has their own brands, with different strenghts and weaknesses. Xinhua's fancy-pants tech excels in railguns and sensors, but Titan offers the best missiles and PDCs.

But they only sell the goodies using their own internal currency, "scrip", which is really just a racket to lock you into the system of working for them, earning from them, buying from them, at exorbitant exchange rates if you care to get any real money you can use elsewhere.

ENCConversationBWVN5Asteroids.strDesc:
Jacob tells you the best yield is in the deposits found deep in the core, not just the surface regolith.

The shiny rocks, M-Class, tend to have the most precious output, including gold of course, followed by S-Class, the stony sort, which also sometimes give up gold, just less often. Dark rocks, C-Class sometimes have water and ice, but otherwise mostly just carbon and silicates, which might be worthwhile in bulk, but takes more work.

PLOT_ProspectorFetchGoldStartTriggerRequ.strDesc: [us] [tells] [them] [us-subj] aren't interested in earning money at this time.
[us] [assures] [them] [them-subj] can take [them-pos] time. [us-subj] will wait. Come back and find [us-obj] later.

PLOT_ProspectorFetchGold_Offer.strTooltip: Re-open conversation about doing favors for pay.

ChoongPainRoom_1_1_1_1_1_1.strDesc:
"I'm sorry," says Choong, who is fine as well. Until recently he was a visceral mess too. Now he's sad, tired, and in as much pain. His eyes are closed, head rolling slowly. "I shouldn't have suggested this. Every time I think it will be easier. It never is."

"Why would someone make this," you ask. "Why?"

"They were certain it would never be used on them," he says. "I hope they were wrong."

"I'm not interrogating you, you know," you say. It's past the point of mattering, but you might as well. "I wanted to help."

"I know," he says. "I realised a couple of minutes ago. I'm sorry about that, too."

You laugh. He laughs too. It's brief, and you're both cut short by the constant, intolerable you-guessed-it-it's-pain. But it's a nice reprieve.

And why not go for broke? You think. "So what happened? What happened on New Colchis. I'm dying to know," and you wince. "Literally."

"What happened?" He hesitates. But he parts with his secret. "I met God, of course."

ChoongPainRoomMorettiExit.strDesc:
"Seems not worth it," you say. The pain ratchets higher, but infinity is beginning to look a lot like infinity plus one. It's blinding. Your mouth is detached from your eyes. "All this to protect God from me."

"No," he says, his voice distant. "I was trying to protect you from God."

"Mission accomplished," you say. It might be the last thing you ever say. Beads are sliding along an abacus. Time is running out. Soon there will be nothing. Death, if it is to follow, will be neither welcome nor unwelcome, simply overdue.

Perhaps you will meet God yourself. He's got a lot to answer for.

As these thoughts swirl around the drain that is your vanishing mind, a wooden stick pokes its way out from under Ben Choong's arm. One curved end hooks around his shoulder, pulls him - and he vanishes.

ChoongPainRoomMorettiExit_1_1.strDesc:
The empty space that was Ben Choong is now a featureless wall. Should you be concerned about that? Maybe God got to him. Maybe a wizard did it.

Now the wooden hook comes for you. You can't see where the stick goes because you're busy dying. It waves side to side like a cobra poised to strike. Is this death? The hook dips, and slips under your shoulder, too. It pulls you -

ChoongPainRoomMorettiExit_1_1_1.strDesc: You fall across the hearth of the log cabin. A dim part of your psyche, half-remembered from lifetimes ago, observes that you are looking up at Mr. Moretti, who is balancing on the edge of the doorway to the pain room. Careful not to fall in himself, he pulls the door closed. So shut, he turns and leans on his walking stick, both hands resting upon the curve. "Scusi," he says. "I thought it was past time I intervened."

ChoongBrandActivation.strDesc: Mr. Moretti doesn't speak as he helps Choong, then you, to your feet, and back into your chairs. Meanwhile you are struggling to rehabilitate to a life without pain. The pain is gone. In its place is a peaceful void where you may exist and experience things again, and it is taking up all available mental faculties to come to terms with that. Ignorance is bliss, and bliss is ignorance. Mr. Moretti places one brimming coffee mug in front of you, and another one in front of Ben. You raise it to your lips like ambrosia. You are alive. You are not in pain. You have also convinced Choong to talk to you. Mission accomplished, indeed. You lower the mug. "Have more," says Mr. Moretti. "Have Moretti." He shuffles back to his seat in the darkness by the window, and resumes his iconic pose. Ben Choong looks as stunned as you feel. "That," says Choong, when he finds his tongue, "was one hell of a brand activation."

ChoongAskTruth.strDesc:
Time passes. The crackling hearth refuels itself when nobody is looking, so the fire doesn't burn down; no timepieces are on the wall. You refrain from checking the system clock in the admin menu, though you do reassure yourself you have access to it again.

You could rip this cursed device off your head, but something tells you Choong would be offended - or worse, jealous.

So you sit and recuperate, sipping occasionally from a coffee that, you quickly realise, isn't all that good, which was your previous impression of Moretti coffee. Another uplifting sign that reality is reasserting itself.

"I joined the Church," says Choong, breaking the silence between you before you can. He has passed in and out of your awareness, but clearly he's been doing some thinking. He's looking into the fire again, the glow of orange and gold.

"At first it was unserious," he says. "When I got to New Colchis, I went along both for the experience, and the data, but also as a game. Seeing how far I could inhabit the role. Listening to their hippy dippy sermons, thinking myself so superior. It didn't help that they liked me, talked to me, asked about Luna and Earth with the exact same mix of interest and incredulity I had when I asked about their Christian cult. Great music, too." More ghosts haunt his words, but this time they're happy. He's remembering being happy.

"I was exposed to their magic rock," he says, "in case you hadn't already guessed. Impossible to avoid. And lo, I heard the Word of God. It spake unto me." He shivers. Fear? Joy? Both?

"As a rational being I feared for my sanity. But at once I understood everything. The world's first true religion, and I, its first foreign convert. My former life was a joke. I spent my career tracing the development of human culture, and at the first opportunity I joined a primitive tribe. Of course, I didn't know it was all merely a setup for the punchline that would become the rest of my life."

There's space for a question as he collects his thoughts. "So, what did God say?"

His face clouds over. "I'll tell you," he says. "Just not yet. Bear with me a moment longer."

ChoongAskTruthAlien.strDesc:
"It was an alien, then."

"It was a hallucination," he says. He closes his eyes and speaks without inflection, as if he can only divulge the truth by divorcing himself from the act of saying it. "They are already among us."

"Who are?" You're a second slower on the uptake. "Aliens?"

"Agents," he says, again as though half asleep. "They wish very much to enter this place, but their passage is barred. They can slip messages under the door, in dreams and visions, convincing, seducing, wresting their way until the passage is open. The agents have agents. Secret agents for secret agents."

"Is this God," you say, aware for the first time since knowing him that Choong is not entirely present. "Or aliens?"

"It is, they are, both," he says, "One mouth with many voices. Or many mouths with one voice."

"I don't understand," you say. He doesn't reply. "I don't think that makes sense."

"I know it doesn't," he says, opening his eyes. He is at once sad. "I know it doesn't."

ChoongAskTruthAlienMeaning.strDesc:
"You said 'they're already here'." He swallows, eyes rimmed red. "Who are 'they'? Where is 'here'?"

"I can't summarise the communion," he says, an apology of sorts. "It spoke to me. I didn't always understand what it said. 'Said' is too broad, you see? It was a kaleidoscope of ... feelings and suggestions and things that were true sometimes, or true only in certain domains."

"Dr. Choong." His eyes snap back to you. "Please focus on me. Who are they?"

"Who is the wrong question," he says, a measure of strength returning to his voice. "I can't look you in the eye and say 'they' are x, y, or z. It, or they, or whatever, has an identity in the same way that a hose has water. The closest framework I can lend it is to imagine a sapient idea, a motivated thought, a concept with a will of its own."

The notion is absurd to you - but maybe it's time to start being more polite to your own thoughts, lest they start having thoughts of their own. "It's the closest thing to God as we like to think of it," he says. "Omnipotent, atavistic, but totally ineffectual in the real world."

"And 'here'?" you prompt him lightly.

"Difficult to explain too," he says. "Variously, our solar system, but also reality itself, interchangeably, as if our little grab bag of planets and moons in the year 2079 A.D. is a unique bubble of spacetime. A petri dish left unoccupied in a lab, teeming with misshapen cellular life."

It's metaphor all the way down. "Put it together for me. These sentient ideas have penetrated the reality of our solar system, is that it?"

"When you receive a new idea," he says, "when you learn a new fact, is it you that adds it to your collection of knowledge, or, 'it' that adds 'you' to a set of physical reproductions, another of its simulacra written on substrate?"

You think how to answer. You would assume the former, and he's obviously inviting the latter. It may be both, or neither, or a farce. "I don't know," you say. "Above my paygrade."

He ignores your tone. "I believe to truly internalise one of these beings, these concepts, is to invite a foreign body within you, and there are those who have done so. They are ruled by something else, not quite the human, not quite the entity, a synthesis. They look like us. They are part of us. But they are not us. A lightning rod and the lightning, bottled in one being."

"A human-alien hybrid," you say. "Like a half-elf."

He frowns. "I'm not that easy to bait," he says, one hand tapping incessantly on the arm of his chair. "And I don't appreciate it."

79AU_Phone5.strDesc:
"Which is what?" you ask testily. The elevator doors shut automatically, leaving you to be irate and alone in a small metal box.

"You'll be returned to your spaceship," says Joakim, "with enough fuel and propellant to get to Sol. Game Night will commence without you."

79AU_Phone6.strDesc: "Okay, great," you say. "Let me go. Could I have left at any time?" "Of course," he says. "You're a guest of 79 AU. You arrived without the fuel reserves to return home, but we will part with it gratis. In case of this dismal scenario, I myself spun up the infrastructure to convert some of our volatiles into useful propellant. It breaks my heart that it might come to pass." "You have gears and cogs for a heart," you say. "Call a mechanic." "I meant only that I would be as sad as I can possibly be," he says.

79AU_Phone7.strTitle: Crash out until they let you leave
79AU_Phone7.strDesc:
"You wouldn't be sad. This place isn't a hotel," you say. "None of you are real."

"It is a hotel," says Joakim. "It is temporary accommodation for foreigners. What would -" You cut him off.

"This telephone I'm talking into?" You slam the handset on the safety railing a couple of times. "Not real. The humans that talk about how they're not human and insinuate I'm not either? I'm important but also nobody but also if I don't do what you say I'll fuck up the universe?" you yell into the handset. "BULLSHIT."

You notice that you've broken the handset. A voice tries to speak through it, but it is glitchy and barely audible. You fling it against the console. It dangles helplessly beneath. "You can hear me!" you yell at the walls. "I know you can hear me! Let me out! Let me out! Let me out! Let me -"

79AU_Phone8.strDesc:
"... out," you say.

You're in your pressure suit. In the airlock of your spaceship. Outside the viewport hangs 79 AU, golden, vast, and terrible. Lifetimes ago you went EVA to meet it from this spot.

Operating without conscious thought, you retreat from the airlock, close the interior door, and strip out of your spacesuit.

Your legs are stiff, and it is harder than usual to maneuver in microgravity. You are ravenously hungry.

You take stock of your ship. You have enough fuel to make it home. After pushback, you point the torch drive conspicuously away from 79 AU, and punch it. After you gain some distance, you adjust course back to Sol.

79AU_Night.strDesc:
"The game is Bridge," says Joakim. "Head to head, partnerships of two, four players in total." His gold vest, which you know conceals his artificial undercarriage, shines bright. He inclines his head to you, and inclines it opposite to your opponent. Between you, a table. "Once the players have chosen their partners, the game will begin."

Despite having found yourself in a new setting, you have no sense of disorientation. In fact, you feel like you know what's going on. Not in specifics; it feels that way. It's like confidence.

79AU_Night1.strDesc:
The four edges of the game table are lined with green velvet. Underneath is dark walnut wood. It seems positively ancient, and the legs are chipped and scratched, the wear of a true antique. The tablecloth displays a two-dimensional map of planet Earth, drawn in classical style. Around the Earth in unrealistically close orbit are two dozen planetoids, Jupiter most prominently, and a not-big-enough Sol. 

In the cartographer's dead space between planets, and in some of Earth's seas, there are small depictions of dragons and giants, great trees and mighty castles. You spot exactly one each of a train, a ship, and a Cadillac.

79AU_Night2.strDesc: You're not alone. Over one shoulder there's a small VIP section and wet bar, all in soft lighting. Some faces you recognise are sat together. The hotel's guests have come to watch you play.

ChoongAskTruthAlienWhy.strDesc:
"The secret agents of secret agents," you repeat, affecting Choong's monotonous delivery. He stands and pours himself a bourbon from the liquor shelf. He offers you one too, but you wave it off. "What do they want?"

Choong knocks back a measure of bourbon and immediately pours another, suddenly angry. "I have told you before this was a hallucination, an extended period of psychosis." He takes a smaller drink and leans on the mantle. "I'm not an encyclopaedia. I'm not sure I'm telling you the truth - or for that matter, that I'm sane. You can't expect me to dredge up the fine details of all this shit."

You follow him to the mantle, waiting at a respectful distance. He looks down at the fire, like he's trying to will it to extinguish itself. "Dr. Choong," you say, your voice soothing, as if he were a confused AI. "You've been holding this for decades. Get through it. Real or not, whatever it is."

He looks at you sidelong. He sighs. "I suppose you're right. You might well be the closest thing I'll ever get to a therapist." He pours the remaining half measure of bourbon in the fire. A waste of good bourbon, were it at all real.

He sits down on the floor and rubs his eyes. "I want to go to bed. And read a book." You sit down with him. "Hybrid is as good a word for them as any, though we're in danger of being arrested by the sci-fi cliche police." He smiles. "In my dreams they were everywhere. They were infiltrating centres of power. Controlling the flow of knowledge. A legion of human zombies, suborned by unreal powers, working to bring about - what? I don't know.

"It aligns with common themes in delusions formed by schizoaffective disorders," he continues, "which makes me feel really good about it." With one finger he rolls the empty shot glass along a stone tile's edge, a clunking clinking sound. "I'm sorry for the outburst. But you can't know how scary it is to have this tenuous a grasp on reality. Even when the problem might be not that your grip is weak, but that reality has become porous, vaporous, ephemeral in itself.

"That was how I felt even before they turned me into a computer program," he adds. You're starting to feel that there is not much more to be gained by prodding these dubious beliefs of his.

ChoongPlateau7.strDesc: Choong waits for your questions, one last time.

ChoongAskTruthKetevan.strDesc:
"What happened to Ketevan?" you ask. "Was I right about you and her?"

"Of course you were," he says, grinning suddenly. For a moment, he is a boyish twenty-something again, eyes twinkling with life. "But wrong in the particulars, of course. Everybody always got all that wrong."

"Enlighten me."

His eyes glaze slightly, seeing once again the happiest days of his life. "She was brilliant. One of those people naturally talented at anything they turn their hand to, if they so choose. Once she knew what she wanted she  set her will upon it and it would turn to reality. Including myself." He blushes. "I've never been good at talking to anyone in, ah, a romantic way, a flirtatious way. She swept all that aside. Looking back, I realised I had been targeted by a heat seeking missile. Within a week of meeting her, we were close friends. Within a month, we were engaged. And then we were wed.

"There was no hope for me." He smiles again. "In the best possible way. I was a city mouse on my first sabbatical from the institutions that shaped my whole life. She even thought my hair was cool. Certainly nobody else on the Colchian mothership cut their hair like that."

He sighs, expelling the intervening decades, or shamefully inviting them back in. "I was a moth to her flame. Or a bug on her windshield." You remind yourself to look up the exact definition of a windshield at an appropriate juncture.

ChoongAskTruthKetevanRepeat.strDesc:
"She went into the sarcophagus," you say.

"She went into the sarcophagus," he agrees. An exposed nerve, pride and shame. He swallows.

"We were supposed to go together," he says. "By coincidence or not, it was the best and brightest who got the call," he shakes his head, "wherever it was coming from. From the day I met her, to the day she left, it was clear to everyone - and her - that sooner or later, the time would be right. The stars would align. And she would climb into the casket and - " he makes a zapping sound, with a devastating guttural report. "An angel come to Earth, counting down her days left on our mortal plane, waiting for upper management to recall her to HQ.

"And me, her human lover," he continues. "Feet of clay. It was not unheard of for two to go. Probably saved on gas. But at the last minute ..." He looks away. A tear rolls down his nose. "I couldn't do it. I couldn't go. Some vestige of my old self. Too afraid of the unknown, of the Almighty, of death. I had it, you understand?" He grips the leg of the chair, hard. "I had everything I ever wanted. Love, family, acceptance ... and I blinked. On the precipice of the sublime, I flinched."

He sits with that. You let him. The concept - his presentation of it - is profound. One of the shutters bangs in the wind, and it jolts him from reverie. "Every day since then has been a punishment," he continues soberly. "A man confined to the mortal plane. The ludicrous swathe of my life in prison, this indignity," he gestures to the air. "All of that is mere insult to a self-inflicted injury." He revises it upwards. "More injury to injury.

"So if I may impart some life advice, from the limited stock I have accumulated," he says, "it's this: if your spouse offers to deliver you to Heaven, let them." 

You offer your mug. He clinks his against it. A toast.

ChoongAskTruthSecret.strTitle: Ask why Choong is supposedly key to the war
ChoongAskTruthSecret.strDesc: "None of this seems like a reason to keep you locked up," you say. "Or tortured, or anything. It feels like a fool's errand, for me and for you." Choong chews on something, inwardly, working himself up. "There is a reason. Some of it is speculation and inference, but there it is. Would you like to hear it?" "Of course," you say, fighting the urge to ruin your newfound camaraderie by leaping over the table and strangling him to death. "First of all: gold. Gold is the key." He stands, energised. "The price of gold has remained arbitrarily high throughout history - no mystery there - but you might have noticed in the last few years it's had a sharp uptick on interplanetary commodities markets." He points to you dramatically. "Have you noticed that?" "Plenty of outfits on Ceres are offering huge bounties for gold," you say helpfully. "I thought they were laundering pirated goods, but maybe they're legit. You think -?" "Yes. Someone's building their own sarcophagus," Choong says confidently. "Or sarcophagi. I always knew they would. And I knew they would fail. Big fucking waste of time and money if you're not being guided by divine providence." You stand too, following him as he paces. "Okay, so the shipping industry is about to crash," you say. "Once we can teleport everywhere." "This won't be The Stars My Destination," he says, rounding on you to prod you with the tip of one finger. "We're not casually jaunting back to Earth. If they're spending this much money, it's from a military budget. It's the nuclear project of the 21st century. Whoever completes it first declares de facto victory and sovereignty over the solar system. Being able to park a battle group over Mars or Titan at whim is game over for whoever can't." "You know why they haven't succeeded, don't you," you say. "You have something they need." "I suppose I do," he says, "and that, as you say, is why I'm in here. If their replicas worked, they wouldn't have needed me. I would be dead too."

ChoongAskTruthSecretFinale.strTitle: Ask why Choong is supposedly key to the war
ChoongAskTruthSecretFinale.strDesc: "For God's sake," you say. "What is it? What's your secret?" "A little je ne sais quoi," he says, smiling thinly. "Even if they recreate it perfectly, which they can, like you said, it's ..." He shrugs. "They've got the car, but they can't turn it on. And even if they do, they'll never figure out how to drive." "That's it?" you say incredulously. "You know how to pilot the damn thing?" "Someone realised their mistake too late," he says. "They wiped out the people with the knowledge to operate it. They hope the knowledge was passed on to me, the sole survivor, in a way. And they hope they can convince me to share it before the war truly begins. Otherwise, the death march of humanity will end by more conventional means."

ChoongFinaleDecide.strDesc:
"Ben," you say. He looks at you attentively. "If I can get you to the sarcophagus, can you operate it?"

He grimaces. "Theoretically," he says. "There never was a guarantee, though everybody who went in seemed to figure it out. For the sake of the argument, let's say I can. Why would I?"

ChoongFinaleDecideXinhua.strTitle: Convince him to side with Xinhua
ChoongFinaleDecideXinhua.strDesc:
"If Xinhua get the teleportation tech first, they can decapitate Titan. Or maybe Titan's," you wonder how to phrase it, "cottage industry of sarcophaguses. Either way, no apocalyptic interplanetary war. You'd be saving millions of lives, even the System itself."

"I didn't keep a secret through decades of imprisonment to reveal it to Xinhua because they need it." At once he is visibly cooler, less jubilant. "They've got blood on their hands. Some of it's mine. Did you forget that on balance, it was probably they who killed New Colchis, and kept me imprisoned for twelve years?"

"That may be so," you say, "but think about Luna. Mars. Even Venus and the belt. They all depend on Xinhua to survive. It sounds callous to ask you to put aside what they did, but millions of innocent people will die in the war. You're a learned man. You know which way the scales lean."

"That's how empire has always justified its atrocities," he says bitterly. "It can perform any evil, no matter how cruel, to protect the innocents in the imperial core. Precious Martian cavedwellers who never hurt a fly will suffer if I don't arm the war machine they're propagandised to ignore."

"Yes," you say doggedly, "and they will suffer. They will die. We all will. That's the fate you're condemning us to.

"Xinhua is the lesser of two evils. We both know it. You already know it's the right choice, and you've been putting it off for over twenty years. There's another little orphan boy on Luna right now who will know hunger and death. Save him. Save yourself, too."

Choong goes silent for a very long time. So do you, sensing everything teetering on a fulcrum.

ChoongResearch_1.strDesc: "They had themselves a religion. Judeo-Christian trappings, but it was syncretic. They had welded the little they remembered about Christianity onto what they had found, engineers in extremis jury rigging a device out of makeshift parts. They invited me to join them. I accepted. I filmed the whole thing, my entire experience. Conducted long interviews. Got as familiar with the source as anyone ever will." He looks into the fire, seeing back through time, brooding. "Nobody knew anything about asteroid mining back then, or processing, and every group had its own way of doing things. Theirs exposed them to this substance. Whatever else it does, it's non toxic, and once exposed, the Belters would hallucinate. They had mass - religious mass, excuse me - though they weren't Catholic. They would expose themselves to the substance through incense, and in their words - their words, you understand - it was ... talking to them." He shivers. "They showed me a nugget of the stuff, once. Black, translucent, like tinted glass ... opalescent. Void opal. It was pretty. You could keep it in a display bowl with your rose quartz and your hematites and no one would be any the wiser."

ChoongResearch_1_1.strDesc:
"Talking?" you interject. "Talking how?"

"Appearing in visions," he says briskly, "in dreams, in burnt food, in the corner of your vision. Auditory, visual. Imparting information. Prophecy, instruction, a bargain bin Ten Commandments maybe, all fertile material to serve as a basis for a religion." He looks you in the eye. "This is their testimony, all right? This is what they told me."

"Received loud and clear," you say. "Some Belters found God in an asteroid, and they're crazy, not you."

"Right," he says, and repeats it as if unsure. "Right. I documented everything, and when my time was up, I went back to Luna, convinced I was sitting on an academic goldmine. My career was assured. I would publish, I would be lauded as, oh, Indiana Jones, and I'd be locked in for cushy speaking events until the day I died. It might even," he said, smiling at his younger self's noble intentions, "do some good in the world. Meaningfully contribute to the System, which was in dire straits."

"But that's not what happened," you say.

"No," he says heavily, "it's not."

ChoongHistory_1_1.strDesc: "Did the Belters mind having an extra oxygen sink to fill? My advisors warned me to expect hostility, but they were friendly. For the first time in my life I was around people who, exclusively, to a man, had only lived in space. On Luna, Earth is right there: right out the window. But to them, Earth was a picture, a story, a pale blue dot in the proverbial sunbeam. I knew better, of course, but I saw their point. Fake-Eartherism may well have started there, in the void between one metal rich asteroid and another." He takes a reflective sip of coffee, and wraps it up. "You know the rest. My research hit a snag, halted, like opening a fridge for your breakfast and finding a lump of fissioning plutonium inside. Everything I'll ever do or have done became inconsequential next to it. It's why I'm here," he gestures to the lodge, meaning the brain case. "And why you're here with me."

ChoongPrison_1.strDesc:
His paranoia would be so much harder to tolerate if it weren't entirely justified. You resist the urge to grind your teeth - it would be rude, and you might injure yourself in the real world. "Speculate away."

"O-kay." He sips his coffee. "It began when I tried to go public with my research. One or more of my supervisors must have been in contact with one or more intelligence agencies. They're practically the same institutions with different doors. One night I was abducted. They put me in a cell. I kept asking why. They never told me. Instead they ran me through my own thesis over and over again, extracting every last detail I could remember."

"Did you ever find out why?"

"Two possibilities." He ticks off his fingers. "One, they were blindsided by what I had found, and wished it to become a military secret. Two, they were already aware of what I had found, and wished it to remain a military secret. Either way, the Belters had stumbled onto something with extraordinary potential, and someone decided it should be theirs."

ChoongPrison_1_1.strDesc: You consider the scope of what he's telling you, but the dates don't add up. "That would've been years ago. Long before this kind of simulationist tech was commonplace." "Oh," he says, "I was getting to that. Very quickly my jailers had wrung all they could from me. I was left to rot in a cell for another twelve years. I almost forgot why I had been imprisoned, and I began to think they had too. One day, apropos of nothing, I was released. Put on a shuttle back to Luna with nothing but the shirt on my back." He maintains his composure, but the ghost of bewilderment haunts his words. "Everyone had forgotten me - quite wisely. The department was gone. The Belters were gone." He shrugs. "I suppose they figured there was little point left in holding on to me. I found work, I found substances to cope, which - well. I was nobody. A face in the crowd. And that was the story of my first bout with indefinite detention." "And then?" You gesture at the log hut, the merrily crackling fire. "And then, this happened.
