One day I was a free-ish citizen on Ring Station. The next, I was back in a cell. This time the questioning was ... accelerated. Aggravated. They wanted something from me - still do." He blows air through his cheeks. "Later they told me my body died from the strain. They showed me pictures. Video. That was my first experience here."

ChoongEnvironment.strDesc:
"Why are we meeting in this," you look around again, "wooden house in the cold?"

"It's a log cabin," he says, trying to conceal a smile. "A winter retreat, for wealthy Earthers."

Winter. Sort of an archaic word referring to an Earth season, a disused offcut of the still-extant Christmas and gift-giving. Kind of like spring cleaning, a ritual you've participated in but never interrogated the origins of. Or summer holidays, which only Titanians observe.

ChoongPrison_1_1_2.strDesc:
"That's horrible," you say.

"Yes, it is," he looks at you, his voice laden with irony. "And they said there was no reason it wouldn't continue. That it would continue, until I told them everything. In here, there is no limit to what they can do to me. No limit to cruelty. Even unconsciousness is a temporary reprieve."

ChoongPrison_1_1_2_1.strDesc:
"What do they want?"

"I have no idea," he snaps, "and I'm beginning to think that isn't the point. They don't have to want anything. They just do it.

PLOT_Ceres_Our_System_For_Whom_Trigger.strDesc: [us] [has] begun material support and sabotage within the Ceres Proxy War.
PLOT_Ceres_Our_System_For_Whom_Trigger.strTitle: Trigger for Advancing the Ceres Plot Our System For Whom Beat

PLOT_Ceres_Valkyrie_Trigger.strTitle: Trigger for Advancing the Ceres Plot Valkyrie Beat
PLOT_Ceres_Valkyrie_Trigger.strDesc: [us] [sees] a vision of the world, and all the wonder that was lost.

PLOT_Ceres_Our_Strange_Denouement_Trigge.strTitle: Trigger for Advancing the Ceres Plot Our Strange Denouement Beat
PLOT_Ceres_Our_Strange_Denouement_Trigge.strDesc: [us] [has] used a powerful technology and must decide who it belongs to in order to change the fate of Ceres and The System at large.

ValkyrieSarcophagus8.strDesc:
"Fuck," you say. And louder: "Fuck!" Now the walls are repeating uck-uck-uck-uck, laughing at you.

"Who am I?" you shout. "Who are you? What is this?"

A garbage bin discovers it is not so securely bolted to the ground as it thought. You wrestle it to your hip and heave it through the window of a city bus. The glass shatters and trash spills everywhere. The sounds of destruction are a welcome reprieve from the silence.

The silence returns, cautiously, now that it knows what you're capable of. You feel better having got that out of your system.

ValkyrieSarcophagus9.strDesc:
Something catches your eye overhead. There are letters in the sky, English alphabet, in tall white clouds of vapour.

I LOVE YO, it reads.

As you watch, a long vertical begins to form, the start of a letter U.

You laugh until your head hurts.

ValkyrieSarcophagus10.strDesc:
You tour the silent streets at random. Your burning questions ebb with each step taken, and you find yourself simply taking in the scenery. It is dreamlike, though not a dream. You're more awake than you've ever been.

Even the smallest building has an impressive cap of spires and stonework. Closer to the ground, though, they're just as likely to sport shopfronts and advertising, large meaningless signs plastered above display windows. They're offering baked food, books, craft supplies, phones, kitsch and memorabilia, alcohol, groceries, menswear and its alternatives, shoes, camping supplies, and banking services. You grab a couple of pastries. You find them perfectly edible, though whatever is preventing spoilage, you can't begin to guess.

When the bells sound again, as they must do on the hour, you set a course for the largest cathedral you can see. The bells are the only positive motion in this whole place, so it follows that you might as well check them out.

You enter through a gatehouse into a square interior lawn, a path crossing it and subdividing it into smaller squares. On the other side of the square, you see a door to the cathedral itself.

ValkyrieSarcophagus11.strDesc:
The vaulted ceiling takes your breath away. Real or fake, or whatever shade of in-between this place is, you're certain that the stonework above was derived from some original, an authentic article. Real people must have made this. The gravity here is crushing. How the hell did they get up there to chisel it?

The sound of a human cough obliterates the quiet.

You proceed down the aisle between row after row of empty pews. Someone is sitting in the front row, just to one side. They're facing away from you. They're dressed in white. The back of their head is thick brown shaggy hair, topped by some sort of headpiece.

ValkyrieSarcophagus12.strDesc:
"Hello?" you call. "Who are you?"

Their head turns slightly. They have heard you, but they do not answer.

ValkyrieSarcophagus13.strDesc:
The closer you draw, the harder it is to avoid the obvious, and ridiculous, conclusion: the person in the front row is a conventional rendering of Jesus Christ, a deity made famous by the Abrahamic religions, though not without a lot of controversies along the way.

You reach the front row. Yep: it's Jesus. He has a beard, a crown of thorns, a white robe - He's in full religious mode. Does He ever get to dress down, or is He always obligated to wear the full regalia when meeting fans?

Jesus can't ignore you now without being incredibly rude. His tranquility breaks as He sneaks a glance at you. He favours you with a tiny wink.

"At last," He says. "I wondered who would get here first. Welcome to Heaven, my child."

ValkyrieSarcophagus15.strDesc:
"Take off that ridiculous getup," you say.

'Jesus' pouts. "Aww. I thought it would be funny." Still, he takes off the crown, a plastic prop likely from one of the gift shops outside. "That thing's itchy. I can see why He hated it."

"What are you doing here?" you say.

"What do you think? I'm praying," he says. "Though whether it's to myself or someone else, I have no idea. D'you think Jesus knows he's a lesser partner in his Trinity, too?"

"No," you say.

"Me neither! I've -" he agrees readily, and you cut him off.

"No. I'm not doing this again. I'm not asking one more person what is going on. Everyone else has been holding all the cards, and I'm playing with an open hand," you say. "I'm sick of it."

'Jesus' nods sympathetically. "True," he says. "We can switch it up. You tell me what you think is going on, and I'll only stop you if you're wrong."

"Take off the fucking beard, Smiley," you say. He smiles, and does so. He removes his beard, his hairpiece, his eyebrows, and smears the makeup on his face enough to signify the facade is no longer necessary without actually fully removing it. He rubs his eyes; out pop some coloured contact lenses. 

When he's finished, the Lord and Saviour is gone, and in his place is a hairless human doll, devoid of distinguishing marks or features, with a pan-ethnic complexion. The smile never leaves its face; it lives in the eyes, in the sneering intellect that guides this creature through its facsimile of life. It stares out at you now, all barriers between you removed.

"Nice to finally meet you," it says.

ValkyrieSarcophagus17.strDesc:
"You're the thing that Choong warned me about," you say. "A person possessed by an idea."

"Right!" says Smiley happily. "I might pick you up on a few details but, broadly, that's correct, so far as you understand it. He's got all kinds of theories, our Ben, doesn't he? What was your favourite?"

"You're an alien," you say. "Trying to enter our reality, or destabilise it so you can inhabit it. I don't know how to destabilise reality, but that's what you're doing."

Smiley shrugs, fingering the crappy plastic crown of thorns. "Ah, 'reality', pshh. It varies from person to person. Everyone's got their blind spots. There's no big conspiracy. It's all legions of useful idiots, fed exactly the right mix of wrong ideas. If I have one preternatural talent, it's engineering stuff like that." Its smile turns bashful, humble.

"The only thing I don't know is why," you say. "What's so good about humanity and Earth that an alien would come here?"

"You've got me there," says Smiley. "I'm also not privy to that information - hand on heart." It places its hand over where its heart ought to be. "The mothership tells me the winning lottery numbers, it doesn't tell me why."

ValkyrieBorderCool.strDesc:
You straighten your posture, smooth your gate, and push the screeching terror to the back of your mind. Your walking pace is brisk enough now that one of the guards is going to have to move, or else be shoulder checked by a very confident traveler.

Just before that happens, the centre guard steps aside to let you through. You give her a friendly nod, which she returns. 

"Welcome to Calico," she says. 

"Happy to be here," you reply, and walk off towards your rendezvous point.

ValkyrieBorderReactor.strDesc:
Opting for the more private route, you bolt ahead through an increasingly narrow and labyrinthine length of corridors. Before long, you've taken so many turns that you couldn't go back the way you came even if you wanted to. Somehow, you still hear the agents in pursuit behind you, drawing ever nearer as your pace starts to slow.

Suddenly the corridors open up into an expansive chamber with an aging reactor at the center. Knowing this is your only chance to hide, you duck behind a particularly knotty tangle of pipes and conduits. 

As you sit and catch your breath, you hear the agents in pursuit slow their advance. Though you can't make out their words, you hear a muffled conversation in alternately pleading and demanding tones. After a moment, the voices stop, and you hear their owner's footsteps going back in the direction they came.

In the pit of your stomach you find a cold and growing nausea. It's a surprise to you, as you're expecting to feel only relief. With your wits about you now, you look around the room you've decided to make your refuge. 

The reactor is in bad shape. In fact, you wonder how it is even functional. Most of the components are rattling in their operation, choking out what you're sure are some of their final cycles. One of the two laser arrays has broken loose and is now pointed at the wall. The housing of the pellet feeder is so thin and rusted that you see gaps exposing the inner mechanisms.

With horror, you realize that you've sheltered yourself beside the failing cryo pump. Coolant leaks from every surface. An inch from your face, you see the toxic mixture gather, droop, and drip into a pool at your feet. You scrabble away from the lethal sludge as fast as you're able, knowing the damage is already done.  

As the sickness unspools from your stomach and begins to thread outward into your extremities, you stumble out of the reactor room towards the rendezvous point , brain case in tow.

ValkyrieBorderFight.strDesc:
Go time. You turn a corner and try to catch your breath, listening as the clatter of bootsteps thunders towards you. When the first agent turns the corner you step forward and swing the brain case in a long arc that begins at your feet and ends at their chin. The strength of your swing collides with the momentum of the agent running full speed, knocking his head straight back and taking him off his feet. 

Briefly you wonder if Choong can feel it in there, if his whole digital world shudders as the case crashes against the world in meat space. 

Before you can finish the thought, a second agent rounds the corner and trips over the first, his head slamming into the corridor wall. The third agent, not so clumsy, turns and stops before you, pistol at the ready. 

They settle into a firing position as you charge. You hear a shot and your left shoulder is forced backwards as you torque at the hips. You slam into the agent, managing with great effort to bring him down to the ground. The crook of your elbow finds his neck in a rear naked choke, and you squeeze with all the strength you have left.

As the agent hammers away at your head, legs kicking, the only thing you feel is a white hot stinging in your left arm that occasionally gives way to dull, radiating tremors of pain that cascade through your entire body. 

The agent gives a final pitiful kick before going limp in your arms. You wait a few moments to finalise the blood choke, then drop him.

As your wits return to you, you realise the path to the rendezvous point is back the way you came. You pick up the brain case and hobble in that direction, hoping you can reach it before more security finds you.

ValkyrieSarcophagus3.strDesc:
The sky is blue.

That used to be a truth so self-evident someone would have to be a liar or crazy to deny it. This is your first time seeing it. 

But for the thrust holding you back, you would fall toward it, there to turn to vapour in the perfect empty blue.

You have a feeling that in your immediate past there was an awful tumult, and you remember nothing but that it happened.

You're lying on grass. Moreover, you're awake. Your eyes are open and you exist. It's a lot to process lying down, so you sit up.

You're on Earth. Sitting in a wide green field ringed by a white fence. And there's that blue sky everyone's been talking about.

ValkyrieSarcophagus4.strDesc:
Who are you? You try to remember your name.

"My name is [us-firstname]."

So far, so good.

You get to your feet. No roof overhead. You wait to feel a sense of vertigo, but on the contrary, you've never felt surer. 

A bell peals, shortly joined by uncountable others. Beyond the field where it meets a line of trees, spires stretch up into the sky.

You can see nobody else.

ValkyrieSarcophagus5.strDesc:
You cross the grass, past painted white lines and freestanding white rectangles. A football field.

Venturing past the treeline, you learn not all wooded areas are created equally. Some you can walk through, while others are totally impenetrable. You roll your ankle on an exposed root, and that convinces you to hobble back to the field, and to walk beside the trees instead. You're relieved to discover a stone path cutting through the forest. Now if you roll an ankle, it'll be your own damn fault.

The path seems to know where to go. It curves back and forth, the spires drawing closer and taller. Before too long, they disappear behind the tree canopy. A keen grasp of trigonometry spoils that you are about to reach the end of the path. The path joins a tarmac road, and standing in the middle of that road, you see the town.

ValkyrieSarcophagus6.strDesc:
Small residential buildings squat next to each other. Behind them larger edifices loom. All of them, big and small, are bedecked with stone spires, reaching up into the endless blue. The largest building you can see is about the size of a Martian mining barge. They're all made from yellow stone bricks of uniform size.

None of this can be real, you think, your feet carrying you into the town proper, along streets lined with classic cars. Empty windows stare back at you through iron spiked fences. If this is Earth, everything here should be shelled to bits by meteorites. No PDA on your wrist to identify any of this shit. And where is everybody?

The bells peal again, making you jump. Hundreds of them, from every direction, all at once. It's not quite loud enough to be painful, but it is unnerving and terrible for your train of thought.

When the bells finish you are enveloped in silence.

ValkyrieSarcophagus7.strDesc: "Hello?" you call out. It rebounds off the squat cottages and returns to you as echoes. "Is anybody here?" Besides these aural vestiges of yourself, nobody replies. You repeat the question in Mandarin. Again nobody replies, but this time with Xinhuan characteristics.

ValkyrieSarcophagus115.strTitle: Decide what to do with Smiley
ValkyrieSarcophagus115.strDesc:
Smiley looks like a petulant child who's been put in a corner for disobedience. That may actually be how it feels.

"That was touching," it says. "Can you put a bullet in me, too? I just fulfilled my last purpose for existing. I don't have any more, and I kinda hate it."

Ben called it Keti. His lost love, who went first through the sarcophagus. It's galling: the bleak irony of a life spent regretting their separation, all the while in captivity orchestrated by the thing she has become. An amoral being, completely without regard for the humans it's so desperate to join.

ValkyrieSarcophagus116.strDesc: You point the gun at its brain. In there, you surmise, in that cosmically engineered device, all these events happened a priori more or less exactly as they came to pass. You having the gun now is an ephemeral detail. It looks back at you, waiting patiently. "If you're anything like your God," you say, "we don't want you. We'll hate you. Go away." Smiley nods. "Oh, I entirely understand," it says. "Our coming will be disastrous for humans in the mold of Keti Giorgadze and Benjamin Choong. But eventually there'll be a new kind of human who's only ever known things our way. And that'll be the way things are." You feel the grip kick before you register your decision to fire. Red mist billows out from the back of Smiley's head. It swirls in the air above the altar. The gory cloud hangs there like the head of an enormous red rose. You look at the gun in your hand: it is gone. Smiley's corpse grins back at you. "What?" you say. "I'm dreaming -"

ValkyrieSarcophagus117.strDesc: You train the gun on Smiley. It waits patiently for you to pull the trigger. Something about that empty, useless stare. You find yourself lowering the gun. There would be no point. It would be like shooting a glass bottle. Smiley rolls its eyes. "'Kay," it says. What is left? you wonder. Here you are at the outer limits of life, of reality. All you have found is a dark, entropic hunger. It's a nightmare that would itself like to end, just as much as you want it to. "Why did you kill Ben and not me?" you ask it suddenly. "Why did you humour me?" Smiley looks puzzled. "I don't understand the question." "Why would you help me on K-Leg? Why even talk to me now?" You think of Smiley's careful patience, guiding you toward this conclusion, even as you resented it, or feared it. "You're possessed by an alien intelligence." "Yeah," says Smiley, as if stating the obvious. "Aren't you?" Before you can reply, you cease to exist.

ValkyrieSarcophagus118.strDesc: You're in the interior of the sarcophagus again. The amniotic liquid that surrounded you sluices away. The heavy lid creaks open. There's a growing sound of cheering, applause.

ValkyrieSarcophagus119_Titan.strDesc:
John's face appears above you. He grabs your hand, but instead of helping you out, he shakes it. "Knew you could do it."

"Do what?" you ask belatedly. One second you were there. Now you're here. Both claims quite unverifiable, of course.

"Take a look." He pulls you up. Slimy fluid drips off your shoulders.

The screen is hanging over the flag again. It's showing a vectorised display of the System, Mars in focus.

Some kind of console output is running along one side. It reads:

X-53 LAUNCHED
X-54 LAUNCHED
X-55 LAUNCHED
X-56 LAUNCHED
X-57 LAUNCHED
X-58 LAUNCHED
X-59 LAUNCHED
X-60 LAUNCHED
X-61 LAUNCHED
X-62 LAUNCHED
X-63 LAUNCHED
X-64 LAUNCHED
...

More numbers scroll by every second.

The analysts at the equipment banks whoop, cheer, hug each other.

John raises your hand. Victory. The analysts cheer for you, too.

You look down in the sarcophagus. Ben Choong's brain case is gone.

"John?" you ask. "What did I launch?"

ValkyrieSarcophagus119_Xinhua.strDesc:
Ortega's face appears above you. He pulls you up from the sarcophagus, slime dripping from your shoulders. The marines and the scientists cheer, for each other, for you, for Mars.

"What happened?" you ask. An apposite question. Ortega takes it that you mean 'out here', when the truth is more complex.

"You did it," he says. "You won."

One of the marines towel-dries you, and you are given a couch to lie on and a hydration aid. Someone has the questionable idea to give you a PDA with internet access. The internet is talking about one thing. A video:

From Virginia, Titan, the President begins his weekly fireside chat. "My fellow Americans," he says. "In these dark times -" he breaks, squinting at a commotion offscreen. His media presence snaps off, instantly annoyed at the interruption. "Annie, who is that?"

His head explodes. A soup of red and pink gore expands for exactly one frame before the feed goes dead.

The internet isn't quite sure what to make of that.

You watch the sentiment shift in interplanetary time, as more and more observers report Titan ships moving erratically, or failing to change course. There's one massive collision above Virginia, and a handful of deadly 'oopsies' scattered across the Outer System.

Ninety minutes later, plus light lag, Congress' designated survivor appears on an identical soundstage to deliver some disturbing news.

ValkyrieSarcophagus1110_Titan.strDesc:
A view of the Martian surface, high overhead. A wing camera from an unmanned atmosphere scoop, trawling for what little Mars has.

A hundred bombs, fifty megatons apiece, detonate above, below, and inside the underground cities of the Tharsis plateau. Hundreds of cubic kilometres of rock vaporise in three microseconds. The cavity of gaseous rock expands, straining at its solid extremes, crushing within milliseconds the outlying human structures not consumed in the initial blasts. The many fists of God clench tight around the frail tubes until they are indistinguishable from any other pocket of molten rock.

The plateau is pockmarked by a dust cloud hundreds of kilometres wide. Three large hats obscure the mountains. They are becoming craters. Ejecta streak up to the sky like millions of escape pods outrunning the thunderous red dust below. 

Mars is no more. The Revolutionaries cheer like it's the 4th of July.

You allow them to get you very, very drunk. You have become the lynchpin of the most successful military operation in history. There won't be a press tour, but a distressingly broad band of the intelligence community will repeat your name in hushed whispers forever. Maybe if the records are ever unsealed, the children of humanity will know your name too. You try not to speculate if that's as a hero or a villain.

How to explain the implications of everything you saw within the sarcophagus? Do you even know someone who would hear you out? Is it ... is it even important, anymore?

You try cornering Pan Tan at some point during the night. He's half cut and so are you, but maybe - no. You needn't have tried. He dismisses your garbled retelling of the events as a dream.

"We won, man," he says. "By a lot. You're guilty. Survivor's guilt."

He shrugs. "They woulda done the same to us. Have another drink."

You get no better advice.

The telemetrics recorded of your brain, and that of Choong, provide the basis of a functional system for teleportation. After its debut in Operation Valkyrie, Congress deadlocks itself discussing how to roll out this technology in the immediate future. 

The disappearance of Choong's brain, and the activity monitored in your own brain as it apparently failed to disappear, was a crucial factor to the theoretical physicists in observation. You don't understand any of the words they've coined to describe it, insofar as the comparison between you was a useful A/B test. They note your testimony that subjective death seemed to be a crucial mechanic in its operation, but whether anyone takes that seriously is hard to say. They're satisfied with their synthetic substitutes; indeed, you can't argue with the results.

In the System, the tables turn.

The coring of Xinhua's central command scatters their forces into cells across the System.

Ceres comes entirely under Titan control. A Congressman is elected to speak for Ceres, and shipped off to Titan in good order. Titan blockades are established at Mars and the twin Hangzhou/Suzhou orbitals, turning cargo smuggling into a lucrative profession.

Rewards follow. Immigration fast-tracking. A full suite of top tier weaponry and munitions. You accept them. It would be impossible not to.

None of it is a relief. All of it is hollow. A dark intelligence hovers at the edge of your understanding. It is not content to remain there. It is becoming. 

Humanity has been gifted a new vice. Soon they will indulge it. Once weakened, it will be colonised by a thing from beyond. All you know will be swept away by the coming tide.

You are the only person who knows the truth. There is nothing more lonely.

ValkyrieSarcophagusWilling.strDesc: You walk to the sarcophagus flanked by an escort. Like an astronaut of yesterday. Or a criminal of any day. They assist you in to the box. The lid swings shut. The light goes out. Liquid, heard and felt but not seen, sluices in at your hips and ankles. It's breathable, they said, but how the fuck would they know? Your breathing accelerates, the nightmarish sensation of a water level crawling up your neck. You press your face to the lid, desperate for the last pocket of air - And then it's streaming down your throat, through your nose, in your ears - We're skipping straight to human trials! crows a giddy, oxygen starved part of your brain - "Breathe, [us-firstname]," says a muddy voice through an internal speaker, and about a thousand litres of ALIEN GOO. "Breathe!"

ValkyrieSarcophagus2.strDesc: A moment in time curves back into itself. You curve with it. You're spinning. Angular force strips your perception apart piece by piece. The feelings of the liquid in your lungs and the sounds of it in your ears tumble to the floor, and you stare down at them. The moment repeats and repeats and repeats. The you that is staring at your other senses is lying on the floor alongside them, looking at nothing at all. The synapses in your brain don't know each other. The electrical signals that constitute your soul are separated, laid out in serried ranks, and unit tested one by one, by you. The first hundred trillion is the hardest. There's a lot of dead wood. "Ego death," says a voice. It might be yours. There must be some other you, here, on a separate registry. Perhaps it's a future self doubling back to verify. "Am I talking to myself?" you ask. "No," you say. "It's Ben." Oh; not you, then. Could've fooled you. "I still exist, don't I?" you ask. Another heartbeat scurries past, during which you relive your life from three to six years old. "Could I ask that if I didn't exist?" A crack, like wood on wood. A crowd of people cheer. The infinite procession of your self halts, and a great heaving breath rockets through your lungs. "Define exist," you reply to yourself. The world is light. Bells are ringing.

ValkyrieBorderInitialTruth.strDesc:
"I'm in possession of a strange technology that could turn the tide in the War. Also there's a very irritating man inside that box."

The first agent blinks his wet eyes twice, then exchanges a glance with the second agent, who begins tapping at her PDA even faster. 

"Is this your official declaration?" the second agent asks. "Let me remind you that we are authorized agents of the CCRE customs house."

You glimpse a suite of family tattoos beneath the cuffs of her jumpsuit, a few of which bear the scars of an ongoing removal operation. Must have been a mighty betrayal to her Calicoan elders, shedding their toxic brands to land a coveted municipal job. Proves she's taken the hard road to get to where she's standing, and she's not going to let you or anyone else fuck that up. 

"Papers, please," she says before you can reply.

ValkyrieBorderInitialFalseID.strDesc:
"I'm a tech consultant to various multinational corporations, usually investment and fintech. I have a meeting with a representative from the Harper Jiang group. They're bidding on a contract to lease an asset I have in tow."

The first agent blinks his wet eyes twice. 

"Papers, please," the second agent says. You glimpse a suite of family tattoos beneath the cuffs of her jumpsuit, a few of which bear the scars of an ongoing removal operation. Must have been a mighty betrayal to her Calicoan elders, shedding their toxic brands to land a coveted municipal job. Proves she's taken the hard road to get to where she's standing, and she's not going to let you or anyone else fuck that up.

ValkyrieBorderForgedCreds.strDesc:
You dutifully pass the agent your data card with the fabricated manifest. Thanks to your forger, it lists the brain case as a sophisticated, self powered market analysis platform used to model trade indexes in real time, an overcautious bit of redundancy to ease the minds of finance drones during their long haul travel. You wouldn't want to miss the trade of a lifetime after a micrometeorite severs your power on the way to Venus, after all. 

The agent stares at his PDA for what feels like an eternity. Just when you think he's about to be finished, he waves over the second agent, who does the same. The partners look to one another, then back to the PDA, then back to you. 

"What is that," the second agent asks, and nods towards the brain case in the corner. 

"It's a sophisticated, self powered market analysis platform," you say. "It's used to check trade indexes in real time. You wouldn't want to miss the trade of a lifetime after a ..."

She waves away your explanation. "Not that," she says. "That," and points to your transponder. They must have pinged it before the random search. "You're a long way from home. Rare to see anyone make it off K-LEG these days." 

"Everybody has a home," you reply.

"And where's home now?" the second agent asks.

"Wherever there's money to be made," you tell her.

She spends a few more moments examining the manifest, dashes off a quick few lines on her PDA, then looks to her partner. He offers a backwards nod you can't quite interpret.

"Continue down the airlock," she says, and clears the way for you to pass.

ValkyrieBorderGuards.strDesc:
You see them the moment you leave the customs agents: three armed guards, shoulder to shoulder, standing at the end of the corridor. Two of them hold automatic rifles to their chests. The third, you can't help but notice, is idly thumbing the handcuffs dangling from her hip. 

You're still walking, it appears. A cold sweat gathers on the back of your neck. The guards aren't exactly blocking your route, but they aren't clearing a path either. 

If the nosy customs agent blew your cover, you're about to find out.

ValkyrieBorderBreak.strDesc:
Your faith in the forged credentials evaporates and leaves behind a vapor of cold fear. Staring into the agent's discerning faces you hear blood pumping through your swimming head, each heartbeat crashing against your skull like the tide against harsh cliffs. Only one way out: run.

Recalling something you saw in a Breakout highlight, you tuck the brain case under your arm, lower your shoulder, and charge through the blockade at full speed. The quickness of the manoeuvre catches them flatfooted, and you manage to knock one off balance while the others grasp for their weapons. You've already turned a corner when the first shots ring out. 

You've already taken two more turns before you realize you have no direction, no plan for escape. But with the fate of the war under your arm, you know you have to keep running. 

Three more corners and a couple unlocked doors later you find yourself in a darkened industrial corridor. Markings on the floor beneath you indicate a fork up ahead: it's either a reactor substation or a crowded residential zone. That, or you could take matters into your own hands.

PLOT_Merga_WhispersFound01Reply3.strTitle: Watch the Biography of Miss M
PLOT_Merga_WhispersFound01Reply3.strDesc:
According to the broadcast, Camellia Middlemist was born in 2049 on NewCal, the year of the aerostat's establishment. Although there is ample evidence disputing this fact, many consider her to be the first person born to Venus, and for that reason she grew up as a child star in the system.

After acting in various feature films for the Xinhua media conglomerate Peacock Pictures, Middlemist abandoned the film industry and struggled with addiction in her teenage years. She fell into obscurity for almost a decade before emerging, somewhat suddenly, on the Encantado aerostat in 2076, where she began a singing residency at the Sol Vermelho Lounge, a bar overlooking the Encantado Grand Prix. 

Because the Vermelho is owned by imprisoned crime boss Helio Hora and is the primary haunt for the Briar Rose piracy syndicate, it is rumored that organized crime is at least somewhat responsible for Middlemist's return. 

Her reemergence created an immediate media sensation, a redemption story that has captivated the hyperactive Venusian tabloid press for years and created a loyal and sometimes ravenous fanbase. In 2078, a year before her disappearance,  she began a very public relationship leading to a whirlwind marriage to champion Encantado Grand Prix racer Rex Korin. 

As Weihan closes his segment, he sends the broadcast back to Banks, who offers a heartfelt plea to anyone watching with information on Miss M to please contact authorities as soon as possible. 

Enraptured by the program, you look around to find that most of the spacers are still standing with you. A preview of the next program flashes on the screen: "Spotlight: Blood on the Rose, a History of Helio Hora"

PLOT_Merga_WhispersFound01Reply4.strDesc:
OWNG "Spotlight" is the network's premier interview program, featuring trenchant conversation between host Pierce Wilcox and an array of fascinating guests. This week, Wilcox has managed to pull a former member of the Briar Rose criminal syndicate: Breno Oscar Vaz.  

It's a rare get. Most syndicate members die in service to family, and those who manage to escape it are rarely brave enough to talk.

This one, however, seems compelled by the disappearance of Miss M to speak out. He is an aged man, nearly 50, with fading face tattoos and sunken eyes. His shirt is too large for him, and it looks like the first time he's ever worn a tie. The entire ensemble makes the neckpiece look like an inverted noose.

Vaz presents himself as an authority on Helio Hora, a former friend and associate. During the back and forth between himself and host Wilcox, you glean insight on Hora's background.

The now imprisoned crime boss was born in 2023 in São Paulo on Earth. Details of his early life are mostly unknown. In the early days of Venusian aerostat development, Hora worked in contracting and eventually materials acquisition, and was thus vital in the construction of both NewCal and Encantado.

Using resources and relationships cultivated in the construction of the latter, Hora began the Encantado Grand Prix and eventually established the nearby Sol Vermelho Lounge, where Miss M would eventually perform in residence. 

According to the case built against him by law enforcement, at the time of his arrest Hora's criminal empire included race fixing, labor bribery, contract embezzlement, intimidation, piracy, and contract killing. As part of the terms of his arrest, most of Hora's assets were turned over to a still active Venusian business mogul, including ownership of the Sol Vermelho Lounge. 

The current owner of the famed lounge was in close contact with Miss M up until her disappearance.

ValkyrieTitanIntro4.strDesc: "I did," you say. "We talked. He told me all about that." You nod to the sarcophagus. "Musta taken a shine to you," John says. "He never told me shit." "You knew all along," you say. "Ever since I got here, you've kept me in the dark, all the while planning this whole affair." "Yeah," says John. "So?" The moment lingers. He spreads his hands. "So, what? This is my job. I'm here to win the war before it hurts anyone I care about. I've done worse. Going to do worse still." "Speaking of," you say, pushing the case into his arms. "He thinks this was your decision. Good luck explaining it." You walk away. John calls after you. "Uh, yeah. I'm not going to talk to him."

ValkyrieTitanIntro5.strDesc: You separate from the revolutionaries and the Titanians and sit against one wall, watching the room work. A familiar face appears and sits next to you: Pan, your contact on Mojave. "Fancy running into you," he says. "It's been a crazy few days." Not exactly keen on anyone here, but Pan is maybe the closest thing to a friend. "What's going on?" you ask. "Mojave was deserted." "Closed, now," he corrects you. "You got out right before it went into lockdown. Calico's in full revolt. Ring Station's busy putting out fires, literally - they got nobody to spare for us quarrelsome natives. You and me are talking here, now, and as we speak? The regime's coming down. There's a guillotine in Times Square." "A guillotine," you say. "Aren't they gravity-fed?" "Traditionally yes," he says. A glimmer of pride in his voice. "Some psycho built one running on conductor rails. Bzzt, shiiing!" He makes a chopping motion. "Thock," he adds. "And then the blood goes everywhere. Way more than you'd think." You consider it. "Yeah," you agree. "That is crazy."

ValkyrieTitanIntro6.strDesc:
There's not much to do, it seems. Your part in this is over. At least you can compose your reply to Isambard: yes, I found him. No, he's not okay. No, I don't know why he was in that video. All it took was destabilising the whole system.

Maybe that's unfair. If you hadn't been here, this could've played out the same. Choong and the sarcophagus, in the hands of Xinhua or Titan, would have brought things to a head. Warships launching. Drums in the deep. 

They set up spotlights around the sarcophagus. One of those lights is eclipsed, and a shadow falls over you. It's John. "Hola," he says. "Got one last job for you."

"Get someone else to do it," you say reflexively.

"No can do," he says. "Ben's being a good sport. Not sure he knows what's going on, but he's talking to us finally. Cut a deal. He's going in. Willingly."

"Great."

"It is great," he says. "You're going with him. That's his price. I was right: you left quite an impression on the old boy."

He hooks his thumbs in his belt, the stupid cord-leather fake he's been wearing since day one. "I gotta say," he says. "Me as well. Don't know how often you hear this, captain, but you're the most self-possessed son of a gun I ever met. If anyone can do this, it's you."

ValkyrieSarcophagus119.strDesc: Ben Choong is lying flat in the aisle of the nave. A pool of blood seeps out from under his body. You crouch by him. He's whispering: "Oh God, oh God, oh God ..." "Ben. Can you hear me?" His eyes flutter open. "You," he says faintly. "I know," you say. "I'm sorry." "Sorry for what?" he says softly. "You don't care. You're ..." he coughs. "You're empty." "I didn't have a choice," you say. "This wasn't supposed to happen." He shuts his eyes, with more finality than demanded by his condition. "I cannot ... believe ..." he says breathlessly, "I'm to spend my last ... moments ... with you." His breathing stops.

ValkyrieTitanIntro7.strDesc:
There's not much to do, it seems. Your part in this is over. At least you can compose your reply to Isambard: yes, I found him. No, he's not okay. No, I don't know why he was in that video. All it took was destabilising the whole system.

Maybe that's unfair. If you hadn't been here, this could've played out the same. Choong and the sarcophagus, in the hands of Xinhua or Titan, would have brought things to a head. Warships launching. Drums in the deep. 

They set up spotlights around the sarcophagus. One of those lights is eclipsed, and a shadow falls over you. It's John. "Hola," he says. "Got one last job for you."

"Get someone else to do it," you say reflexively.

"No can do," he says. "Ben's a vegetable. And the logs show you did it."

"-" you say. A lacuna where a rejoinder, one you don't have time to think of, should be. Whoops.

ValkyrieSarcophagusUNWilling.strDesc: They drag you to the side of the sarcophagus. You don't have a lot of say in the matter. John follows to one side, halfway apologetic. "For the record, this isn't my best idea," he says. "But I've got 12 Martian warships breathing down my neck, and I'm throwing shit at the wall to see what sticks." Once you're within the tomb, he removes the gag from your mouth. "For the record," he says over your protestations, "I kinda liked you." The lid swings shut. The light goes out. Liquid, heard and felt but not seen, sluices in at your hips and ankles. It's breathable, they said, but how the fuck would they know? Your breathing accelerates, the nightmarish sensation of a water level crawling up your neck. You press your face to the lid, desperate for the last pocket of air - And then it's streaming down your throat, through your nose, in your ears - We're skipping straight to human trials! crows a giddy, oxygen starved part of your brain - "Breathe, [us-firstname]," says a muddy voice through an internal speaker, and about a thousand litres of ALIEN GOO. "Breathe!"

ValkyrieTitanIntro8.strDesc:
John shakes his head. "Disappointing."

He gestures.

ValkyrieBorderCoolNoCreds.strDesc: They scan your credentials. You smile and think cool thoughts. Ice cubes. Fast ships. Jazz, maybe. They whisper to one another. Exchange a significant glance. "There a problem?" you ask. "It's just going to take another minute," says the first agent. The second agent glances toward the case at your side, and then at the door. "Can we get you a ... anything?" Oh, fuck. They're being nice.

PLOT_Merga_Present_Evidence_Journalist_C.strDesc: [us] [says] you don't have much. Try pressing them for an alibi as a start.
[us] [says] running that alibi against the lawyer of a big shot club owner might be an uphill climb. Sounds like a dead end, for now.

Plot_Whodunnit_CollectCluesSplitNoMore.strDesc: [them-pos] killer left no more obvious clues that [us] can find.

ValkyrieSarcophagus18.strTitle: Tell Smiley what this place is
ValkyrieSarcophagus18.strDesc: "We're in the paradise the Colchians were promised, or one they made for themselves," you say. Scraps of memory sidle back into your brain, mostly of Choong describing the Colchians, but also snatches of the videotape you discovered. "And it's a replica of an Earth city." "Heaven is a place on Earth," Smiley says, as if it's snidely quoting something. "Oxford, England, circa the early millennium, warts and all. An intellectual property lawyer's wet dream. It makes sense, I suppose. A bunch of illiterate miners trying to recreate the Garden of Eden - you could do a lot worse than a university town from before the world went to shit." "Where is it?" you ask. "Where are we? Physically, mentally, spiritually, digitally, what is happening right now?" "Relax," says Smiley. It's said in the mode of an interlocutor who does truly want you to relax, for your own sake, before you hurt yourself. "You don't have the vocabulary. Think of it like an antechamber. A private cosmic room with the physical laws your genes expect, even if your socialisation doesn't." "An antechamber before what? What is it ante to?" Smiley just shrugs wordlessly. You get the sense that even it doesn't know.

ValkyrieSarcophagus19.strTitle: Tell Smiley it's connected to Choong
ValkyrieSarcophagus19.strDesc: "You know Ben Choong, and the Colchians. You're connected to them somehow." "Of course," it says. "I'm one of them. The last of them, if we're being technical - Ben's a pretender. Touring the slums and picking up our women with his fancy city talk. He makes me sick. I'm a Colchian born and raised." An unexpectedly venomous take on the divisive problem of Dr. Choong, you think. Your mouth voices the conclusion as it comes to you. "You're the one who tortured him." "Bingo! Correct! Big points to the Appellant! That's you," it adds, sotto voce. "I was killing two thousand million birds with one stone. I handed him to Xinhua State Security, I had him released, I gave him to the CIA, and had him killed. The form you found him in was by design." "You wanted the Great Powers to develop teleportation technology," you say. "We need more mass transit solutions," Smiley deadpans. "I can't stand spaceships."

ValkyrieSarcophagus110.strTitle: Tell Smiley it started the war
ValkyrieSarcophagus110.strDesc:
"The war isn't a coincidence," you say. "It's your doing. Your plans need us to be fighting each other."

"Haha," says Smiley. It doesn't laugh. It says 'haha'. "Not quite. I needed everyone distrusting each other, viciously, not actually at war. You won't like to hear it but I'm the System's greatest peacenik. I prevented the mouthbreathing morons on either side from knifing each other to death, multiple times." Smiley laughs brittily. "You have any idea how desperate you all were to throw a bunch of relativistic asteroids at each other? How hard I had to work to stop it? Of course not. They'll never build me a statue."

"The cold war, then, is your doing," you say. "Kept everything in homeostasis on the brink of destruction."

"Oh, yeah, that was me, for sure." Smiley's woe-is-me attitude vanishes, its mood turning on a dime, back to flippant disclosure. "Not solely my work, but I had a hand in it big time."

ValkyrieSarcophagus111.strTitle: Tell Smiley it made the videotapes
ValkyrieSarcophagus111.strDesc:
"You made the videotapes," you say. "It was you."

"Holy shit," says Smiley. "It's a big swing and a big hit! Yes, yes, I did! Did you like them? What did you think?"

"You're insane," you say. "You're not human. You don't care what I think."

Smiley looks hurt. "Don't say that. Of course I care what you think. That's why I asked."

You're dizzy, all of a sudden. You sit down on the first step of the altar. You put your head in your hands. It all led to this; it all led here. A cynical, circuitous loop, a mystery perpetrated by the object of the mystery. You'll ask why, now. You have to. But no answer could possibly satisfy. The very act of inquiring further was doomed from the start.

"Why?" you ask. "Why would you do this to me?"

"Ah-ah-ah," says Smiley reproachfully. "It selected for inquisitive minds, which are the only kind worth having, I think you'll agree. People are incurious by default. Most people would see those tapes and go, wow, crazy, and move on with their lives; mostly to work and back. You, though? You had to know more about the tape, about the people in the tape, about the circumstances behind it, and so on."

Nausea mounts, and you feel the urge to throw up. You close your eyes. Smiley continues. "The other Colchians had to go, of course; they were too far indoctrinated and most unhelpfully so. I needed a fresh batch of believers running on void opal, hunting down more, and so on, snowballing until the material requirements for my project were met. It talks to us. It tells us how to find it. You've had the dreams, you know what I'm saying. I spiked Abacho's ganja grow-op and pretty soon we were all having a wonderful time on our way to recreating the Colchian miracle. And I wasn't alone. There'll be cells like us on Mars, on Ceres, on Titan, wherever there are souls we can co-opt into useful service, there'll be a guy like me, dutifully co-opting."

You open your eyes. Whatever Smiley sees in them, it tries to modulate its tone. "Don't look at me like that. I was inspired by MK-Ultra. A human program designed for other humans! You might think little of me right now but I promise, I'm far from the worst of humanity."

ValkyrieSarcophagus112.strDesc:
Doors at the far end of the cathedral open. A sliver of daylight disrupts the soft ambience of the cathedral. As it shuts, your eyes readjust to the gloom.

"Hello?" says a voice. It's Ben Choong. "I heard voices. Where is everybody? Why am I in Oxford?"

Ben appears at the other end of the nave. He's damp, as if he was recently dunked in a river. Arriving in this place has granted him a human body, not the digital construct with a high resolution face map in which you met him. His real human face crinkles in confusion as he sees you with Smiley, an uncanny humanoid half out of costume as Jesus Christ.

He approaches you both. That funny feeling in your stomach is back. "It's me, Ben," you call out. "It's [us-firstname]. I think ... I think this was a mistake. It's all someone else's plan ..."

Ben slows as he nears you. He squints. He blinks very hard.

Smiley's bald head is fixed on him like a hunting dog.

Recognition dawns for Ben. He whispers: "Keti?"

Smiley sneaks a wink to you over its shoulder. "Sort of!"

It shoots him.

ValkyrieSarcophagus113.strDesc:
A bright red gout of blood explodes from Ben's chest and back. Smiley draws the gun out from the white robes and goes to fire again -

But you are on your feet, and before you know it you have grabbed Smiley's arm. The shot goes wide and high, making a cloud of masonry in a far corner of the cathedral.

Smiley doesn't fight back at first. It says, "What the hell are you doing?" When it realises you mean to take the gun for yourself, it struggles. The gun goes off. "What are you doing?" repeats Smiley. "This isn't right!" You grapple, Smiley spitting its words between grunts of exertion. "You're not - supposed - to -" The gun goes off again, and pierces clean through Smiley's bicep.

"Oh," says Smiley, and its arm goes slack. Blood sprays over the pews. You take the gun from its fingers. It sinks down into the pew, cradling its limp arm, white robe soaked with red. Smiley looks up at you in disbelief. "What was all that about?"

"Shut the fuck up," you say. "Or I'll kill you."

Smiley grimaces as if it only made a faux pas. It runs a finger along its lips and locks its mouth shut.

ValkyrieSarcophagus114.strDesc:
Ben Choong is lying flat in the aisle of the nave. A pool of blood seeps out from under his body.

You crouch by him. He's whispering: "Oh God, oh God, oh God ..."

"Ben. Can you hear me?"

His eyes flutter open. "I don't understand," he says faintly.

"I know," you say. "Neither do I, really. I'm sorry."

"Hold my hand," he says. You clasp it. His grip is weak. "I appeared in a river," he says softly. "Nearly drowned. Now this."

"I'm sorry," you say. It's not enough. Nothing you can think to say seems worth saying.

"I found my way here," he continues. His breathing gets weaker and weaker. You glance down at the wound. Shot through the heart, or damned close to it. "For the past hour or so, I had a body again. I was on Earth. I was wet, and I got dry in the sun." He smiles.

"It was worth it," he says to you, as clearly as he can. "It was all worth it for that."

"We're in a cathedral," you say desperately. "You were dunked in a river. Maybe you could convert."

His eyes shut. His breathing slows. "Absolutely not," he whispers. His breathing stops, and his hand slips from your grasp.

ValkyrieBorderIntroTorture.strDesc: It's okay. Act natural. You go through customs with a Renbao Cerebral Armature every day, for all anyone knows. It's not, yet, a crime.
ValkyrieBorderIntroTorture.strTooltip: PLACEHOLDER: The player sees this by stepping on a zone trigger on BCRS_ROOF. Zone triggers have no strPlot set, so we set it manually.

ValkyrieBorderIntroCase.strDesc:
Two uniformed agents emerge from the security office to stop your approach. The first, an older gentleman with a soft body and very wet eyes, takes a good long look at you. The second agent is a youngish woman, and at no point does she stop tapping away on her PDA.  

"What is the reason for your visit?" the first agent asks.

ValkyrieBorderIntroEmpty.strDesc:
Realizing you don't have brain case to smuggle through security is a bit of relief, even if it just means kicking the can down the road a bit.

You pass without incident this time.

ValkyrieBorderInitialJoke.strDesc:
"Can't be pleasure if I'm heading to Calico, can it? Business, then."

The first agent snorts. A good sign.  

"Papers, please," the second agent says. You glimpse a suite of family tattoos beneath the cuffs of her jumpsuit, a few of which bear the scars of an ongoing removal operation. Must have been a mighty betrayal to her Calicoan elders, shedding their toxic brands to land a coveted municipal job. Proves she's taken the hard road to get to where she's standing, and she's not going to let you or anyone else fuck that up.

ValkyrieBorderFinish1.strDesc:
Your body is in bad shape, but your will remains undaunted. With the brain case dangling from your arm, you drag yourself through the corridors with only a vague understanding of where you're headed.

First you turn a corner. Then you turn another. The pain now is less localised, and has begun to distribute itself across your entire body. Your pace slows. You put your free hand along the wall to maintain what's left of your balance. 

Your vision begins to darken at the edges, creating a tunnel ahead of you. At the end of that tunnel is a door. It is open. There is light inside. 

You use what's left of your energy to stumble towards the light and collapse inside.

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing1.strDesc:
"All clear!" is the first you hear from them: a squad of Xinhua marines storms the rendezvous point before you realise what's happening, moving with cybernetic swiftness and silence. Lucky they're on your side. They surround you, while a vanguard pair bound ahead to cover the exits.

"You're late," you say, keeping your cool.

One of the marines ratchets open the faceplate on her helmet. You recognise her. "So are you," she says, equally detached. "I'd call this longer than fifteen minutes. Wouldn't you?" Tragic. Two ships passing in the void.

"Figures," you say. "You got a name?"

"Sure," she says. "But you can call me Banzhang." It takes you a second to realise she means 'squad leader'.
ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing1.strTooltip: PLACEHOLDER: The player clicks on something to begin approaching the sarcophagus, possibly a character or door or computer.

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing2.strDesc:
The squad patches you into their comms on a managed channel. They shepherd you through enemy territory, flitting ahead and behind as you travel through Ceres tunnel by tunnel. You, personally, don't witness the action. "I'm not sure what's going on," you say into your mic.

"Ortega's up ahead with team two," says one of the marines. "We're delivering you to him."

"Why?"

"That's the mission," comes the curt reply.

PLOT_Merga_Present_Evidence_Mogul_Clue0.strDesc: [us] [says] you don't have much. Try pressing them for an alibi as a start.

PLOT_Merga_Present_Evidence_Mogul_Clue1.strDesc: [us] [says] breaking an alibi with a lawyer involved is almost impossible, especially that lawyer. Sounds like a dead end, for now.

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing9.strDesc:
Springing into action, you subdue the surprised marine, grab her weapon and spray the room with lethal automatic fire; that's the impulse that passes through your nervous system, anyway, in the same instant she's jabbing you with a subcutaneous sedative.

Darkness descends, and you go with it.

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing10.strDesc: You surmise, correctly, that it was a careful choice to have her relay this information to you. As opposed to, say, any of the other personnel in this cave less capable of tackling a runner. Sometimes the messenger is the message.

ValkyrieTitanIntro1.strDesc: Mojave is quieter than usual, perhaps due to the chaos on Ring Station. A TV news bulletin interrupts the ads to say Xinhua's Outer System Fleet is redeploying. The chyrons scroll over long-lens footage of incandescent torch plumes, a dozen ships in Yangtze's class vectoring hard. And this time, there's no quasi-lovable scamp waiting to guide you into the heart of Ceres.
ValkyrieTitanIntro1.strTooltip: PLACEHOLDER: The player sees this by stepping on a zone trigger on BCRS_ROOF. Zone triggers have no strPlot set, so we set it manually.

ValkyrieTitanIntro2Case.strDesc:
"Fuck it," you say aloud. The empty lounge does not object. You grab the braincase and set out.

You remember the way, to a point. The port's civilian thoroughfares give way to maintenance access, which give way to disused maintenance access, which give way to the tunnels, the endless smoothbore tunnels, empty but for trash and stale air.

ValkyrieTitanIntro2Empty.strTitle: Return Later with the Brain Case
ValkyrieTitanIntro2Empty.strDesc:
Which is probably for the best, seeing as you don't have the brain case with you anyway.
		
		You resolve to return later with the brain case in tow.

ValkyrieTitanIntro2.strDesc:
The first stage of being lost is not knowing it. The second stage is suspecting it. You're at stage five or six of the process.

Stations and ships are difficult to get truly lost in. They're usually relatively small, and every part of them was intentionally designed. Ceres and its subterranean features are neither. Clans of tight-knit engineers worked the tunnels for generations, and rarely in communication with one another, creating a labyrinth to put Mother Nature and her aeons of geological incrementalism to shame. How the hell did that kid manage it? He looked at each tunnel juncture and just knew.

In the end, you're rescued by the Revolutionaries' lookout. You hear her yelling first. It's an eerie wail emanating from nowhere at all. It sets your teeth on edge, but she spoils the tension by arriving red faced and panting, hauling herself hand over fist. "Don't go that way," she says between breaths, bracing against a wall. Or the ceiling - you can't quite remember which it is.

"You almost missed us," she says. She drains half a water pouch in one go, and spritzes some of it on her face. "You're about half a mile out, twelve degrees up, thirty around," she continues. "Where's your guide?"

"Didn't show," you say. "I had to chance it."

"You nearly 'chanced it' right into the badlands," she says grimly. She points down the tunnel you're following. "Another ten minutes that way and you're gone for good."

You look again along the tunnel, which looks identical to the others. "What's down there?"

She clams up. "Follow me. We need to get out of here ASAP."

You follow her. She sets a more measured, but still urgent pace. She guides you back up the tunnel five minutes, taking the third juncture you reach.

"Really, though," you say to her, if only to break the silence. "What's down there? People?"

"No," she says stonily. Then, "Yes. We don't have time to get into it. They're ... different. Drop the subject."

A story for another time. Before you know it, you're at the headquarters, and John is welcoming you with open arms.

ValkyrieTitanIntro3.strDesc: "About time you showed up," he says, loud enough to be heard across the cavern. "They got their shiniest tin cans pushing 2Gs to stop us. Get the fuck over here!" You're struck dumb as you enter. Things have changed in your absence. The HQ is buzzing with activity. There must be fifty people milling around, not just more militia, a new flavour of unassuming technical guys fretting around batteries of electronic equipment. That's all on the periphery: in the centre of the cavern, the Colchian sarcophagus rests. The oversized American flag hangs above it, and the two massive icons do not share the stage well. "Just you?" says John. "Where's Ben?" "He ... I've got him," you say. You hold up the case. John looks at the case, double takes between you and it. "Fuck me," he says. "That's what they meant by a special diet." He raps his knuckles on the case. "Didja have a look inside?"

CeresP3FinaleMothman.strDesc: The Steward inclines her head to one side. Then: "Mothman has entered the killzone. Again: Mothman is in the killzone." She looks up. "General?" Everyone looks to a four star general, head resting on two crooked hands. He speaks up for the first time, almost lazily. "Astra." The Steward repeats: "Astra. All units, Astra, Astra, Astra." At once the POV monitors wink out. No signal input. They switch over to analysis summaries, trawling social media feeds. "Moving," says a new voice, tense, from nowhere in particular. There must be a tightbeam link to a commander on the ground. That's all: the room is silent. The lights flicker again.

CeresP3FinaleNudge.strDesc: A nudge at your shoulder almost makes you jump: it's the junior officer. He whispers. "Tea, coffee?" An unfathomable question.

CeresP3FinaleTea.strDesc: He places a pouch of chai tea in front of you and moves on.

CeresP3FinaleCoffee.strDesc: He places a pouch of coffee in front of you and moves on.

CeresP3FinaleIgnore.strDesc:
You stare at each other mutely. He places a tall glass capsule of chilled water in front of you and moves on. 

Droplets bead on the side. It's sweating.

CeresP3FinaleMothman2.strDesc: "Our team is moving into position." The Steward is fully in shadow, has become another voice in the darkness. You can see nothing more than her hands resting on the table only. Her long graceful fingers are covered in scars. "We're about to see their diversion." Something flickers on a CCTV feed of a convenience store. The feed takes prominence, occupying four monitors at once. There's a bright white flash, an explosion rendered in grayscale against the lit signage. Then little flashes around it, emanating from somewhere indistinct. "Blast doors!" says the voice on the ground. Harsh in the background are terrified screams and automatic gunfire. "I need a -" it cuts out. You watch the dots of friend-or-foe milling about on the schematic. From overhead it looks meaningless. "So far, so good," says the Steward. "This is good?" says the Captain. He puffs on the pipe, revealing it to be a convincing electronic replica. "It doesn't sound good." "With respect, Captain," says the General, still hunched, "if it were not good, we would hear nothing at all." The statement precludes further discussion, even the Steward's sparse commentary. The wardroom lights flicker again.

CeresP3FinaleMothman3.strDesc:
The lull draws so long that you start to wonder if there isn't some kind of rhythm to the flicker. You find yourself counting the seconds between. 17, 22, 17. What does it mean? Reactor cycles? Something about the revolving station? 

Your paranoid fantasies are interrupted. A woman's smiling face, covered in grime, winks on to the monitors. "Home free," says the face, and pans down to a bodybag at her feet. The wardroom exhales collectively, and there's scattered applause. A fistbump.

The Captain leans forward. "This is a secure line, right?" A nod from the Steward. "Hey, kid. Good work down there. How are your people?"

"Banged up, but we're good, sir." A magboot nudges the bodybag harder than necessary were she simply indicating. "Our friend had some surprises ready for us. Nothing we couldn't handle." She wipes a layer of grime from her brow. "We're going to move to our secondary exfil if it's all the same to you."

"We read you," says the Steward. "Good luck. Out."

CeresP3FinaleMothman4.strDesc:
The screens return to the operating system's default background, the Xinhua insignia with the Navy dragon coiled around it. Behind you the officers file out, chatting, happy with the play. The house lights come up, and when you look for her, the Steward has already disappeared. You wait, not knowing what to do. Finally it's just you, the General, and the junior officer hovering at your shoulder.

The General sighs and shakes the tension from his hands. He leans back in his chair, and seems to notice you for the first time. His eyes slide to the ceiling, to the symmetrical navigation strips there. "This was your idea, huh?" he says, as if to himself. But he's talking to you.

His eyes slide back down to you. "What the fuck," he says, "are you still doing here?"

The junior officer helps draw back your chair, and leads you out.

Plot_Scholar_Flat_Enter.strDesc:
Isambard's instructions take you to Benjamin Choong's apartment without much difficulty. The residence is a small econo flat nestled among dozens of others in a relatively high rent area of the station. The line of identical doors gives you no reason to pause but Choong's, near the end, is the only one flashing with a green indicator. Clearly, it is unlocked. You step inside.

The place has been ransacked. What clearly began as a tidy living and work space now shows signs of intense struggle. Every bin and rack in the flat gapes open like a yawning mouth. The floor is covered with the guts of terminals: power sources and leads and motherboards. No drives in near sight. Whoever came here knew what they were looking for.

Choong is nowhere to be found.

Perhaps something here will give you insight into what happened. Where do you look first?
Plot_Scholar_Flat_Enter.strTooltip: The door panel reads Benjamin Choong

Plot_Scholar_Flat_Corner_Bed.strDesc: The bed is high quality, expensive, but unmade. You wonder if Choong was here when he was spirited away in such a hurry. Must have been a rude awakening.

Plot_Scholar_Flat_Workbench.strDesc:
Of all the spaces in your vision, the workbench is the most ruined. Stripped terminals, shattered labware, and tangles of electronics cover the surface. In the center of the table, a clear lack of debris. Even the light layer of dust around the rest of the apartment does not reach here.

Below the vacancy you find a matchbook. It is from a bar here on Port Mojave. Inside, a note written in faint ink. A contact number, and initials below it: PT.

Plot_Scholar_Flat_Kitchenette.strDesc: You see a half open fridge, a small dining table with a single chair, and various kitchen items clearly thrown to the ground during the haphazard search.

Plot_Scholar_Flat_Kitchenette_Fridge.strDesc: It remains relatively untouched. Expensive high nutrient foodstuffs are aligned in neat rows. You see about a dozen water bottles, all full, along with a batch of refrigerated supplements, some of which you do not recognize. Choong clearly knew how to take care of himself. Why do you find yourself thinking of him in the past tense?

Plot_Scholar_Flat_Kitchenette_Table.strDesc: You find an empty coffee cup, a handheld terminal smashed beyond repair and stripped of its drive, and a paperback book. Not cheap, those. Something called The Day of the Triffids by John Wyndham.

Plot_Scholar_Flat_Kitchenette_Ground.strDesc: Broken dishware, shattered glass, and assorted papers litter the ground here. You rummage through the papers but they present in a language so erudite as to be illegible to you. Mentions of rare mineral compounds standout, as well as their properties when combusted at certain temperatures. Just as you are about to give up here you glimpse a splash of vibrant color in the wastebasket. You take a closer look. A bouquet of flowers? You retrieve the arrangement. You lean down to smell them but find no odor. They feel fragile, cold, crosshatched. Paper, then. An impressive feat, creating all these by hand. Inside, there is a note: Thank you for meeting with me. No need to look me up next time you are on The Ring. I will find you. - Francisco Ortega

AVClub_FirstWatch_Extras_FF2.strDesc: He fast forwards again, throwing out a comment here and there, and holds it on the sarcophagus. You take a good minute and study it in closer detail, as close as the resolution and uneven lighting will allow. "Now," you say, "what's ... going on, here?" "That is the million dollar question," he says soberly. "We don't know." "That's all you have to say? You don't know?" His smile dims a little. "That's the long story short. The short story, um, medium, is that the sarcophagus comes up here, in #2, and again in #8. The numbers are meaningless." He corrects himself. "Not meaningless, but not chronological either." "What is it?" "A big gold human effigy," he says. "I don't know. They - the people in the videos - seem to revere it. They worship it. In the other video they put all kinds of science gizmos around it and talk to it or pray to it, but there's no audio. It's like a gnostic, new age, high tech religion. If only the Ancient Egyptians could see us now." "There must be a reason," you say. "People don't worship things for no reason." Smiley mulls over that idea. "I suspect," he says, "people worship what they're told to."

AVClub_The_Return_Cops_MakeBreak_Keepgoi.strDesc: The crowd steadily funnels into a disused cargo bay on a mining ship once known as the Primary Consumer. The Flotilla community has set up a makeshift aid station. Displaced residents float to and fro, calling or texting or intensely questioning one another. An awkward contingent of Ayosec goons are here, too, temporarily on their best behaviour, while their lieutenants liaise with harried and haggard community leaders. You grab a patch of wall and make yourself scarce. The show is over, even if it's outstayed its welcome as particularly bad shows do. You listen to the churn of the rumour mill. Nobody knows what's going on, except that Ayo's strike has run out of steam, and they seem to be losing interest in the whole affair. With nothing to do but wait, you ruminate. The timing of the sweep seems far from coincidental. Was this about the videotape? Smiley's club? Could this be, even, about you? Ayotimiwa's bottom line would be impacted by this; a vast expense carried out for what are, as far as you can tell, intangible returns. Surely it's not to do with the contents of the tape, part of you insists. A glitchy soi-disant ARG can't be worth killing for ... unless it can. Does that possibility recontextualise the tapes? What part of them was important? Your thoughts chase themselves in circles, so that you barely notice when an Ayo drone scans your ID and instructs you to return to your ship of origin.

AVClub_The_Return_Cops_Slipthrough.strTitle: Try to slip through Ayosec's lines
AVClub_The_Return_Cops_Slipthrough.strDesc:
Doubling back, you move oblique to the danger, searching for an uncovered exit, a gap in the dragnet.

Unfortunately for you, AyoSec know this particular warren better than you do. Whenever you get on to a promising route, you wind up face to face with fast-setting foam barriers set from the other side, totally impenetrable with the time available to you. Reversing course, your options narrow, and narrow again, until eventually your luck runs out.

AVClub_The_Return_ShieldWall.strDesc: The men and women on the front line brace behind an row of interleaved ballistic glass shields. They themselves are kitted out in Testudo hardsuits, the helmets bristling with bugeyed imaging tech, and their snub-nosed weapons peek out of eyelets in the shield wall. Further down the passageway you glimpse the bulk of the skiff, the oddly boxy boarding craft Ayo uses for infantry support. A voice crackles over the loudspeaker, sharp and accustomed to command. "Advance!" A thin, reedy whistle sounds out, blown by someone safely behind the front line. The shields ripple, suit thrusters hiss. The wall advances slowly, inexorably, toward you.

AVClub_The_Return_ShieldWallSurrender.strDesc: You lay down sharply, hands behind your head. "Citizen!" you yell into the floor, spittle bouncing back into your face. "Azikiwe citizen!" "Advance," booms the officer's amplified voice again, somehow terse while also verging on bored. "Drop anyone moving." They open fire: a series of sharp cracks followed by the eerie whistle of subsonic rounds zipping by your head. Rough stippled gloves, and a boot to the head, transfer you behind the line as the shields float above you. "Subdue, restrain, verify," says the officer's voice. You're turned around to face your captors, slammed back against the wall in the process, your skull ringing like a bell. Once your ID is processed, you're fed head-first into a human storage cube, where you have plenty of time to think, and not a lot to do.

AVClub_The_Return_ShieldWallSurrenderPro.strDesc:
An unknown amount of time passes in the cube. There's just enough space and ambient motion that you are constantly, literally, bouncing off the walls.

At the end of the unknown time period, which couldn't be more than half an hour, the viewing port slides up. An Ayo street Judge peers in. She reviews your case in twenty-three seconds flat. You're found noncompliant with eight of Ayotimiwa's core values in key growth areas of time management, interpersonal communication, and respect for authority. "What does that mean?" you ask. She taps the screen of her PDA, where your appointed HR rep is idling in a voice chat.

"Roughly, it means, wrong place, wrong time," says your HR rep, his audio icon jiggling with each word. "All told, you'll be out of pocket $523."

"Five hundred dollars?!"

"And twenty-three," he says smoothly. "If you want we can try and bargain them down, but as your representative, I'd advise you to take the rap and pick up some extra shifts."

You grit your teeth. It's difficult to bargain when you're crammed into a cube like a dehydrated mushroom. "Guilty as charged." The Judge nods, and the viewing port slides down.

After another four minutes, you're released to the tram station.

AVClub_The_ReturnRefuseSmoke.strDesc: "Hell no," you say. "I'm not smoking your shit." He flicks it at you dismissively. It glances off your temple just hard enough to sting. "Have a good evening, officer." "I'm not a cop," you protest, aware it's falling on deaf ears. "I just don't want to smoke weed right now!" Abacho lays down, hands behind his head, preparing to be arrested. "It's not weed," he says. "But I think you know that." "I didn't know that!" He keeps his face to the floor, pointedly. "Then if I were you, I would start running."

AVClub_The_ReturnRefuseSmokeBack.strDesc:
Back in the common room, the party's over. The futons are scattered, popcorn floating through the air like confetti. 

The riot police outside sound awfully close. With no other avenue available, you go outside to meet them.

PLOTLEOSnitchTargetSkeptical.strDesc: [us] doesn't trust the information and [asks] [them] to reveail the source.

PLOTLEOSnitchTargetGratefulAccept.strDesc: [us] [reveals] [3rd] to be the source of the compromising info.

PLOTLEOSnitchTargetGratefulDeny.strDesc: [us] [refuses] to reveal the source of the compromising info.

Plot_Snitch_Mojave.strDesc: [us] gets a bizarre message from [them], the Mojave station tech. [them-subj] would like to speak to you about someone named [3rd].

Plot_Snitch_Mojave_Offer_Reply.strDesc: [us] asks [them-pos] opinion on a recent capture of a Gal Con stronghold by CCRE forces.

Plot_Snitch_Mojave_Offer_Reply_CCRE.strDesc: [us] praises the courageous efforts of the CCRE and the glory of the Xhinhua empire.

Plot_Snitch_Mojave_Offer_Reply_GalCon.strDesc: [us] praises the valiant defenses of the Gal Con forces.

79AU_DeadUniverse2.strDesc:
Your ship limps back to Sol for another span of weeks. You are as glued to the scopes on the way back as you were on the way out.

The system is silent. Ships on Brachistochrone trajectories never finish them, spiralling the sun in crazy arcs, doomed to fall between the planets for the next billion years. Hundreds of ships make planetfall, funeral pyres streaking across the skies of Mars and Venus and Titan. At least two of the major ports become clouds of debris, docking attempts that should have aborted. Hangzhou is the only one to remain totally unscathed. Is automated systems assume control of incoming traffic, an emergency feature the station long denied it possessed.

Throughout weeks of carnage and aimless destruction eclipsing all solar history hitherto, you pick up no S.O.S., no distress calls, not even any complaints or arguments over who was at fault.

79AU_DeadUniverse3.strDesc:
K-LEG looks pretty much the same as you left it. The derelict graveyard has a handful of new, unlicensed headstones. Some of them might need intervention within a year to avoid a nasty collision, but until then everything seems fine ticking over. Whatever contingencies the station planned for, and this was certainly not one of them, the automated systems have handled it.

You coast in to dock as you always have. Ignoring the warnings, you override the clamps. You'll have to fix that. Perhaps you can take the Harbormaster's codes from his quarters.

The docks are quiet and empty for the first time in your life. The air is cool, almost cold, a feat never achieved by the long suffering environmental team. As you stroll past familiar haunts, the unattended kiosks and crew lounges and vending machines and dorms, you find the floors littered with objects that had been held by your former colleagues until the instant they disappeared into thin air. The usual culprits are PDAs and rotting food, power tools, an extra garment or two. They had no idea. They never knew it.

You watch the footage in Station Security, more for something to do than for enlightenment. The clips are uniform, almost boring. In one frame the station is teeming with life. In the next frame it is not. The PDAs float like an afterthought. Everything sets course for 1036 Ganymed below, eventually to be intercepted by the station floor.

79AU_DeadUniverse4.strDesc:
You are the last and only human. Did Nietzsche conceive of the ubermensch having to feed themselves, use the bathroom, clean their clothes, shave? Does the last man brush his teeth? These needs demand your attention. Some you address out of habit. Others slip now that they're not for anyone.

This station, any station, anywhere you can go, houses more material wealth than one person could ever hope to attain or exhaust. It is yours by default.

You have an embarrassment of riches, a freedom surplus. You can go anywhere, do anything. All you have lost is the observation of others. Whether that is a win or a loss is entirely, solely, your opinion.

79AU_Ose1.strDesc:
You wheel yourself into the elevator and take it to the second floor. There, a long hallway stretches out and presents six doors, each of them illuminated from above by light fixtures casting a dim orange glow. At the end of the hall there is a final door, and it is ajar. 

Your chair struggles against the carpet. Pushing yourself down the hallway the only noise you hear is the occasional creak of the metal straining against your effort. 

The elegant label on the final door reads '208'. It's already open, which suggests an invitation or a disaster.

79AU_Ose2.strDesc: The room is beautifully appointed, with every object carrying the certainty of taste emboldened by infinite resources. The carpet is an emerald green with notes of golden filigree. Plants and drapery climb the walls. The rest of the space is populated with low slung, blonde wood furniture in organic shapes, many of them topped with upholstery in earthy, terracotta tones. You're trying to place the fragrance (sandalwood?) when you see him, a lithe figure sitting near a bookcase and a bonsai tree, one leg crossed above the other. His left hand balances a book in the crevice between his legs and his right rests on an end table near a tumbler full of what you assume is whiskey. The man is wearing a silk kimono tessellated with a pattern of cranes. You're so fascinated by the design that it takes you a moment to notice that he has the head of a black panther. His yellow eyes glance up at you over his glasses, expectantly. "I'm sorry," you stammer. "I'm looking for ..." "Ose," he says. "Great President Ose, apparently. Ruler of thirty legions? Although I've not met them yet. And you are ...?" "[us-firstname]," you say. "Not as exciting as my name, but we can't all be so lucky," Ose says, and closes the book. "Are you from here?"
