"It's my first time in the hotel." "No, no, not here. Here," Ose says, and makes a broad gesture with both hands. "Oh. Yes?" "I see. I'd ask you to take a seat, but ..." He nods towards your wheelchair. Suddenly feeling like a bad house guest, you roll your chair closer to his, hoping the spot you choose doesn't damage the immaculate feng shui. "A human, then," Ose says, and swirls an ice cube in his glass with a long forefinger. "I've been reading about you. Your kind has quite the imagination. Authors of such varied and exotic worlds. Tell me, why are there so many kings?" "I don't know what you mean." "I've just yet to come across a story that doesn't involve some kind of hierarchy," he says, and tosses the book away in disgust. "Even the heroes are peasants. At least they start that way. Before they become kings." You have no idea what to say. You find yourself falling into his voice. The sonorous and melodic timbre suggests pride for the old world along with fascination with the new. Plus, you must remind yourself again, he's got a bespectacled cat head. "Tell me about Earth," Ose says. "I've never been," you tell him. "A paradise, it seems. Positively teeming with life. Trout in the brooks, birds in the sky. Clouds of gnats. Innumerable microscopic herds of, what did I read...waterbear?" "Not anymore," you say. "Oh, don't be so grim! It's true you've nearly ruined the place. Such a shame. All that grubby infighting. Not the kind of thing a king can solve, unfortunately. But that lesson is hard won. Usually over far more generations than your kind has under their collective belts."

79AU_Ose3.strTitle: Who could solve the infighting, then?
79AU_Ose3.strDesc:
"It's a good question. The right one," Ose says. "Truthfully, that kind of thing has a way of working itself out after a time. Assuming, you know. The babies aren't strangled in their cribs."

"Is that what we've done? Strangled ourselves?"

"I haven't decided yet," he says. "Perhaps we'll know by the time I finish this drink."

79AU_Ose4.strDesc:
"Why are you, um..." you think for a minute. "Is your head...?" Still nothing. 

"I should be asking you! I wouldn't think too much about it. Suffice it to say that new worlds come with altered contexts. This one is yours, believe it or not. A very old one. But human nevertheless. Does it frighten you?" he asks.

You don't know what to say.

"No," he muses. " You don't seem the type."

ChoongAccuseWar.strTitle: He's lying about the end of humanity
ChoongAccuseWar.strDesc:
"I've never heard of this Earth surplus before today," you say. "And even if it's real, I've never seen signs it's running out."

He frowns, and shakes his head like he can't believe what he's hearing. "You grew up on a rock floating in the middle of nothing," he says viciously, accessing an untapped well of condescension. "Everything you ever ate, drank, or breathed, was shipped to you at a massive expense. You have no idea what you're talking about, no idea how tenuous your life really is."

"I'm a ship's captain now," you say proudly. "I don't need anyone for anything."

His mouth actually falls open, an expression you've read about but never seen. "You're as doomed as I am," he says, after snapping it shut.

ChoongAccuseVideotapes.strTitle: He's lying: he made the videotapes
ChoongAccuseVideotapes.strDesc:
"I don't know why, or how," you say, "but you must have made the videotapes. Perhaps to lure people to you. Perhaps as an escape attempt. After all, it worked: I'm here."

"It took me a second to remember what the hell you're talking about," he says. "This is the first I've heard about your stupid tapes. Zero marks, see me after class."

ChoongDontCareLying.strTitle: Say you don't care if he's lying
ChoongDontCareLying.strDesc:
"I think, in your situation," you say, "anyone could be forgiven for lying. Putting your brain in this device was cruel, and bizarre."

"No argument here," he says.

"That's all I wanted to say. Whatever your secrets may be, you're entitled to them, if nothing else."

"Forgive me," he says tonelessly. "But I couldn't care less what you think."

ChoongDecide.strDesc:
Choong, as it stands, seems like a dead end. He has no answers for you about the videotape mystery, nor how it interfaces with the incipient war, besides the origins at New Colchis. Whatever he's hiding, you may have to content yourself that it is beyond your reach ...

His life is in your hands, in the most literal sense.

ChoongTortureHim.strTitle: Torture him to see what he's hiding
ChoongTortureHim.strDesc:
"I'm running out of options," you say, for yourself as much as him. "The Great Powers are convinced you hold the secret to the war. Even if they're wrong, I have to try. The cost is too high."

"No," he says quietly. One pitiful little no. Even after it all, he still didn't see this coming. He wanted to believe. He had hope.

"Then tell me!" you explode. "Tell me what you're holding on to! Tell me why they did this to you!"

He closes his eyes, processing, some internal battle between release and guilt, punishment and fear.

His expression firms. He opens his eyes. "No."

ChoongTortureHimInvestigate.strDesc:
You take off the rig. Blinking away the last images of Choong and the log cabin, you stretch your arms, wondering how long it's been.

The device is forthcoming about how to proceed. There are logs of prior sessions, and it's not difficult to recreate one.

The scenario they used the most is titled The Pain Room. The application byline calls it the gold standard in the field of Computer Assisted Interrogation, and has many quick setups and user guides to get you started.

ChoongTortureReconsider.strDesc:
Is there such a thing as morality? Is there really? 

This much is obvious to you: evil, 'immoral' things happen on the daily, everywhere, and you always hear the same line: everyone thinks they're a good person. They can't both be true - rather most of those people thinking themselves good have to be plain wrong, ipso facto. Good people do evil things, and pretend it was okay afterwards, or that it didn't happen. If it were really so wrong to hurt someone, there would be no war, and if a veteran soldier broadcasted everything they did when they returned home, they would be shunned. We keep right and wrong around when it's useful, and when it's not, we try to ignore it. You could do or say whatever you want, and never tell anyone afterward.

So why do you feel so totally averse to this? Why are your hands poised to command it to shut off?

You have justification. Primarily, he's concealing information that could decide the fate of millions. Secondarily, he's annoying. Third, or tertiarily as Choong might smugly put it, the damage has already been done, and by whole cadres of state actors from both sides, no less. Who really cares what happens to him? If you have to put anyone in something called The Pain Room, it might as well be someone who's been there plenty of times already.

Still, with all that rattling around in your head, your hands execute the command, and The Pain Room quits.

ChoongTortureHimReadme.strDesc:
Before you torture him, you decide to torture yourself, first.

The Pain Room's readme describes a featureless room where the subject is immobilised and various parts of the brain are directly stimulated to induce pain. There are many different kinds of pain it can do. Vast swathes of grey matter are devoted to modelling damage and abrasion on every other part of the body, and all of them are fair play, each detailed in dedicated chapters. 

The skin, broad surface that it is, has many different notes to strike - cuts, boils, bruises, burns, all the way up to nasty stuff like degloving and neuropathy.

The extremities, lips, mouth, fingers, genitalia, all have trillions of nerve endings to bother, and a forest of subheadings detailing the different ways the program can do it, none of which you feel compelled to expand. 

The gut has a lengthy chapter on simulating acute inflammation, or a classic gutshot in a variety of calibers. 

Finally the notes explain the program can simply convince the prefrontal cortex it is experiencing pain on a scale of 1 to 10, and warns that above a 7 risks unconsciousness, and 9 or 10 will reliably cause a coma within seconds.

STKTemplate_Intro_Allow_Faction_Likes.strTitle: Agree to Discuss Favors with Faction Ally
STKTemplate_Intro_Allow_Faction_Likes.strDesc: [us] says I like your faction! Sure, let's talk favors.

STKTemplate_Intro_Allow_Faction_Same.strTitle: Agree to Discuss Favors with Faction Ally
STKTemplate_Intro_Allow_Faction_Same.strDesc: [us] says good to see a fellow faction! Sure, let's talk favors.

PLOT_ProspectorFetchGold_AskQuestions.strTooltip: Re-open conversation about mining and Ceres.

PLOT_ProspectorFetchGold_OfferReply.strDesc:
[us] describes to [them] [us-pos] deep need for gold.
[us-subj] [is] willing to pay good money for any gold nuggets you can bring by hand. [us-subj] [says] it's most often found by mining the deep deposits on the shiniest asteroids. There are a few asteroids around here, but thousands more gathered at Ceres.

PLOT_ProspectorFetchGold_OfferTrigger.strTitle: Trigger for the ProspectorFetchGold Offer Beat
PLOT_ProspectorFetchGold_OfferTrigger.strDesc: [us] should bring [them] gold ore, a mining laser, a PDC, and a radar.

InspectBraincase4.strDesc:
You jack in to the case's OS, not entirely sure what to expect.

The biometric software has little to say. The brain is unresponsive and likely in a coma.

If anyone asks, you think, you'll say you found him like this.

ChoongPlateau3_Exit.strDesc:
Silence falls in the cabin between you. The wind whistles at the window, buffeting the heavy shutters, a reminder of the dreadful cold all around. It's easy to imagine this pocket of warmth and light is all that exists, that reality itself will cease to unfold a dozen steps in any direction - and for at least one of you, that is accurate.

"Is that it?" asks Dr. Choong. "Have I aided the war effort?"

"You've been very helpful," you say. "I'm sorry it took so long."

"It's not every day I meet someone new." He smiles. "For the most part, I actually enjoyed our conversation."

"However," you say. He blinks. "There's a couple things you haven't been entirely honest about."

"Ah." A single sound, but it betrays a crushing weight of expectation. "May I be permitted to know what it is you think I'm lying about?"

ChoongTortureHimReadme_1.strDesc:
A section break, and the readme continues outlining its more experimental fare. 

Broad emotions and qualia can be stimulated with reasonable precision. Starvation, thirst, fatigue, nausea, those are all easy. A pull-quote details one test subject’s account that a complete loss of internal balance was the worst of the lot. 

More difficult - which is to say, less precise - is simulating fear, guilt, shame, despair, and higher order social feelings like rejection or alienation. 

The readme takes care to warn that these effects may linger with the subject, and compared with the physical pain trials, had a much higher rate of attrition on test subjects.

ChoongTortureHimReadme_1_1.strDesc:
The readme concludes by referencing another document, not loaded on this device, which reported the fair weather success rate of securing an accurate confession, based on controlled trials where test subjects were instructed to conceal specific information: 

22%. 

The report compared it favorably against traditional methods like waterboarding or hammering thumbs, which the program readily simulates, but laments that the scope of inquiry was sorely lacking, and would require follow-ups with more funding. 

It stressed that for the time being a good law enforcement agent should exhaust all his or her available alternatives of information gathering before using the program for its intended purpose.

ChoongHair.strTitle: Ask him about his unusual hairstyle
ChoongHair.strDesc:
"What do you call that?" you ask.

"Call what?" he says. "My hair?"

"It’s so round."

"Very good. It is." He sounds pleased you can recognise shapes.

"I mean," you say, "it’s not common where I’m from."

"It’s not common where I’m from either," he says stolidly. "They cut it like this in creche, ten children at once, bowls for guidance. Easy to tell who was an orphan and who wasn’t."

"You’ve kept the same hair for over forty years?"

"I always thought I’d wear it until I died," he says. A belated note of pride accompanies his afterthought: "And I did, didn’t I?"

ChoongLeaveAndEnd1.strDesc:
You pull off the Renbao electrode rig. Choong and the log cabin and Moretti disappear, replaced by the familiar dull wall of your ship.

The braincase sits in its same place, making its steady quiet noise. You ride the wave of vertiginous self-doubt customary when emerging from lengthy simulations - was that real, did that really happen, where did it happen, et cetera - and consider everything you've learned.

You think you will be unlikely to encounter again in your life another conversation that will challenge your understanding of the universe as much as that one did, minute to minute. That wasn't a category you were tracking, but now that you are, it's got the number one spot.

At the same time, your situation and your needs are prosaic. You have to track down the sarcophagus, and get Dr. Choong inside of it, possibly under the watchful eye of a battery of specialists to record what he does, or what happens to him. No small feat, but no viable alternatives, either.

Plot_Ceres_The_AV_Club_Watch_News.strTitle: View News on Strange Watch Parties
Plot_Ceres_The_AV_Club_Watch_News.strDesc: [us] [watches] [them] more closely and learn about a group of eccentrics who gather in secret to watch what they describe as rare and mind altering video footage. The segment B-roll shows a makeshift theater on Flotilla full of viewers with blurred faces watching the footage and smoking from large shared pipes.

Plot_Ceres_The_AV_Club_Lookup_Watch_Part.strDesc: [us] tries scouring local and social media sources using [them] for info about the drug fueled watch parties around OKLG.

CeresP3FinaleMothman5.strDesc:
The screens return to the operating system's default background, the Xinhua insignia with the Titan Navy dragon coiled around it. Behind you the officers file out, chatting, happy with the play. The house lights come up, and when you look for her, the Steward has already disappeared. You wait, not knowing what to do. Finally it's just you, the General, and the junior officer hovering at your shoulder.

The General sighs and shakes the tension from his hands. He leans back in his chair, and seems to notice you for the first time. His eyes slide to the ceiling, to the symmetrical navigation strips there. "This was your idea, huh?" he says, as if to himself. But he's talking to you.

His eyes slide back down to you. "What the fuck," he says, "are you still doing here?"

The junior officer helps draw back your chair, and leads you out.

CeresP3FinaleMothman6.strDesc:
A familiar face passes you at a bulkhead. Of all people, it's Francisco Ortega, dressed in military fatigues. "I'll take [us-custom-characterGenderCond|him|her|them] from here, Lieutenant," he says. The lieutenant shrugs gratefully and disappears before someone can assign them any more busywork.

"Ortega?" you ask. The stencilled name on his suit reads HARRISON.

"Don't," he says. "Don't call me that here. I'm doing you a favour. Follow me."

CeresP3FinaleMothman7.strDesc: He takes you on a path notably distinct from the maze you travelled to get here. You pass other military personnel who defer to Ortega, letting you past. He's tense, and it shuts down any questions about what's going on - something you're getting tired of asking all these people anyway. You arrive in a cavernous bay filled with smaller craft attended by teams of engineers. He guides you along navigation lines to one such craft, which in addition to dedicated crewmen conducting a post-flight examination, has a tired looking squad of marines lounging nearby, waiting for debrief. You recognise some of their faces from the final call in the wardroom. You look to Ortega. Intercepting your look, he passes you a PDA with a document open on it. "Smile for the camera," he says, and walks ahead of you. "Well done, marines!" he says brightly to the squad, who come lazily to attention. "At ease, we'll keep this brief ..." The document open on the PDA is titled FOLLOW THESE INSTRUCTIONS OR WE'RE BOTH DEAD.txt

CeresP3FinaleMothman8.strDesc:
TAKE THIS CASE TO THE SECURITY OFFICE CHECKPOINT ON CERES.
		
		CHECKPOINT IS ON THE ROOF LEVEL/THE MOUTH.
		
		DO NOT ALLOW THE CASE TO BE INSPECTED BY PERSONNEL THERE.
		
		YOU WILL BE CONTACTED ONCE PAST CHECKPOINT.
		
		HAND THE PDA BACK TO ME NOW. AND LEAVE.

CeresP3FinaleMothman9.strDesc:
You look up from the PDA. Ortega has a magged whiteboard and he's drawing big looping lines of enemy movements, narrating the op play-by-play. The marines are mostly paying attention.

You hover at his elbow and slot the PDA back into his grip, which he takes with a nod. Then he nods you toward one of the marines.

Under her arm, there's a grey-black case. You glance back at Ortega. He is ignoring you.

You approach the lead marine. Her eyes slide from the whiteboard to you.

You hold out your hand.

After a moment, the marine hands the case to you.

You turn and walk away.

CeresP3FinaleMothman10.strDesc:
Each step proceeds robotically with the momentum of the last. Case tucked under one arm, light as anything in freefall, you wend your way back along the half-remembered route to the exit. All around you the Navy buzzes with activity, welding and loading and delivering and joking and arguing and lazing around bored.

"Hold up!" you hear behind you.

You turn.

The lead marine catches up to you, serious expression on her face.

"Let me see that," she says.

"I'm supposed to have it," you blurt out.

"I know. Give it here," she says.

With no other way out, you hold it toward her.

She eyes it critically.

She produces a rag from a hip pocket and rubs a dull brown patch of gore from the top surface of the case.

"That was bugging me," she says. "Now, how 'bout I buy you a drink?" She winks.

"Oh," you say. "Yep. Yes. Sure." The marine looks at you. "What about," you say, clutching at straws, "I meet you back here in fifteen minutes?"

"Fifteen. Got it," says the marine. "I'll be waiting."

You turn away again, trying not to hurry. She'll be waiting a long time.

CeresP3FinaleMothman11.strDesc: You disembark from the Yangtze-3 unchallenged. What in God's name was that all about?

79AU_Basement13.strDesc:
"Does part of this fact-finding expedition involve me talking to it? I know it's against the rules," you say. "But you're not going to put me in there, are you?"

Ariel laughs. "No." And an aftershock laugh, verging on a giggle. "No, that wouldn't help at all."
79AU_Basement13.strTitle: Do you want me to talk to it?

79AU_Basement14.strDesc:
Following your last exchange of words, her head snaps to the glass. It's the fastest you've seen her move. "Put the glasses on," Ariel says quietly.

You put them on. The humanoid outline, which had appeared to stand appreciably far back, is much, much larger; the entity is standing directly on the other side of the wall. It is as close as it can get to you both.

"What's it doing?" you ask.

She doesn't reply.

"Does it do this often?"

Again she doesn't reply. She goes to the locking mechanism and engages it. The doors slide shut. She spins the wheel counterclockwise, and when it stops, she strains against it until it absolutely does not budge.

Climbing into the driver's seat, she reaches over her shoulder for the glasses, which you return.

79AU_Basement15.strDesc:
"I suspect that was not good," you say. The car eats up ground at the same frustratingly measured pace. "Maybe even bad," you say to her unresponsive back.

Ariel does reply, but it's after a hard thirty seconds of silence. "Hostile entities are kept in panopticon," she says coolly. "For their protection, and ours. If we choose, they can't tell they are being viewed. Observation goes one way, outside-in." She is silent for another long while. "Or so we believed."

You can see how that might unsettle an entity styling itself as a warden. "Nobody's perfect," you offer.

"My record was," she says. "Until today."

79AU_Basement16.strDesc:
It's not until the elevator is in sight that the thought occurs to you. "I didn't break your rules, did I? Even by accident?"

"No," she says right away. "I'm not some martinet out to punish you on a technicality. Although if you did do something and got away with it, you're cheeky asking about it." She pauses, perhaps considering herself fallible, to see how that would feel. "But I don't think you did. The fault is mine."

"Maybe it was a coincidence," you say. You don't believe it, but there's a chance these alien things don't consider probability the way you do.

"Coincidences are rare. This was close to impossible," she says. Another similarity you can bond over.

Maybe you're learning to read her body language after so long with nothing to stare at, because something else occurs to you. "You called them antisocial, paranoid, and arrogant," you say.

"Yes," she says. She parks within reach of your wheelchair. "If we ever manage to converse, I hope to find the respect is mutual."

She helps you back into the elevator without delay.

79AU_Phone1.strDesc:
On the elevator console, there's a small red handset hanging in a cradle beneath the floor buttons. As you look over the buttons, considering your next move, a small bell rings from within the handset.

You pick it up gingerly and look into one bulbous end of the crescent. There's a star pattern of speakers within. A tinny voice speaks from it. "Hold it to your ear," says the voice.

You press it to your ear. The voice comes through more clearly. It's Joakim's voice. "Now put the other end by your mouth." You do so. "You can reply to me."

"Understood," you say.

"Game night is beginning," he says. "Would you please join the other guests in the VIP Lounge?"

79AU_Phone2.strDesc: "There's some things I'd like to do. Is it, ah," you say. "Mandatory?" "Technically, no," says the automaton. "But I'm going to level with you. You really, really, really, really shouldn't miss it." "I see," you say. "And it has to happen now?" "Yes," he says. "It has to happen now."

79AU_Phone3.strDesc:
"I don't think I want to play a game," you say. "I don't want to do Game Night."

Joakim is silent for a moment. "I can convey your wishes to the other guests. But I advise against it. Are you sure you can't bring yourself to attend?"

79AU_Phone4.strDesc:
"You know what it sounds like to me," you say. "It sounds like you're trying to lure me into some kind of high stakes scenario that I don't understand, where I do something I regret, because this mixed media reality attaches bizarre significance to," you bite the words, "random stuff."

Joakim pauses before answering. "That's an ungenerous rendition of it," he says. "But not far from accurate. I still think it's better than the alternative."

AVClub_The_Return_FindSmiley.strDesc:
Where the hell did Smiley go? He was standing right there, not a moment ago.

"Smiley? Smiley!" you yell into the furor. It occurs to you that that was a forum handle. What was his real name? He introduced himself at one point.

You grab someone's shoulder in passing, knocking them off their axis. "What?!" they say. It's Xavier, the club's resident simulation theorist. 

"What happened to Smiley? Where'd he go?"

"Get the fuck off me!" says Xavier, righting himself, before he hurries after the rest.

Something bumps your shoulder: the light kiss of objects in space. It's Smiley's enormous glasses. You snag them on the rebound. Yep, it's the same pair, alright. Did they get knocked off?

Looking around, you spy another odd accoutrement, peeking out from underneath a futon. Something sleek, on bulbous fabric. You tug on one end.

The curio comes loose. It's a prosthetic bald cap, attached to a distinctive hairpiece with a receding hairline.

In either hand, you hold the two most recognisable features of the man you knew as Smiley.

AVClub_The_ReturnAcceptSmoke.strDesc: The man is dead serious. You must smoke this drug or else. "Fine," you say, biting the word. "Fine! Give it." You inhale on the pen. One Tharsis City, Two Tharsis City, Three ... you glance at Abacho. He motions keep going. You glare at him, and keep inhaling. Eventually it is enough. You hand the pen back. "That wasn't weed," you say. Do the corners of your vision blur a little? No. "What is it?" Abacho shrugs. He stands aside from the vent shaft. "Left, two rights, left. Remember. Get going while there's time."

PLOT_Ceres_Ask_Prove_BCER.strDesc:
You approach Pan Tao at his usual smoking spot and ask him how someone like you can prove your loyalty to the Titan cause.  

"Few options," Tao says. "First is territory. The whole belt is in a kind of King of the Hill situation. If you trade for a Titan beacon, you can take it out to unclaimed space near some profitable asteroids. Deploy it and we have eyes on those rocks. Keeps our supply lines open."

"Xinhua likes to throw out their own beacons, so you could always blow those up. That's kinda fun, and the brass gets a big kick out of it."

"If you're feeling froggy, you could always jump. By that I mean: sieze or destroy a Xinhua allied vessel. Demand their surrender or, ya know. Boom."

"Lastly, you can hit the mines. Plenty of good rocks left. Get some ore and sell it to one of our faction kiosks here. That gets you good scrip, plus attaboys from the right folks. 

"Besides that, you could try and run special missions for Mr. Wayne. He doesn't give them to everybody, so if he trusts you to handle it, it's probably a good bet. Check the planter up near 'The Mouth' for messages."
PLOT_Ceres_Ask_Prove_BCER.strTooltip: [them-firstname] may have advice for how to prove your loyalty to Titan.

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strDesc:
Pan Tao is physically slight for a dock worker. You find him leaning against a wall, lit cigarette in a hand beating a staccato pattern against the rock face.

"Pan Tao," you say, not quite a question.

"Shoot," he says, not quite paying attention.

"How do you know Benjamin Choong?"

Pan squints in your direction, taking a drag from the cig. "Drinking buddy of mine. Why, what's he done?"

"Nothing for quite some time," you say. "He's missing. Some buddy you are."

"Hey pal," he says, "fuck you. I don't know you. Why don't you make like Ben Choong and get lost." He goes back to watching the cargo drones scooting up and down the bore. 

You snap your fingers in his face. "Cut the shit. Whoever turned his place over didn't catch the handwritten sheet of paper with your name on it. Was it you, dumbass?"

That gets his attention. "You're serious," he says. You are. He groans. "That fucking moron ... I don't get paid enough to deal with this shit." He shakes his head. "There's a bar in downtown Calico. Angel Wings. Go there. You'll find the guy you want to talk to. Now leave me alone," he says tiredly, "this was supposed to be my break."
PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strTooltip: 'Pan Tao' ... that was one of the names on the note in Choong's apartment.

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strDesc: [us] gives [them] a startled look and says to follow them to somewhere more private and await further contact.

You arrive at Angel Wings in seventeen minutes. There's one man at the bar. It's a big hat he's wearing, a white Stetson homage, to go with the blue flannel shirt and jeans. He pumps your hand and the shirt cuff brushes your fingers - perfectly smooth. There's no way it's real flannel. "John Wayne, at your service, sir." He holds up two fingers. Two shot glasses full to the brim slide down the bar, not spilling a drop. He's tall and gaunt, almost cadaverous. Brown skin which could be a tan job or some melanin in his family tree. He downs his shot and waits for you expectantly. It burns your throat. He nods slowly. "If you can hold your liquor we'll have no trouble." He's already holding up a hand for two more. "Now listen to me," he says, his hand held up, before you can get a word in edgewise. "We're going to do shots here until we can't see straight. Then we'll go down the street to Palmers. A few more there. Then upspin to The Red Door. Two there, and then I'm gonna get in a fight. You watch my back. Xinhua sailors are loaded with scrip, we take it, it's ours. We hit the Aphrodite. I'm on a hot streak, I won 5 grand this week. We go big, yeah? Follow my lead. After that, I know a guy, Muhammad or Mustafa or something. He knows guys, girls, whatever you like. We put all that together," he says, taking his delivered shot, "and our night is set." You leave your glass where it is for now. "Did you kill Benjamin Choong?" He grimaces. "I dunno, maybe. What's he look like?" "If you don't know, you're wasting my time." "Alright, alright," he says, waving a hand. "Settle down. Cool customer, you. No, I di'nt kill him. He went missing on Ceres. All kinds'a people do." He pulls up his shirt to show the ivory white revolver at his hip. "I'm carrying. You should be too." "You're not even trying to hide what you are. Why?" You look him up and down, the ridiculous caricature of a man. "You stick out like a sore thumb." He considers you at length. It's a surprisingly canny gaze from someone consuming that much liquor. "Well, son," he says slowly, "this is a war. You best know that by now. And war has rules." He sees your expression. "Oh, sure, folks break 'em. But they're there. Least for a little while. And hell, I'm alive, ain't I?" He grins. "'He clasps the crag with crooked hands, close to the sun in lonely lands, ring'd with the azure world, he stands.'" "What was that?" His face darkens. "That's poetry, fucknuts. Now," he steadies his gaze on you. "In the words of the late great Mr. Seger - Pete, not Bob mind you. I hate that Night Moves shit - Which side are you on?"

AVClub_FirstWatch_Intrigued.strDesc:
"I have to admit," you tell him. "It's pretty cool."

"Yes!" he says. "I knew you'd say that. You have good taste."

AVClub_FirstWatch_Rubbish.strTitle: Say it's a load of rubbish
AVClub_FirstWatch_Rubbish.strDesc:
"What a load of crap," you say flatly. 

Smiley nods, his smile fading to a rare grimace. "Of course, sure," he says. "It's not as if ... no, you're right, of course."

AVClub_FirstWatch_Leave.strDesc: You leave in search of Isambard Cruz.

Isambard_Start.strDesc: This is definitely the address Smiley gave you, a hole in a ship wall with a sturdy door bolted on. Who exactly has he sent you to meet? You hit the buzzer. A moment's pause before a woman's voice replies: "Yes?" Surly, clipped, not entirely hostile. "Smiley sent me," you say, "if that's his name. I found a videotape. You've seen these before?" "Hold it up to the camera." You angle the 'Inhalants' label toward the tiny red bulb. Another moment as your offering is considered by the disembodied woman. The door unlocks with a loud ker-chack!. "Enter."
Isambard_Start.strTooltip: A red light glows, the recording signal of a bespoke security system.

Isambard_InsideShop.strDesc:
Isambard Cruz puts you in mind of a schoolteacher you had on Arithmetic Disk 2. Tall, old, a bit too thin, a speaking voice so soft as to enchant and annoy you. She turns the video tape over in her hands like a fossil. "Yes," she mutters. "I know what this is."

Without breaking concentration, she beckons you closer. She indicates with her pinkie finger. "You know VHS, yes? Here, and here - fake studs. Not real, hah, reel." The homophones bounce off your skull. She looks up and scowls. "Fake."

"Why would someone make a fake video tape?" you ask. 

Cruz snorts. "Earth freaks, fetishists. They love car dice and I<3NY ballcap. They pay for it. Paid for it. Earth's the past. Market's dying." She sniffs again. "Good riddance." She was probably old enough to have come from Earth, you guess. She doesn't miss it.

"So what's on the tape?" You reach for it, but she turns and shuffles deeper into her shop. "I want to play it." You follow her, breathing in a mix of machine oil and incense. You trip over a cat, which hisses at you before returning to its idle animation. When you catch up to her she has the shell open on a workbench. She holds up a segment of tape to a single powerful lightbulb. 

"Is something," she mutters. "Old eyes can't see. You look, come." She bids you take the film. You hold it to your face, turning it this way and that. She continues to herself. "Real tape, magnetic." Chimes sound from the corner, turning in front of a desktop fan. The cat meows. "The fakes have film. Like what you see?"

The image resolves in a rush. A white-gold humanoid, the sarcophagus in miniature. The suggestion is so bracingly evil you lurch as if from an electric shock. Cruz laughs softly. "Yes," she says sadly. "It's never good."

Isambard_InsideShop_1.strDesc:
She collects the offending strip of tape from you and shuffles over to another machine. She click-clacks on its oversized keypad. The machine, a gunmetal gray box with an LED readout canted toward her, whines to life.

She holds up one end of the length of tape to you, as if you have any idea of what she's doing and are keen to follow along, and inserts it into an aperture at the top of the machine. The machine's whine crescendos, and a deeper grinding thrums through the floor. Is she ... destroying it?

She senses your distress. "Digitisation," she says happily, stumbling a little over the English word. With one hand she feeds in the tape, the sound oscillating back and forth. "Cameras, inside," she says, running a pinkie along one edge. "And blades. Film, goes chop-chop-chop-chop poof! All the little pieces, tracked by little lasers. We get perfect copy at the end."

"You can't just photograph it?"

The machine screams. Isambard shakes her head. "That way is not perfect. This way it will live forever in the cloud."

It only takes a minute to digitise the rest. You hold a hand out to the Petware cat. She regards it dutifully. "How old is she?"

"Six months past warranty," says Isambard. "Like me!" And she laughs herself silly.

The machine sounds cease. Just as quickly she's handing you a data card, and inexorably chivvying you out the way you came in.

"Don't you want to see what's on it?" you ask.

"God in Heaven, no," she replies, and shuts the door in your face.

AVClub_The_Return.strDesc:
Smiley flags you down eagerly. "Come in, come in!" he says. "The gang's all here." 

He ushers you inside.
AVClub_The_Return.strTooltip: He's still here. Doesn't he have a job?

Plot_79au_First_Approach.strDesc:
At long last, you approach the location of your many visions.

Before you you see an enormous golden sphere. While it's the size of a large asteroid, you're certain it is not a natural formation. As you stare at the strange object, you find your senses stunned and your reason stupified. Who could have built such a thing? And why?

You find yourself compelled to get closer to the surface of the object. To touch it's surface. But you feel equally a palpable dread, a stupifying fear of the unknown and impossible.

Plot_79au_Spacewalk.strDesc:
You spacewalk to the object, feeling an ever growing sense of terror the closer you get. 

The surface is a gossamer knit weave of golden threads pulled taut and rigid to the touch. Above you is a platform sticking out of the sphere, the only irregularity to the curve of the object. 

You float to it and see a strange interface above the platform. A hexagonal pillar beside a hexagonal hole. You take the pillar from the surface and hold it in your hand.

Plot_79au_Leave.strDesc: Overwhelmed by terror, you decide to leave the strange object. For now.

Plot_79au_Pillar.strDesc:
The golden weave loosens before you and begins to open. The hole before you reveals a bright purple light, and as it grows larger you see there is a shimmering liquid inside of the same color. The opening grows and grows, eventually becomes as large as your ship.

You have a vision of an infinite plane suddenly pockmarked with other purple nodes in a network, of which this is just one. You feel a sublime expansive terror, as if you are an ant on an anthill and the camera zooms out and you realize your world is tiny in comparison.
 
You have a terrrible certainty that suddenly you are being observed by trillions of eyes, and most of them are curious. Many of them are coming. Very soon. Perhaps now.

Plot_79au_Enter.strDesc:
Following a feeling of naive optimism and a willingness to risk one's own life, you enter the sphere. You know that humanity is flawed, failing, but has an ineffable essence that should expand and continue. Going through, even if it kills you personally, is worth it.
 
You find yourself in a bureaucratic metaphysical switchboard  in which you must imagine your ship's essence.

You blink to ... somewhere? Silence. You hear your ship nav pan sound but it is panning like crazy, faster and faster as it scrolls out to your new location, lightyears away.

Plot_79au_Others.strDesc:
Following a perfectly rational pessimism and a drive to protect one's own life, you wait and see who arrives. You're certain Humanity is failing itself. It can no longer be trusted to decide its own fate. Anything coming through must be better than what we got. Let Daddy come home and sort it out for us. 

The Entity comes through and asks you "Are you Merga?" Before you can answer, and without any emotion, The Entity harvests all of humanity in the blink of an eye. You enter a dead system as the only remaining human in the universe.

79AU_Approach20.strDesc:
The Object grows larger in your scope with each passing day.

You find yourself watching it for hours. You studied the readouts, the videos, the decades of identical reports made by astronomers assigned to observe it. Those methods became insufficient. 

The optics suite has an eyepiece which, when you look through it, is as close as possible to the unfiltered image captured in the hull-mounted scopes. You keep your eye fixed to that scope until you fall asleep in your chair, and then you watch it in your dreams.

In moments of lucidity you realise you are losing track of time. When you are not watching the Object, you're tending to the needs of your ship, and those of your own body, in that order. When those are taken care of, you return to the scope. 

A rational part of your brain observes that this is not healthy or safe or particularly sane. Unfortunately, your rational brain is fully on board with the irrational parts of your brain telling you to watch the Object, and these observations are abandoned as quickly as they're made.

It's not like there's anything interesting to watch. From any distance it is the same uniform circle. A child's drawing of a gold coin, or the closed eye of a sleeping dragon. You might as well be watching the O2 light on the NAV console; it's a similarly amber-coloured LED that, should it ever change to red, would convey the information that you are about to die. That would be something.

But you return to your position at the scope; what is interesting for you and what is not has become irrelevant.

79AU_Approach40.strDesc:
A revelation! You're no longer confined to your seat at the scope. This is because the image of the Object at 79AU has burned into your retina. That's your best explanation for how you can always see it, even while you're doing inconsequential things like eating or going to the toilet. 

This has freed up your hours aboard the ship, and in the nick of time too, for several runaway processes were leading to a total breakdown, both in the ship's systems and your own. You're able to put most of them to rights.

You try to get a few hours a day at the scope to keep your hand in, but that's only because you're an overachiever.

Your ship has pushed deep into the Kuiper Belt. You receive mail from the scant human souls who've ventured out here. It's mostly friendly, but it dries up once word gets around that you don't reply. Afterwards you get the occasional ping curious about what you're doing, or where you're headed, or sad to see you go. You get a heartfelt message from, if the header is to be believed, the only Trans-Neptunian psychiatrist.

You try to write back about the Object that has eclipsed your vision, but as you put metaphorical pen to paper, it all falls apart. Reading your drafts back, it's as if another writer has surreptitiously accessed the document and muddled your thoughts. You can't include any of it in a reply. You'd look insane.

79AU_Basement6.strDesc:
"Joakim said you have terrestrial emanations here," you say.

"Yes."

"You're taking me to see them?"

"Yes," she says. "One."

"What is it?"

"We don't know," she says. It's perhaps the first time she’s revealed vulnerability. "That is probably why Joakim mentioned it."

79AU_Basement7.strDesc:
Ariel stops the car at a door the same as any other. She takes a moment to stretch her legs. You decide it's not worth the hassle to do so yourself. "Refreshments?" she asks. She reaches in to open a glove compartment, which is full of energy bars and DND Cola.

You take an energy bar and a drink. Whatever the extraordinary features of 79 AU, it must not keep you fed and watered, or why would they offer? Start the countdown to needing an alien restroom. She pockets an energy bar for herself, and lights up another cigarette.

When the break is over, she walks to the door and repeats the opening process. The doors slide apart. Immediately on the other side, there's a transparent divider. You can only tell it's there because you're reflected in it. Through the glass, darkly, there is nothing.

You look at her, wondering what it is you're supposed to see.

79AU_Basement8.strDesc:
"Can't see anything?" she asks.

You shake your head. "They like to shroud the cell in darkness," she says. "A simple defensive involution protocol. It doesn't know where it is, or what's happening to it. The one-way manifold doesn't exist in there." She raps her knuckles on the glass, which you suppose is not glass at all. "Okay. We've humoured it long enough." 

She fishes some packages from a pocket on her coveralls. She rips one open and hands it to you. Inside is a disposable pair of glasses. She rips open the other and puts another pair on.

She taps the rim of her glasses to demonstrate. "Cycle the scanner. Set it to gamma."

You put the glasses on and tap the rim. Your vision is overlaid with familiar blue-cold/red-hot blobs of infrared. The space beyond the glass is blue, or empty - take your pick. You glance at Ariel experimentally, but if she's anything other than human, it's not apparent. Her yellow-hot face tilts at you. You hurriedly tap the glasses and cycle through the spectrum.

Passing out one side of radio and arriving back at gamma, there's a change in the room beyond the wall. In its centre there is a faint humanoid outline in white. Within the outline is a white blob which might describe a face. The centre of its chest is a luminous purple. Emerging from the outline is a prickly white aura, stabbing at the darkness around it, peaking and receding like an audio waveform.

"I see it," you say. Your mouth is suddenly dry.

"Good," she says approvingly. "What is it?"

79AU_Basement9.strDesc:
"I have no idea," you say.

"You've never seen one of these before? Or heard about them? No records of it in media, traditional or modern?" You shake your head at each question. "Yeah. That's where I had my money." You open your mouth. "Figure of speech." You shut it.

You take off the glasses. The entity's silhouette is not a calming presence. 

Ariel takes a long drag on her cigarette. "This was a bust, then."

79AU_Basement10.strTitle: What do you know about it?
79AU_Basement10.strDesc:
"What do you know about it?" you ask.

"Not a whole lot," she says. "We can't get close. It has supernatural capabilities, which as best we can tell, it vastly overestimates. Catching them and overpowering them is trivial." A grim smile plays at the edge of her mouth. "They all operate from the same playbook, which was as outdated on First Contact as it is today."

"And it came from Earth?" you ask.

She tilts her head noncommittally. "Tracing the signal is a dead end, but all the dead ends are on Earth. Besides, it's shaped just like you." She looks at her body. "And currently, me. We put two and two together."

79AU_Basement11.strTitle: Why can't you get close to it?
79AU_Basement11.strDesc:
"You can't get close to it?" you ask. Feeling particularly out of the loop, you point at the glass. "It's right there."

"Silly me," says Ariel. "We never thought to walk up and shake its hand. No, it doesn't want anything to do with us. We tried contact you would find conventional, and we tried ways you would find unpleasant. Sincere attempts to forge a bridge between worlds. All were rejected. The instant we get past defenses they consider vital, we hit a dead man's switch, and we're talking to the void."

She puts her hands on her hips, ash flaking off the end of her cigarette. "Embarrassing. It kept happening. We had no idea what we were doing wrong. We were forced to conclude their kind is fundamentally antisocial, paranoid, and arrogant. We had no choice but to shove them in storage."

79AU_Basement12.strDesc:
"Joakim said you had hundreds of this thing. Whatever it is."

"He did, and we do," she says. She takes a contemplative drag on the cigarette, sizing up her opponent. "Going back a bit, when 79 AU arrived they swarmed us. A hail of arrows from the undergrowth met by sixteen-inch guns. I took no pleasure in it." The cigarette coal flares. A trail of smoke streams from her nostrils. "Since then we'll get one every few years testing our defences. They're all here. Every single one. Alive and unharmed, assuming they entered that way."

"Joakim said they were 'free to a good home'." An unpleasant thought, the kind of place this being would consider a good home.

"We don't want them," says Ariel. "Storage is unlimited, our patience is not."

79AU_Ose5.strDesc:
"Of course!" Ose says, and rises to his feet. "Where are my manners?"

Several bottles sit atop a mirrored sideboard between the bookshelf and a large, curtained window. Ose busies himself there as he continues speaking.

"I've never been good at these," he says. "First Contacts. I always find myself bored by the big picture and respond by fixating on the tiniest of details. Here."

He passes you a brown spirit in a short glass tumbler with a single ice cube. 

You take a drink, confirming your suspicion. Whiskey. Real whiskey, even.   

"Crown something, according to the label," Ose observes. "And I'll admit to having never tasted anything like it. Cheers," he says, and raises his glass before sitting down again.

79AU_Ose6.strDesc:
"Beautiful, isn't it?" Ose says. "Our host presented a range of options. Eras, styles, motifs. Mid century modern leaped out. 20th Century, I should say. Well before our time. What did you think of our host?"

"Joakim? He was...accomodating."

"Yes. That part doesn't change. An entire species whose sole purpose is just that: obsequious accommodation. Rather pitiful."

79AU_Ose7.strDesc:
"I didn't, I'm ashamed to say. I was following someone else. The much-too-free spirits in Room 103. We don't get along, but they have a knack for turning up new friends that I find useful. They keep wondering why I show up when they do. I'm beginning to wonder whether they have the capacity to realize I've been doing it on purpose."

"How did they find us?"

"You'd have to ask them. As far as I can tell they just like to wander."

79AU_Ose8.strDesc:
"It's more about what you want, I'm afraid," Ose says, then looks at his nails. They're perfectly manicured, and filed nearly to a point.

"How so?"

"How to put this? You are the first. The vanguard. More of an outrider, really, to preserve the metaphor."

"The first to do what?"

"To come here. To meet another. The Great Cosmic Handshake. We all had one, otherwise we wouldn't be here."

"Did you have one?"

"No, no ..." He waves the question away and takes a delicate sip of his drink. "That was eons ago. You're early to the party, relatively speaking. Must be that special human ambition I've been reading about."

"What does it mean to be first?"

"Ah. That's a privilege, isn't it." Ose leans forward, points a long finger at you. "It means you, my friend, are temporarily in possession of a heretofore hidden knowledge. You and you alone. I'm jealous, really. Discovering such knowledge is the sole purpose of my kind."

"Why?"

Ose stands up and indulges in a long, languid stretch before walking to the bookshelf. He runs a finger along the spines of the volumes there.

"Suppose we return to all those kings for a moment."

"Do we have to?"

"It appears to be your highest aim. Power over others. But in all those stories, can you recall even one happy king?"

You think for a moment.

"What I...what we offer isn't power over others. Such power is a trap, in the best of cases. We offer power over the self. No, that's not right. Still feels hierarchical. Even your language is bound by ideologies of domination. We offer power from the self. A kind of...congruency. Within, but gained from without."

79AU_Ose9.strDesc: Ose lets out a frustrated sigh. "If you're asking after my shape, this might help." Ose scans the books and pulls a decaying tome from among them. He tosses it over to you. It lands in your lap with a painful thud. "The ... I can't pronounce this," you stammer. "Pseudomonarchia Daemonum," Ose says. "Not a fan of 16th Century grimoires I see. Neither was I, until I got here. I didn't choose my shape any more than you did. You'd do well to keep that in mind."

79AU_Ose10.strTitle: You didn't answer my question. What do you want?
79AU_Ose10.strDesc:
"I want you to stop pretending. Pretending that you're some hapless bystander on the banks of time, watching as the currents pass you by. I'd like you to step into the river."

"Is that what you did?" you ask.

"Of course! Did, and do. It's the only true safety. You'll hear plenty of complaints about our kind, but nobody can say we aren't the agents of our own fortune."

"So that's what you're offering? Safety."

"It's the only promise I'll make."

79AU_Elevator2.strDesc:
The elevator readmits you, the chair jolting uncomfortably as you cross the gap.

You have perfect recall of Joakim's information. Where do you want to go?

79AU_Ose11.strDesc:
"This has been ... edifying," you say. You begin to wheel your chair towards the door.

"So soon?" Ose asks. "We were just beginning to come to an understanding."

You're not so sure about that.

"I'm not so sure about that," you say. "But I appreciate the hospitality."

Ose offers no reply. Just a long stare through narrowed eyes as you exit the apartment and wheel yourself back to the elevator.

As the platform climbs to your floor, you think back to what President Ose was trying to tell you. Despite the chasms of misunderstanding, the conversation carried with it a vapor of significance that is already evaporating. You have the feeling that you'd better grasp it quickly, because soon it will be gone forever.

AVClub_The_Return_VentEscape2.strDesc:
After an indeterminate length of crawling, you hear a dreaded noise that wakes you from the monotony.

Down the length of shaft behind you, a horrible whining. "Wasps," you mutter, nonplussed. "Wasps!" you yell again to those ahead of you, and you push heavily on their boots.

"Wasps, wasps!" shout those in front, taking up the cry, and suddenly silence is forgotten, you're racing hand over hand as fast as you can.

There's little use. The first bogey zips past you, seeking the head of your formation. You catch a glimpse of it, an evil little bug with a needle-fine proboscis. The latest in AyoSec's compliance toolkit.

The air wing descends upon you, an uncountable number in the swarm. You writhe, desperately shucking off the needles burrowing into your clothes and skin. The first needle to find purchase slides into your left shoulder blade. A horrible pinprick of pain; an ocean of blissful numbing calm overwhelms your body. The wasp falls from your back, dead, its payload delivered.

In eerie unison the swarm moves past you, seeking their next victim, but it's a bad stick, too close to the bone. You can still move. Groggy, you watch as the woman in front of you is stung, and goes limp.

AVClub_The_Return_VentEscape_Help.strDesc:
The simplicity of your objectives has you locked in. Each step arrives to you as a lucid, concrete action, activating a survival routine your mushy consciousness never fully knows. Push feet aside. Wriggle until parallel. Hook arm under arm. Use other arm to pull. Use pulling arm to try to prevent crash. Crash anyway. Recover, barely. Repeat.

Memory ceases recording. The body remains in motion. A kaleidoscope of vents and fans and bodies splits and reforms.

The blackwhite orb from Videotape 3 takes up residence inside your eyelids, surfing along novel circuitries of serotonin. "Come to me," it says. The girl goes inside the sarcophagus. Voices join in sweet harmony. "Come to me."

"I said I would," you mutter. You feel your hands waving, trying to swim. "You don't have to repeat it."

"I'll see you soon," it says.

AVClub_The_Return_WakeUpSafehouse.strDesc:
"I can't move," you say. Your eyes are closed.

"You're strapped to the wall," says a man's voice, "because you're still asleep."

With effort, you open your eyes.

You're in a sleeping strap on the wall of a hard plastic blister. Half a dozen people are with you in the tiny space, trying to stick to its surfaces; to either side, sleepers are strapped against the wall - including the woman you saved. You rest your head. Your heart swells.

AVClub_The_Return_WakeUpSafehouse_Leave.strDesc:
You pass in and out of sleep. The other occupants of the safehouse are less agitated each time you wake, and the sounds from the rest of Flotilla less distressing. In time, you regain most of your motor functions. Soon enough, you're able to leave the safehouse in ones and twos.

You leave with the woman you saved - Molly Oladele, whom the AV Club had dubbed Molly Two. You rejoin the flow of foot traffic on Flotilla. It's depressed, deflated; emergency crews are at work on every other bulkhead, and battered-looking people wander aimlessly or weep in the corridors.

The time comes for you to part ways, you to your ship, she to a shift on station. An uncomfortable frisson passes between you. "Thank you," she says at last, "for what you did."

You demur as best you can. She ignores your words. "I've been having dreams. All this will come to an end."

She looks in your eyes, suddenly intense. "Spend your final days wisely. Make them count."

You have to bite your tongue as she, having said this, leaves for work.

AVClub_FirstWatch_Extras.strTitle: Ask to hear Smiley's Extras commentary
AVClub_FirstWatch_Extras.strDesc:
Smiley eagerly runs the video back and begins pointing out every detail to his knowledge, along with a few guesses masquerading as knowledge.

"We've tried tracking down where we are, to start with," he says, gesturing to the asteroid and its starfield. "Molly 2 spent weeks trying to triangulate the co-ordinates from the constellations and the angle of the sun. I think it drove her a little bit mad."

"What did she learn?"

Smiley snorts. "That it was somewhere in the Belt," he says. "Fat lot of good that did us. We had better luck with the grapple rigs. They're rare enough that there's only a couple of Belter communities that use them, in a couple of asteroid groups, since their heyday in the colony rush. Of course, if it was filmed then, which we don't know, then we're back to square one."

"What will you do if you find it?" you ask. "Go there?"

Smiley laughs, but the mirth fades quickly. "Nah. We're stuck here."

AVClub_FirstWatch_Extras_FF.strDesc:
Smiley skips through until the university advertisement. "Okay, now this, this is Voltaire University, right? On Luna. That's Earth up there," he says.

"There it is," you agree.

"So with this part, what's crazy is, there is no such ad, officially," he says. "I did the legwork myself. Kinda went nuts calling around everyone I could who'd answer a message on Luna, asking to dig through archives and so on. I watched a lot of ads, looking for this." Something in his tone tells you, it was hundreds and hundreds of hours of media.

"So it's a fake ad?"

Smiley chews some popcorn thoughtfully. "Dunno. There's a small holy war in the club over whether this part's AI or not. It's an offshoot from the main war over whether all the tapes are AI or not."

A total quagmire, then. You study the CEO's frozen smile, and compare it with Smiley's. Perhaps there's kinship there. "You seem to have an opinion on it," you say.

"Oh yeah," he says readily. "I know it's not AI, because it's not trying to sell me something."

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strTitle: Ask What In God's Name He Is Talking About
PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strDesc:
"Moles, fucknuts! Xinhua rats. Place is lousy with 'em. Sometimes we scare 'em up hackin and other times, well. Measures more drastic, if you get my meaning."

"Now here's how you suss 'em out," Wayne leans in so close you can smell the Bismertnaya on his breath. "They train em up good back on Mars. Computer shit, like I said, but fightin' too. Hand to hand, real close quarters. They like to get in and out unseen, so keep an eye out for the sneaky ones. They're cruel little bastards, but they aren't dumb. Most of em are a hell of a lot smarter than me, and that's sayin' something."

"Anyway," he says. "You meet someone like that, more than likely that's our mole. Drop your half of the Xinhua code phrase and if they know the rest, well? That would mean somethin', wouldn't it?"

"Lemme ask you: Where is true west?"

"Depends where you're standing," you respond.

"Nope. Where is true west?" he asks again.

You hesitate to answer.

"Personally, I'd say to follow the evening redness. But that's just me," Wayne says, and gives you a wink.

"So, the dead drop," Wayne continues. "You know the embassy on this station? There's a ship and home kiosks next door with a planter in the corner. Ficus or some shit. If you really want to show loyalty to God's Great GalCon, rummage around in there, sneaky beaky like. Had to move that thing like ten times last month and honestly I'm gettin' a little tired of it."

Wayne leans back, tips his cap and holds up two more fingers. "Shot for the road?"

He drains the little cup like he's done it a million times before. You eye your own drink with obvious suspicion, given the circumstances. 

"More for me then, I guess," he says, and drinks your glass down before sauntering out of the bar without paying.

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Discuss_Tradecraf.strDesc:
Pan Tao rolls his eyes at your approach, then lights a new cigarette using his first. "How'd that go?" he asks without looking at you.

"About as well as you'd expect," you reply.

Pan Tao frowns and nods. "Yeah," he says. "Wayne loves his little 'aw-shucks' hayseed act. Don't let it fool you. Guy probably has eyes on us right now."  

Less attitude than before, at least. Helpful, even.

"If there even is one," Pan says. "Rumors, hearsay. Every drunk on this rock has a story. I've damn near lost track."

"Tell me one," you say.

"Well. Couple days ago an atmo system near residential hit the fritz, right? Not so abnormal at first. The station is a shithole. But then, all the way across the rock, another one went down. Then another. You see where this is going."

"Not a coincidence," you reply.

"Could be! That's the rub. Look, if there's really a Xinhua rat this deep in our network, they'd be smart. Very smart. A skilled enough hacker to do that and more. They'd know how to talk, too. Good with oligarchs, good with the military brass. A real 'friend to all' type. Otherwise, how would they get access to intel?"

Useful. "Any other advice?" you ask.

"Shit," he says. "We didn't even have this conversation."
"A fellow painter I see," Pan says. "I'll tell you what I tell everyone: start with the exit plan. Things always go down faster than you think. Once the deed is done, I mean."
"Not my area," Pan says. "I'm more of a hands-on kinda guy."

ENCFirstDockBCRSHmm.strDesc:
"Sorry, can we run this back?" you say. Something is bothering you. Something niggling at the edge of memory and time.

"Mm? To what, or where, my friend?" She smiles.

"It was something you said before," you say. She's playing with her necklace again. The glassy pearls sliding along the string, clinking softly as they rub against their mates.

What was it she said? Something about Calico City. "I'm sorry," you say, blinking. "It's not coming to me, whatever it is."

"That's perfectly alright."

ENCFirstDockBCRSHmm1.strDesc:
"Have we met before?" you ask her suddenly. You don't think you have - it's a sensation, an impression, rather than a recollection. Perhaps you've met her sister. "Have you ever been to K-Leg?"

"Oh, certainly not," she says. "I've been there once or twice, but I would remember if we had crossed paths."

"That makes sense," you say. "Yeah. Forget I asked."

79AU_Inside17.strTitle: Can you tell me the other thing you said?

79AU_Inside18.strDesc:
"What?"

"I offered you two perfectly good options there," Joakim says, "and you went with 'what?'"

"Um," you say. "Yes." That is, after all, what happened.

"Then I'm going to give you some free advice," he continues. "You'll get exactly what you ask for. If you ask for nothing, you'll get nothing."

"Can I choose one of them now," you ask hopefully, "'exhibit' or whatever?"

"No," he says.

79AU_Elevator1.strDesc:
The elevator admits you, the chair jolting uncomfortably as you cross the gap.

You have perfect recall of Joakim's information. Where do you want to go?

79AU_WakeUp.strDesc:
Smooth as anaesthetic wearing off, the next thing you're aware of is you, lying in a bed.

You awaken slowly, wrapped in soft cotton. A machine beeps to let you know you're alright.

You're in a medical bed surrounded by diagnostic equipment. You are not, however, in a hospital ward. The bed and equipment - you look around slowly, serenely - are in a hotel lobby. It's functional, modern, glass and marble, neutral colours, a transitional style.

At the far end of the lobby, lifts travel up and down a transparent shaft. Closer, doors lead from the lobby to adjoining wings. The one with signage near enough to read, written across an arch above the door, says 'Pool'.

Much closer is the front desk. A man stands at ease behind it. He returns your gaze, but gives no other acknowledgement.

79AU_Boheme1.strDesc: You hear the music before the elevator has even reached the first floor. When the doors part you're hit by a wall of sound, and sympathetic vibrations rattle the chair. You wheel through the hall past empty rooms to 103. Even if it were unlabeled, and it isn't, the door rattling in its frame is a dead giveaway that somebody is home. Uncertain how a knock could be heard, no alternatives spring to mind, so you knock. The music turns down sharply, then sharply again, as someone hurriedly turns a volume knob. You hear whispers. Then a bright voice, a man's: "Come in!" You hesitate. Women's voices harmonise in a major third: "It's open!" You push the door open.

79AU_Boheme2.strDesc:
A generous soul would call the room bohemian. A miserly soul would call it a mess.

In the centre stand a group of black megaliths, which at second glance are hi-fi speakers. Piled around them is dilapidated furniture, low-slung couches and divans, and cushions on the lam. Piled on top of all that is a sedimentary layer of takeout food containers, empty record sleeves, and paperback novels. 

The room has a pungent, verdant aroma. It's not unpleasant, but it is impossible to ignore.

The occupants leap up, excited to see you. "Come in, come in!" they cry. "Do you want something to eat? Drink? Cool cast, man!"

They seem human. Sanguine, a tall thin man with a sensitive face and a pencil moustache, got first billing from Joakim, but seems not to talk so much. Most of the talking is done by Emerald, an intense woman with an unambiguous colour scheme. Fire, wearing red, wanders over to a divan and lays down, and says little after that. "She smoked too much," says Emerald. "Don't worry about her."

"We're so happy to meet a human in the flesh!" she continues. "Are you from Earth? Who's your favourite Beatle?"

"Let them breathe, Em," says Sanguine. He's wearing a powder blue suit. "Humans need to breathe."

"I'm not from Earth," you say. "I'm from Ganymed Ten Thirty Six."

"Oh," she says. "Is that near Earth?"

"Sometimes," you say.

"Cool," she says, derailed. "... anyway we love Earth music! We loved your record. Amazing stuff on there. All over the place conceptually, but it put us on to some of your less mainstream artists, and then we got it!"

"Record?" you say. "What record?"

"The Golden Record," she says, as if it's crazy you've never heard of it. "By Voyager 1."

79AU_Boheme3.strDesc:
"You're aliens," you say.

"That's right," says Emerald.

You're unable to be amazed. The closest you can get is credulous. "What is an alien?"

"It's often hard to say," says Sanguine. "In the interstellar, it helps to have an open mind."

"You three," you say. "Are you a race, a species, a society? How many of you are there? Is everyone at the hotel one of you?"

"Steady on!" says Emerald. "Yes, yes, it's complicated, we don't know, and no. What Sanguine means is, set aside assumptions. In your planetary system, physical feedback loops developed into an individualistic spacefaring society. You're relatively rare! You shouldn't expect to meet, oh," she casts around, looking to Sanguine for support, "bipedal humanoids much like yourself with just a few cardinal differences."

"Which isn't to say those don't exist," says Sanguine. "But subluminals tend to stick to their own, um," he says. "Context? Birthright?"

"Homeworld," moans Fire.

"You know that's not right," says Emerald crossly. "You're only going to confuse the poor thing."

"It's good enough for now," says Fire, and rolls over so her back is to the rest of you.

79AU_Boheme4.strDesc:
"If you had to pick one or two differences to distinguish you from me," you say, "what would they be?"

"Oh, very well," says Emerald. "You take this one. I'm going to fix us drinks."

Sanguine cocks his head, and leads you to one edge of the room, where tall glass doors open onto a balcony. Beyond the balcony is empty space, and the Milky Way. You roll outside cautiously.

"Let's get some air," he says. It's a joke about the vacuum, which you find breathable. "We need clear heads. If you were desperate to label us, you could call us Aesthetes. Do you know what teleology is?"

You shake your head. "It's a Greek word," he says, "for investigating the purposes of things. A useful concept. We search for experiences, for novelty. That's who we are and what we do. When we heard Voyager 1, it was a glorious day. There's a whole galaxy out there aching to hear that quintessentially human sound, you dig?"

Plot_Ceres_Clandestine_Interventions_Xin.strDesc: [us] [seems] confused by the question and [offers] a confused answer.

Plot_Ceres_Clandestine_Interventions_Dea.strDesc: [us] [looks] beneath a discarded coffee pouch near [them] to find a data card and a small tablet.
Plot_Ceres_Clandestine_Interventions_Dea.strTooltip: Look for instructions hidden at this kiosk.

Plot_Ceres_Clandestine_Interventions_Dea.strDesc:
Stuffed beneath the coffee kiosk you find a discarded drink pouch, just as your contact indicated. Inside there are two folded up napkins. Finding a quiet corner of the station, you unwrap the first. It is a small data card. 

You slot the card and set it to Ears Only. Your PDA flashes through an authentication process so swift you almost miss the output.

"Good morning, comrade. Health and prosperity to you." A smooth synthetic voice speaks to your inner ear. Ring station spacers pass around you none the wiser. 

"Parameters: target is an unknown Ceresian citizen working on behalf of the Galilean Counter Revolutionary Commission, also known as 'Cyanide Street', in and around Port Mojave, Ceres. In addition to being suspected of sharing valuable Xinhua intel with GalCon loyalists, the target is believed to be a former human trafficker guilty of crimes against humanity during the Galilean unrest.

"Target can be located via blackhat network infiltration or neutralized via executive action depending on the agent's skills and discretion."

The synthetic voice continues.

"Retrieve the lethality kit included in this package and hide it on your person. It is one half of an instantly toxic nerve agent. Another cell will identify and apply the first component of the nerve agent. It is your task to identify the target and apply the otherwise non-lethal second.

"To ensure accurate executive action, target must first be identified using a recently acquired Tinitian code phrase. The target will respond to the Titanian codephrase, 'Where is true west?'" The voice repeats the phrase twice more. "Their response will be, 'Follow the evening redness.'

"Past Titan agent profiles indicate the target will likely have skills in engineering and various forms of trained subterfuge and persuasion. Psychological evaluations suggest GalCon intelligence seeks out strong willed, dishonest, but otherwise gregarious personality types.

"With the target so identified, crush the included blister between your teeth and breathe. The nerve agent will strike them dead immediately. Exfil rapidly and as you see fit.

"Upon mission success, leave an after action report at the dead drop."

WIP: Writing assumed the target was on Ceres, not Ring Station: You slot the card and set it to Ears Only. Your PDA flashes through an authentication process so swift you almost miss the output. "Good morning, comrade. Health and prosperity to you." A smooth synthetic voice speaks to your inner ear. The Ceresians pass around you none the wiser. "Retrieve also the lethality kit and hide it on your person. It is one half of an instantly toxic nerve agent." "Parameters: target is an unknown Ceresian citizen working on behalf of the Galilean Counter Revolutionary Commission, also known as 'Cyanide Street', in and around Port Mojave, Ceres. Another cell will identify and apply the first component of the nerve agent. It is your task to identify the target and apply the second." You watch a Public Security Officer in hi-viz clothes upbraid a coverall-clad citizen for spilling liquor on the edge of the tram station. The man begs on his knees for forgiveness. The other Ceresians avert their eyes, pretending not to see. "The target will respond to the Titanian codephrase, 'It was a bright, cold day in April'." The voice repeats the phrase twice more. "Their response will be, 'and the clocks were striking thirteen.' So identified, crush the blister between your teeth and breathe. The nerve agent will strike them dead immediately. Exfil as you see fit." "Motivation: The target is a human trafficker guilty of crimes against humanity during the Galilean unrest. Payment: Standard third party wetwork contract." "Addendum: substrate will reset to factory default in fifteen seconds. You may keep the blank card. Message ends." You roll your eyes and disconnect the card.
You deny the Wet Work mission. For now.

ChoongInformWarDemandExplanationEnd_1.strDesc:
"And then?"

"The wartime footing will never be relaxed, even without an opponent," he says, rubbing his temple. "Nor will the rationing. They will try to redirect public attention to the vanishing remnants of the loser, but we would expect central authority to degrade further. No matter how repressive a ruler gets, they cannot control a starving populace."

ChoongInformWarDemandExplanationEnd_1_1.strDesc:
"And then?"

"Solar trade, already disrupted by the war, will cease, and the tenuous cultural identities of the United States and/or Xinhua will dissolve completely, replaced by frightened regional authorities. A bit like K-LEG," he adds. "Everywhere will become K-LEG. A tiny fiefdom ruled by a despot."

ChoongInformWarDemandExplanationEnd_1_1_.strDesc:
"And then?"

"And then we starve," he says. "One by one, our little lights in the darkness will flicker out."

ChoongPleaWar.strDesc:
"There must be something we can do," you say. "That someone can do. Things can't end."

"You pretend that they won't," Choong says, false and bright. "And do what you were going to do anyway. After all, human civilisation has never ended before. It's crazy to think that it would now."

"That's it?" you say incredulously. "Embrace fatalism?"

"I did my best to move the social needle," he says. "Look what happened to me."

ChoongSarcophagus.strDesc:
"The golden sarcophagus," you say. "What was it?"

"A human effigy," he says, warming to the subject. "Their idol, an object of worship."

"And a mode of transport."

"I doubt we'll ever see its like in a secondhand dealership," he says drily, "but yes. That also."

ChoongSarcophagus2.strDesc:
"Where did it come from?" you ask eagerly. "They didn't find it buried in an asteroid too, did they?"

"I expect, given the negative phrasing, you thought I'd make fun of you for proposing something so absurd," he says.

"It crossed my mind."

"Well, I apologise for giving you that impression," he says with sincerity. "I think it's a very good question, with a complicated answer."

"So ... did they?"

"No. They made it themselves." He smiles, enjoying some private joke. "But after what I've told you about the hallucinogenic substance, it's not so unreasonable to imagine aliens secreting mystical artefacts across our solar system. Perhaps on Earth, too, at Giza, or Palenque."

You fight back a sigh. "Does it get more complicated than that?"

"Yes, it does," he continues. "I believe the idea for the sarcophagus was conceived through that shared hallucination. They built it, yes, but it was a colossal undertaking, not the whim of one leader or priest, and certainly not the product of one man's labour."

"A fab on Titan or Mars could spin that up in a day or two," you say, on solid ground for once. "And most of that time budget would be spent in CAD."

"A valid argument, but not sound," he says, and he's terribly happy to say it. "You're missing something. The entire piece was gold."

ChoongSarcophagusGold.strDesc:
"Gold gold?"

"Gold gold," he confirms. "Elemental gold."

Three thousand years ago, that was an irresponsible allocation of resources. It still is today. "Why?"

"I have no idea!" He's overjoyed with the mystery. "It's something I've always wondered about. It took them months to find a sufficiently rich asteroid, explore it, and extract what they needed, all the while continuing to meet obligations to their creditors. The project might have bankrupted them, especially without a return."

It was always natural to assume it simply had a gold exterior, not that it was totally composed of the metal. "It was their vessel for teleportation," you say. "Perhaps that was why."

"I'm a layman metallurgist," he says, "but I'm certain that gold alone doesn't confer the power of teleportation."

ChoongAskAboutGod.strTitle: Ask if the Colchian God is an extraterrestrial
ChoongAskAboutGod.strDesc:
"Do you think it's aliens, then?" No point beating around the bush. "Instead of secreting artefacts throughout the system, they secreted their magic rock around the place. Same difference."

Choong leans back in his chair, and stares at the ceiling. He interlocks his fingers, and for a moment, says nothing, deep in thought. "... Dr. Choong?" you ask, after a while.

"Sorry," he says, blinking and returning to the present. "It's a question I've turned over in my mind for a long time. Decades. My considered opinion: ascribing extraterrestrial means to the New Colchians' actions does go a long way to explaining how unlikely they are, but, well," he sticks a finger in his ear, somehow contriving it to be thoughtful. "I think it merely kicks the can down the road."

"Meaning?"

"It delays real answers."

"Right."

79AU_Boheme13.strDesc: You go to the record player and remove the disc from its spindle, replacing it with the one bearing your name and face. The conversation peters out. You replace the tonearm. It settles into the groove. "Hello again, [us-firstname]. You remember me: Isambard Cruz. Happy to find you with friends of mine. You are safe but not long now. I hope Ben is alright. Too much happening, too fast." "79 AU called for a long time. At last someone answer. You. Hoped not for your sake, hoped yes for mine." "Earth doomed itself. Nothing we can do there. Can save Earth's children. Speak for us. Someone must." "Time of false-facing will pass. When there are no barriers, we rejoin our shadows. Another night. Another day." She coughs. It's wet, not the cough of a healthy person. "The cloud is humming. I hear it. Hope you hear it too." "Take care of yourself, [us-firstname]. Make sure you eat properly." It ends in pops and crackles of dead air.

79AU_Boheme14.strDesc:
Like all experienced partiers, the Aesthetes know to leave while the going is good.

You find yourself at the door, hovering on the threshold, as you all say your goodbyes. "This was fun," says Sanguine. "You're welcome any time."

"Don't be a stranger!" says Emerald.

"In fact hold on," says Sanguine, and disappears for a moment. He returns with one of the pizza boxes so crammed full of leftovers that the lid can't close. "Someone needs to eat these. Please take it. You'd be doing us a favour."

You refuse as graciously as possible, and then it's a short roll to the elevator.

Who are we, in these interstitial moments, between the closing of a door and a solitary journey back the way we came? They don't stick in memory. Before the return of our self-regard, when the party's concluded, it's as if we don't exist.

79AU_Basement1.strDesc:
What was it Joakim said? The "basement" is full of "terrestrial emanations". It seems like something you should investigate. After all, you're terrestrial.

The elevator shaft descends into an environment that, as you scope it through the glass panes, you're immediately familiar with: it shares the mien of every hold, bay, storage compartment - generally any place for dumping stuff you don't want - that you've ever visited, used, or at some stage lived in. They don't build basements in space, but they're there in spirit.

Its surfaces are smooth concrete. Set into the walls are wide metal doors with a diagonal seam, a combination digital and mechanical lock in their centre.

The elevator descends into a corridor junction that seems to go on forever. Far as the eye can see, there is concrete and doors, doors and concrete.

79AU_Basement2.strDesc:
You roll yourself out of the elevator before you notice someone lounging against the call button, a human woman in navy blue coveralls. A lit cigarette dangles from her fingers.

"Hello?" you ask. "I'm here about the ... Joakim sent me."

"He did, did he," she says. She has clipped hair and, somehow, a clipped expression. "Joakim doesn't do anything. None of the staff do."
