"Okay, he didn't send me, exactly," you admit. "He listed places I could go and the basement was one of them." You wonder whether you've misunderstood. "If I'm not supposed to be here -"

"You can be here," she says. She runs a hand across her head. "That's why I've come. Do exactly what I tell you. I represent the warden, and if you break its rules, you'll regret it."

79AU_Basement3.strDesc:
Rules. Good. About time this place had some rules. You voice that thought aloud, and she doesn't laugh. Ah, well. "Come on," she says. She punches a button sequence on a door keypad, then casually shoves the wheel in the centre of the lock. It spins easily out to its fullest extent, and the doors draw back, long diagonal partitions sliding left and right.

Inside is a motor pool, with four conical ground cars in various states of maintenance. She goes to the most roadworthy one and, reaching inside the cockpit, heaves, so that it slowly rolls into the corridor while she walks alongside. When it's outside the motor pool she reaches in and engages the brake.

It's a deeply unimpressive vehicle. It has no paint job, unless that paint was an uneven grey. Once she has helped you out of your chair and into the back seat, she presses the accelerator, revealing the car is not particularly fast either. The alien designers must have carefully weighed both form and function, and decided to put both last.

"What happened to the leg?" she asks.

"I drove my spaceship into it," you say.

"Ah," she says.

You putter along in this crappy vehicle with some time to kill.

79AU_Basement4.strDesc:
"The warden runs a tight ship, huh," you say.

"Believe it," she says, watching the speedometer, which doesn't change.

"If you wouldn't mind telling me those rules?"

"I was going to," she says. "There's no gotchas. Number one, don't talk to anything in a cell. No communication of any kind. Number two, don't disturb the panopticon. Number one is a subset of two. Number three, remain under my supervision at all times."

"What happens if I break one?"

"You get a cell in the panopticon."

79AU_Basement5.strDesc:
The car travels at a perfectly fixed speed, and the shift between wall and door and wall and door grows faintly revolting. You focus instead on the woman in dark blue, who despite paying you no mind is easier on the eyes.

"You work for the warden?"

"I am the warden," she says. 

"You said something different before," you say.

"I did. That doesn't mean I work for it."

"'It' meaning 'you'.".

"Find someone else to clarify how it works," she says without heat. "My job is to interface with you because the warden can't."

"I only asked to make conversation," you say. "Do you have a name?"

She looks back at you, a lingering and uncomfortably penetrating stare. "You may call me Ariel," she says at last, and refocuses on the road ahead so that it does not invite a follow up.

79AU_Inside10.strDesc: "What is my purpose here?" you ask. "It's up to you," he says. "What is?" "Everything." "Everything is up to me?" you repeat slowly. "Or ... everything is up to me?" Joakim smiles warmly. "I will carefully misuse human analogies and idioms," he says. His eyebrows go up and down. "A superficial human seeming with the suggestion much more mysterious. You may appreciate the full weight of implication." Never has someone been so up front while indicating the reverse. "Okay." "In the here-and-now, avail yourself of the facilities. Take a well-earned break. Mingle with the other guests." "Other guests?" "The other guests," Joakim repeats. "I can enumerate them for you."

79AU_Inside11.strDesc:
Joakim ticks off an item, beginning with his ring finger. "In room 103, we have Sanguine and his backing vocalists, Emerald and Fire."

He ticks off another finger, the pointer of his other hand. "The gentleman in room 380 eschewing the convention of a name, designated The Beast, has requested its room be inimical to life. Please avoid room 380 for your own safety."

"Let me see," he says, holding his thumb. "President Ose is in room 208. And there are several hundred terrestrial emanations in the basement. You won't get much out of them, but they're free to a good home if you're interested."

"Are there any humans here?" you ask.

"I don't know," he says, looking down at you. "Are there?"

79AU_Inside12.strDesc:
Joakim slides a keycard over the desk. "I'm not at liberty to talk about the guests out of turn. You can visit them if you'd like. Oh, and they will shortly gather in the VIP Lounge for Game Night. You're invited to attend."

What are they going to host? Alien croquet? Multiplayer DOOM? You take the keycard and try not to fret. "I won't know how to play."

"It's a game called Bridge," he says. "Do you know it?"

"I've heard of it."

"You'll pick it up as you go along," he says.

79AU_Inside13.strTitle: Ask if you get a room
79AU_Inside13.strDesc:
"Can I have a room for myself?" you ask.

Joakim cocks his head. "You could," he says. "But you'd only wind up back here in much the same position as before. You've got a life to lead. Best get on with it."

79AU_Inside14.strDesc: "Please specify the mode of explanation," he says. "Exegetic? Or exigent?"

79AU_Inside15.strDesc: "Exegetic," you say. You hope that not all the aliens you meet will be this dead set on five dollar words. "79 AU," says Joakim, "is a Class 13 deep space communications probe of disputed ownership. It has five rainbows transmission, 9th generation intersimulation technology, and over one megabytes of addressable memory, suitable for First Contact, Last Contact, and everything in between. In honour of its eight thousand years of service, including service with distinction in the War Of Two Monads, it appears in gold, a Baryonic element and spectrum of light many cultures associate with the divine." You frown. "One megabyte?" Joakim frowns back. "Excuse me," he says, thinking for a second. "Signed integer overflow. I could start listing zeroes but we'd be here all day."

79AU_Inside16.strDesc:
"Exigent."

"It's your last chance," says Joakim. His air of calculated weirdness is gone. "The Wall is coming down. The enclave will engulf. How? How is your why. It's up to you."

Not for the first time, you're confronted by a monumental concept which evokes no strong reaction from you. You shake your head. "I'm not sure I can make that choice."

"That's the kind of thing you should avoid saying," he says, "unless you want to trigger the worst possible outcome."

ChoongMilitary.strTitle: Ask him about the military applications
ChoongMilitary.strDesc: "You said before that the New Colchians had discovered something the military wanted," you say. "What was it?" Choong blinks. He has a distinctive blink, both eyes really hard at once. "I'd have thought that was obvious, if you're familiar with my footage." "Clean slate rules," you remind him. "No stupid questions." "Fine," he says, "but only if you accept stupid answers in kind. That being, the answer is teleportation." "Teleportation." "From my lips to God's ears," he insists, "without passing through an intervening medium. You saw the video, didn't you? Girl goes in, door closes, machine hums, door opens, no more girl. Where is she? Somewhere else. Quod erat demonstrandum." "It was real?" "Of course it was real," he says impatiently, "or you wouldn't be here, and more importantly, I wouldn't be here." "It's not possible," you say. Choong looks at you. "It's not physically possible." "Then we're done. Can I go home?" he asks darkly. "Put me in a new body, make me the world's first total body transplant."

ChoongTeleportation.strDesc:
"Teleportation, though," you repeat. "How does it work? Doesn't it violate relativity? Causality?"

"I don't know," he says slowly, as if to a slow-witted child. "I'm an anthropologist, not a theoretical physicist."

"It violates common sense."

"Oh, absolutely," he agrees. "Along with the God-rock, it's the single most important discovery in recorded history. It demands a reassessment of common sense itself."

"Occam's razor, then," you say. "It must be a hoax."

Choong eyes you, as would a teacher to a precocious student overstepping. "Put that away, you'll hurt yourself." He puts up a hand, forestalling any more on the subject. "I don't care to talk about this. I've been over it more times than I can count. My best guess is, they discovered functional teleportation. Take it or leave it. If you're of a mind to do it already, send me to the pain room."

ChoongTeleportation2.strTitle: Ask about the destination of the teleportation
ChoongTeleportation2.strDesc: "When this Belter girl went into the sarcophagus," you ask, testing the structural limit of a dubious addition to your reality, "where did she come out?" "No idea," Choong says promptly. "So how do you -," "- know that it was teleportation?" Choong mimics your question. Seems he's heard it before. "I don't. It's an article of faith. However you slice it, if she wasn't in that box, by definition, she teleported out of it." "I suppose the Colchians claimed she went to Heaven," you say. "Her name was Ketevan," he says mildly, "and no, they didn't. There was no Heaven in their theology. Common in modern religion - Gods, yes. Hell, of course. Heaven, no. A world full of cynics has no time for Heaven." "Then where?" "They said, and this was the entire point of the exercise," he says, with the air of someone reciting a flimsy pretext, "that Keti had gone to God. That she was one with God. Transubstantiation, if you like, rather than teleportation." "They sent that poor girl to join with God?" "Yes, and many others," he says. "Anyone who wanted to go, really."

ChoongDisappeared.strDesc:
"They volunteered to get into an eldritch sarcophagus," you say. "They wanted to become one with God."

"Wouldn't you?" he shoots back. Something tells you his heart isn't in it. "Consider it. I don't know your religion - I could make an educated guess, but I won't - but you must understand why they'd do it, even if you're not religious. Consider the hypothetical from first principles. God is real, the Creator of our Universe, and He offers you the choice to become One With Him. Assume that entails immortality, omniscience, changing your participation in reality from that of a mortal subject to that of a supernatural force. Would you say yes?"

ChoongDisappearedReply1.strDesc:
"I've never been a God before," you say. "I don't know if I'd like it. Did He offer a trial period, a try-before-you-buy?"

"Religion is never big on guarantee, as a rule," he says. "Most of them make a virtue out of it."

ChoongDisappearedReplyBack1.strDesc:
"I would at least consider it," he says, "and I'm as atheistic as they come. On the other hand, the Belters were a young community cut off from the rest of their species, further altered by an exotic psychoactive agent. For them it was a no-brainer. They were happy to do it. It was a joyous occasion." 

No, his heart definitely isn't in it. He's arguing for the sake of it, because he can't help but pitch in for the opposite view.

ChoongDisappearedReply2.strDesc:
"There's no way in hell I'm taking that deal without knowing more," you say. "Be God? It could mean literally anything."

"For some, I can imagine that being a plus," he says. "Not everyone is happy with their lot."

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strDesc:
"Ah," they say. "A shame. I had such high hopes for you."

"What is that supposed to mean?" you ask.

"The tides are turning, Captain. You'll find it wise not to be swept up in the undertow," they say.

And with that, they continue their walk up the path.
PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strTitle: Express Loyalty to GalCon and Titan

ENCFirstDockBCRSInfo.strDesc: As you try to work out where you've been deposited, you hear a raspy voice at your shoulder: "Got a light?" A funny little woman waves an unlit Viceroy at you. She has thick white eyebrows, thick black framed glasses, and an accent you cannot place. She doesn't look like the hawkers you narrowly escaped. "Are you going to try to sell me something?" you ask. She gestures with the cigarette. "Probably not." Once the cigarette is lit, she takes a satisfied drag, exhaling a long stream through her nostrils. "You're just off the [us-shipname], correct?" "How did you know that?" "Relax," she says airily. "It's all anyone talks about on the Ring. Every miner here is a fat walking bag of money, and everyone else wants some. Retail surveillance is building your personality profile as we speak. Face, name, how long you'd glance at her tits," she indicates an erotic advertisement you've not yet seen, "how many steps you've taken, where you stopped, where you've come from, where you're going." She gives you a moment to chew on that, then indicates herself. "Eleni Konstantinidis. I'm a trader, like you, of a sort. Us ship captains look out for one another. Let me buy you a coffee."

ENCFirstDockBCRSInfoAccept.strDesc:
Despite her stated lack of interest in selling you anything, or perhaps because of it, you're wary. You follow her unerring footsteps just off the concourse to an equally crowded but less rancidly desperate intersection, and into a dimly lit coffee house there.

Low lighting, better acoustics, and the return of your personal space are all immediate and ongoing reliefs. The clientele resemble Eleni in demeanour if not in look: serious men and women sit one-on-one in private booths, engaged in fierce but inaudible debate. The real deals are made here.

Eleni banters briefly in Greek with the host, who seats you at her favourite booth.

"Let's start with the basics of life in Ceres space," she says, "and this will go much quicker if I don't have to guess what you don't know. Like the war. You know about the war?"

"I don't know," you say. "Do I?"

"Exactly," says Eleni. "So ask me about the war. Thank you, Niko." The host puts a fresh pot and two china cups between you. You take a sip, and have to stop yourself from spilling in surprise, without contest, the best coffee you've ever tasted.

ENCFirstDockBCRSInfoAskWar.strDesc: Eleni fiddles with her necklace, shifting the pearls along the string with one hand. It's a chintzy fake, in your estimation. Perhaps it has sentimental value. "It's like this. Mars and Titan - Xinhua and the United States. They got all the money. They want, they need, metal. There's metal out there, all over, oodles of it, sitting in the asteroids. In the Belt, Jupiter, doesn't matter. But they got problems. It's an ocean of soup, and they've both got tiny little plastic spoons." She holds up a complimentary tiny plastic spoon wrapped in packaging, and tosses it aside. "Ever tried cracking an asteroid, gathering up all the dust and rock, sifting through it all for the shit that isn't worthless? And then, you've got a fuckload of kamacite and your dick in your hands, but you want a steel coil you can sell. Have you got a blast furnace and water enough to swim in?" She doesn't wait for you to answer. "Fuck that noise. It's expensive, time-consuming, and dangerous. They'd much rather us do it for them." "I'm familiar with mining," you say. "Then you'll be familiar with how mining ships go missing around here," she says flatly, "and by 'go missing', I mean they were last seen entering the torpedo envelope of an unaligned ship before suffering complete existence failure. They're not fucking around, my young friend. There's a killing to be made here." She leans forward, peering over her glasses as they ever so slightly slip down her nose. "Be sure the killing's not made of you." "Nice." "Thank you." She sips her coffee.

ENCFirstDockBCRSInfoAskWar2.strTitle: Ask her who's doing the killing
ENCFirstDockBCRSInfoAskWar2.strDesc:
Eleni dips her finger in the saucer. She draws on the placemat: Ring station, and its parent body Ceres, which both look unhelpfully like messy brown coffee circles. She draws another one, big, with a bunch of dots. 

"That's us, Ring Station and Ceres, and that's them, King Jupiter and his moons. As sure as they're here in secret, blasting us to pieces whenever we're nodding off behind the wheel, our brave boys and girls are over there doing the same to the Galileans."

"The station can't stop the Galileans operating here?"

"The station is trying," she says. "Everyone living in Calico City is sick of the corporate yoke, and they're the Coalition's main source of miners. There's a sliver of overlap in the Venn diagram between those pissed off folks and all the happy-go-lucky sods on the concourse outside, in that Bosch painting," she says. You nod like you've seen the painting before, or for that matter, any painting before. Aren't paintings supposed to be beautiful?

"If they push too hard, the people will push back. And the Coalition will find themselves with another revolution, right here on their front doorstep."

ENCFirstDockBCRSInfoAskWar3.strTitle: Ask why the Galileans care so much
ENCFirstDockBCRSInfoAskWar3.strDesc:
"Bigger picture," you ask, "why's the competition so fierce? Why blow up each other's ships?"

"It's the economy, stupid." You frown. She smiles indulgently, as if to a favoured child. "Look it up sometime, I'm not calling you stupid. All wars are fought for money, or things that turn into money, like power or control or slaves. Ceres and Jupiter are selling all this stuff to Mars and Titan, and whoever secures the Belt can starve their opponent.

"Xinhua controls the Coalition, by complicated financial wizardry. Every corp with a stake, if you dig enough, is partly or wholly owned by someone else, and they're owned by someone else again, et cetera, et cetera, until eventually you get to Xinhua."

"And Titan?"

"Jupiter," she says, "or, the Galilean Confederacy, they're calling it these days. They've got more moons than brain cells. Overthrew the Troy-Jupiter Group, declared for themselves, and now Titan's the only thing propping them up. Your guess is as good as mine whether they make it five years, or five more weeks."

"So I've got it clear," you say slowly, "you're saying that Xinhua and the US are in a cold war to control the Belt, but the prize in controlling the Belt, is that it would help win a war over the Belt?"

She mulls over the sentence, then raises her hand to the host for a refill. "That's pretty much it," she says.

ENCFirstDockBCRSInfoRefuse.strDesc:
"Suit yourself," she says. Without missing a beat she veers into the nearest brothel.

Time-to-shop, indeed.

CruzCall.strDesc:
In your inbox, you find a message regarding another message: ZaraFone, an odd little outfit that provides a professional, comfortable environment for interplanetary communication, has a video waiting for you, sender withheld. And of course you may not watch it on your device, no; you must go there physically and sit in a booth and commune. How else can they profit?

When you get a few minutes to yourself, you pass by ZaraFone. A clerk shows you to your booth, activates an incense vaporiser, and leaves a hot pouch of green tea slowly spinning in the air by your shoulder. They close the door behind them.

The lights dim. Your pleather chair has a chunky keyboard in one arm, with which you instruct the room to play the message.

VideotapeOnlineResearchMakePost.strDesc: The K-LEG Q/A boards are awash with a Brownian motion of boredom and moderator tyranny. The top three pages are complaints about questions that have been answered a million times, shoulder to shoulder with posts asking those same evergreen questions.

VideotapeOnlineResearchScrollForumsRetur.strDesc: Trying to view the half-deleted thread throws 404 errors. It's as if that page never existed at all.

VideotapeOnlineResearchMakePostSurreptit.strDesc: Maybe you need to keep it circumspect. You catch more flies with honey. "Has anyone seen Void Inhalants #3?" is the title and body of your post. There's a flurry of engagement. No text, just thumbs down. You pick a fingernail as you wait, listening to the swish and hum of an A/C unit. Finally there's a hit. "Hello! Not 3, but I've seen 2, 7, and 8," says the reply. The avatar is a big upside down smiling face, a match for their handle - 'Smiley'. "Do you have 3? What's in it?" "I was hoping you could help me with that," you tap back. "I don't know how it works." "We absolutely can," comes an instant reply. Who's we, all of a sudden? "You're K-LEG local, right? Come to Flotilla." Smiley attaches a string of numbers. Your PDA helpfully highlights it as a Flotilla residential address. "Any time! Day or night."

VideotapeOnlineResearchMakePostPlain.strTitle: Leave a plain description and request info
VideotapeOnlineResearchMakePostPlain.strDesc:
You jot down basic specs about the video tape, the size, shape, the cursory knowledge you've gained about VHS media, and ask the gen public if they've ever come across such a thing.

All that's left to do is wait for a kind internet stranger to - 

- hold on.

Your post vanishes before your eyes. Refreshing dumps you back to the CCC landing page. What the hell?

VideotapeOnlineResearchLookupManuf.strDesc:
You scroll through catalogues and trade publications of Renbao et al, hoping to come across a niche division or indie outfit producing century-old home media. No dice. As far as the consumer electronics market is concerned, you cannot buy a tape nor player.

An automated sales rep from Renbao opens up a message window and prattles an offer for a bespoke rush manufacturing job to make your own replica VHS device. After a brief Q/A, it admits it has no idea what you (and it) are talking about.

"Can I speak to a human?" you type back.

"We don't have any humans here," it says. Apologetically, perhaps.

VideotapeInspectFinish.strDesc: You pocket the tape and move on.

VideotapeDecideResearch.strDesc:
In the way that a steel pipe pinwheeling forever through an airless cargo bay does not, this feels important.

There has to be an expert on K-LEG who knows more about this ... 'VHS'. Certainly not anyone you know, but someone on the station must.

You could try looking it up on OKLG's local internet. Your PDA can access it, provided you're on one of its affiliate stations.

AVClub_Smiley_Inside.strDesc:
You push through the heavy fabric that many dorms use to segregate their HVAC.

Inside is a wide common room with a low ceiling. Underfoot is a haphazard array of futons and padded flooring, all oriented toward a wall screen. There's a kitchenette in back. Smiley waits for you crosslegged on a futon, halo of hair gently settling around his shoulders. You take a seat opposite him.

"Show me," he says.

You produce the videotape. His eyes light up. "Hot damn!" he whoops. You let him yank it from your hands.

"This is the real deal," he says, poring over it, testing a sticker's binding agent with pinched fingers. "Like I told you, we've got a bunch of others, a 2, a 7, and a handful of 8s. Our first 3!"

You clear your throat. He refocuses on you, eyes blinking behind his enormous glasses.

"Right, right. What is it? It's a video. What's on the video? Freaky shit, man, freaky shit. People doing some kinda ritual. Who am I? Nobody. Who are we? We are, y'know, whoever wants to watch. We get together and we watch them. Compare notes, theorise. Argue. It's like a little club. Get me?"

You nod, considering it. "A ritual?"

He waves dismissively. "I'll show you, if you want. Don't fret. This is a huge day for us. It's been ages since we've had something new. I'm entirely at your disposal."

AVClub_Start.strDesc:
The man has a high forehead and a receding hairline. His hair, where it's growing, is long, reaching past his shoulders. He should be old, but his unblemished skin doesn't put him past thirty. He wears large trifocal glasses, and a wide, placid smile.

"Are you Smiley?" you ask. "From the message thread."

"Namaste," he says, "and jeete raho. I am he."

You murmur noncommittally. "I have the videotape. Do you know what it is? What it does?"

His smile grows wider. "It plays videos. Or it should, but if it's like the others, it's broken."

"But you've watched them."

"I have watched them."

"How?" You keep a lid on your impatience.

Smiley looks up and down the accessway conspiratorially. There's the average amount of people around for a Flotilla accessway, which is to say some, and an average amount of interest in your conversation, which is to say none. "Not here. Inside." Smiley vanishes into a residence.
AVClub_Start.strTooltip: He's waiting where he said he would be.

AVClub_Smiley_Tape2.strDesc:
Smiley never really loses his trademark dopey smile, but it dims and brightens, and it brightens now. "I was hoping you would."

He queues up the video on the wall screen. The playback pauses tantalisingly on the first frame, twin bars of the pause symbol blocking the view. Smiley insists on first making a batch of his special popcorn, 'like how the food carts do it but better'.

While he hums from the kitchenette, you study the still frame.

It's a study in harsh light; the camera and subject are EVA. The top half of the frame is the dark side of an asteroid. The gentle curve of a horizon, where the black body becomes a curtain of stars, suggests it's a small rock, a hundred metres across, if that. A muted pop from behind you announces the first kernel's expansion.

Beneath the asteroid, hanging motionless (the video being paused) is the harsh silhouette of a spacesuit. Their arm is outstretched, gesturing up toward the surface like Adam reaching out to God.

The picture is grainy, pockmarked by imperfection. It could be due to the ISO of whatever this was captured on, but Smiley said this, here, was taken from a cellulose tape like the one you have ... so who knows when the imperfections were introduced?

Smiley suddenly reappears beside you, making you start. He waggles a bowl of popcorn. "Ready?" he says. "First time through, I won't say a thing. Then if you like, we can watch again and I can give you the Extras commentary track." 

He offers you the bowl.

AVClub_Smiley_Tape3.strDesc: "No can do," he says. He indicates your tape. "It's a dud. There's video in there, somewhere. But the first thing we did - this is going back - Abacho and Xavier kitbashed a working VHS player. We had to reverse engineer a head, this little needle thing to read the tape, and order it from a fab on Venus, and then we had to hound down some weirdo on Luna who insisted he had real copies of the PAL and NTSC video standards, and then he ghosted us, blah blah blah. That's kind of how the group got started." "And?" "And, long story short, we made a working VHS player. We think. It worked with some other tape we found at auction. But our damned tape wouldn't play. Know why?" There's no way you could know, but he's enjoying telling the story and he doesn't wait for you to answer. "Because it's a fake! It's not a VHS tape. It's a plastic replica holding a spool of modern, analog, cellulose film. Venus stock, where the cellulose comes from. We had never actually opened the damn thing to check." You have an obvious question coming, but it's been bugging you for a while, so you just come out with it. "Why would someone make this?" "We don't know! That's why it's so fascinating! We're running a pool." He brings up a spreadsheet on the wall screen. "Xavier has 300 on an ARG. Molly Liu thinks it's outsider art. Molly 2 thinks it's aliens. Xavier thinks," he rolls his eyes, "it's final proof that the universe is a simulation that's beginning to unravel. We don't like him very much but he put down a lot of cash, so whatever."

AVClub_FirstWatch.strDesc:
The video plays.

The motionless figure comes to life. At the apex of its arm's reach, a gas jet flares from its wrist. A flicker across the dark suggests a projectile fired up into the asteroid with a long trailing cable. The cable snaps taut, and the spacesuit flies up into the asteroid's penumbra. 

An enormous spacesuit helmet slides in front of the camera as a second figure enters the scene, the faceplate a brilliant reflection of the starry night, evoking that silent terror unique to a spacewalk. It drifts past the camera, offering a brief thumbs up, then fires its own grapple after the first suit.

As the second spacesuit travels, up becomes down, and it's falling. The camera's POV shifts to one side, and the tape abruptly has a -

Cut: 

Inserts flash past too quick to properly read. An alphanumeric string '1-400', a litany of memtest logs, the Voltaire university logo, which segues into a chintzy orientation video ripped straight from the interplanetary net. Audio snaps on, too loud after the silence, playing over Lunar students relaxing in a campus dorm. "- over ten thousand future fellows per intake, you're bound to find a loopmate for life." Students play a friendly scrimmage game of Breakout in a refectory hall. "That's how BNW is securing the future of our System, today."

Students pose in the iconic Voltaire quadrangle, laughing. The camera pulls back past the BNW CEO. He turns to camera, smiling. "Are You Prepared For Tomorrow?"

It seizes on -orrow, -orrow, -orrow, then turns dark and silent. 

Cut: 

A thin stripe of light cuts across the screen, revealing a rock fissure. The torch shines briefly back to the camera, a halo eating everything. It shines away. Its wielder is inching gingerly through the gap in the rock. Judging by the motion of the camera, so is the person filming.

Cut:

A black star. A black sun. The universe around it cast in white. Like a photo negative, or infrared. Its surface roils. Is it Sol? Can't say. Audio builds, an intermittent digital staccato repeating faster and faster until it becomes a voice, and then a cacophonous scream.

Cut:

"O Brave New World," says the CEO, reading from a teleprompter, "that has such people in it." He gestures to his flock of happy undergrads.

"Cut!" someone calls. The undergrads dissolve into a backlit white wall. The CEO wilts against the blank LED volume. "We got it," another voice says reassuringly.

"Thank fucking God," he says, turning offscreen. "I get to the very end - tell marketing to give me simple sentences -"

Cut:

Torches play over another unlit cavern of the asteroid. One of the two spacesuits comes over to the camera's POV. Arms reach out. The POV shifts and settles. Violently? No. It's framing. The spacesuit drifts away.

Overhead lights snap on, bright and powerful. A small prefab room, barely more than a sealed plastic bubble expanded into the rock wall.

In the centre of the chamber, something enormous glitters. An effigy, humanoid, long. A bulbous head. Arms crossed over its torso. Detailed engravings give it the semblance of a slumbering human. An effigy? No, a sarcophagus.

It is made of perfect gold.

The media player reaches the end of the track.

AVClub_Smiley_Tape3_Again.strDesc: "How," you say, accessing a well of patience you never knew you possessed, "do we see what's on my tape, then?" "Easy," says Smiley. "There's a woman here on Flotilla, she digitises them for us. Isambard Cruz. Take it to her, tell her I sent you. Or don't. I don't think she likes me very much." "That sucks," you say neutrally. "In any case, you'll have to call her on her intercom. You'll find it on the door, right down the hall here." Smiley continues. "She, uh. Doesn't get out much." He gives you the intercom door location on Flotilla, down the hall and one turn away. "And can you promise to bring back a copy to us? Finders keepers, salvage rights, et cetera. But," he says apologetically, "I've already organised a watch party, tonight. Everyone's losing their mind, dying to see a new tape. Would you come? You'd be the hero of the hour." "I'll see what I can do."

AVClub_FirstWatch_Debrief.strTitle: Debrief with Smiley about the tape
AVClub_FirstWatch_Debrief.strDesc:
You let out a pent up sigh. What to make of this? It could be anything. It could be nothing. Either way, there's no mystery how it grabbed the attention of a bunch of bored engineers.

You look at Smiley. Smiley looks at you.

InspectBraincase.strDesc: The case is finished in a dark matte. Its only deformities are a seam and an embossed Renbao logo in one corner. The seam opens at a touch. The two halves separate like bookcovers, angling out and down to rest on the surface below. One half holds a white shell with the shape of a brain, a hardened plastic layer which nevertheless seems flimsy, unfit for purpose. An electrician's nightmare of cables connect to the shell's upper hemisphere, flowing out like hair and disappearing into the housing below. Cables, 'tubes' really, plug into the shell at the base, presumably to deliver slurries of oxygen and sugar, and whatever else human brains need to subsist. Besides the obvious comparison (shaped as it is like the brain inside), the shell brings to mind ancient marine life, the first trilobite to venture from the sea to the land. The little telltale LEDs going on-off - its eyes blinking in the sunlight. The case hums, and glugs whenever an internal reservoir resettles. The other half of the unfolded braincase is a hollow depression, a resting place for the shell. Underneath it there are finely printed instructions in ten languages. They outline emergency care for someone untrained in the case's handling. The parts you can read mostly say to find someone who is trained in its handling, but there seems to be detail enough for you to operate it in a pinch.

Braincase1.strTitle: Make contact with the brain inside
Braincase1.strDesc:
The case is compatible with an off-the-shelf Renbao induction rig, a simple mesh of electrodes you slip over your head like a balaclava. It's an effort of will to ignore the background noise of the ship, the ambient warmth of your body, the occasional brush of clothes on your skin - an effort that, once made, becomes thoughtless, instinctive. The red-brown interior of your eyelids is overwritten with purer black, and after a moment, the Renbao logo.

"Hello?" you speak into the void of the operating system. "Testing, testing, hello." You become aware of your own avatar, and that you inhabit it: a 3D model with a poor quality scan of your own face, and a skeletal body mesh roughly based on your own proportions. You note the fine hairs on your arms, which your real body happens to lack - the exhausting reality of default settings catering to Earthers. "Mr Choong? Ben?"

No one joins you to contemplate the slowly orbiting Renbao logo. You rip off the electrodes. Briefly two realities jostle for primacy in the same v-buffer, black squares checkboarding the ship wall. You consult the manual, a dogeared booklet that fell out of the braincase lid. O-kay. Apparently there's a complicated process to setup a digital handshake between the braincase and your rig, and a troubleshooting appendix three times longer than the instructions themselves. You sigh, and get to work.

Braincase1.5.strDesc: It's a less painful solve than it might have been. It takes fifteen minutes, split between puzzling out incantations for the command line, and risking a headache every time you need to quickly switch between the rig and the manual. At two separate junctures, you're convinced that there's a fundamental hardware mismatch and no amount of trial and error will solve it. Experienced spacer that you are, wunderkind troubleshooter of hardware and software alike, you push past these moments because you have no other choice. You double and triple-check the final command: rbc do let ports1n proxok handshake || cat<< "Hello?"

Braincase1.75.strDesc:
The black runs. Patches of near-black reveal themselves, dripping like slime down a wall. Traces of white knit together. The void becomes falling snow.

A log cabin swims into focus from out of the dark, windows dimly lit. It's cold, the air sharp on an in-breath. You start shivering.

An Asian man in his fifties leans against a door jamb, smoking a cigarette, firelight at his back. He sports a classic bowl cut, his fringe a perfect line across his forehead. "Ben Choong?" you gasp, the question mangled by cold sneaking past your lips and into your lungs.

"Speaking," he says. "What is it now?"

"Ah - it, ah -" the sensory overload precludes speech. You hug yourself for warmth, aware that your real body is perfectly temperate. This body you're also in has other ideas.

Choong looks as if he is trying hard not to roll his eyes at you. "You'd better come inside," he says. When your legs threaten to fail you, he loops an arm under yours and assists you across the threshold.

Braincase2.strDesc:
"I don't have time for this," you say, warm enough to trust your tongue again. "Ben Choong. I need your help."

He visibly recalibrates. "That's a first," he says. "I don't see how I could possibly help anyone. Every secret I've ever known, I've divulged. Every confidence betrayed. There's nothing more you people can take from me."

You infer his meaning, though it takes a second. "I'm not here to interrogate you," you say slowly. "I think we may need to start over. I found you - your brain - " What even is the situation? How to describe your current relationship? "I'm ... taking care of it, for the moment. Whatever I can do for you, I will. But I need your help. You have information vital to the war effort." The cliched line rolls off your tongue like a cheap knockoff on a factory line, all the more unsatisfying that it happens to be true.

Choong can't hide the glimmer of hope that sparks in his eyes. It dies immediately, doused in pessimism. "Ridiculous," he says. "I truly don't know what you think this will wheedle out of me. It's a poor effort, a threadbare deception."

"My name is [us-fullname]." You try to project sincerity. Strange that it doesn't come naturally. "I'm [us-age] years old. I'm from [us-homeworld]. I'm a ship captain."

"I'm nothing more than a brain in a jar; I have no way to verify anything you tell me," says Ben Choong. "How can you expect me to believe anything you say?"

ChoongHistory.strDesc:
He begins without any more prompting. His words are confident, but hasty. He seems to have gone over this history many times before, enough to have an answer prepared and ready.

"I was born on Earth," he says, "which I don't remember at all. I was shipped up the beanstalk to Luna when I was a child, with my parents, who worked on a base. I have one memory of Earth: riding in the back seat of a car when it was raining. I remember the red lights of the cars ahead shimmering through the windshield."

This image doesn't coalesce for you - a shield for wind? - before he moves on. "My parents died when I was young, a few years apart, and I became the property of a BNW creche. I excelled in school, mostly in humanities, and got the grades to enter Voltaire University. I was a terrible rego miner," he says, grinning shamefacedly. "The creche was happy to see the back of me. I studied, graduated, was rewarded with a bunch of important letters after my name."

ChoongResearch.strDesc:
"Pretend I don't know anything about what you've done," you say. "What was so important about your research?"

He nods gamely, as if he's heard this exact 'clean-slate, start-from-the-start' line of questioning before. "There is a substance," he says, "and don't ask me anything about it because I swear I can't answer the technicalities. But it has exotic properties of some kind. I don't understand them. It's magic rock, to someone like me. And it exists in our solar system."

"The Belters called it 'void opal', because in solid form it's opalescent, and - you get it. I suppose I'm directly responsible for alerting the powers-that-be to its existence. That's the short version." He looks at you for encouragement, sees incomprehension, and starts on the medium length version.

"When I was living with the Belters - I lived with many tribes, but the one in question called themselves New Colchis - I discovered they had a secret. Not by design, but in practice. They simply didn't talk to outsiders about it, and traded with Inners for air and water without ever bringing it up. I'm sure they would've happily told anyone, had anyone thought to ask."

ChoongKetevanPress6.strDesc:
"No, probably not. That would've been an ethical dilemma."

No reply. He looks away, brimming with murderous anger.
ChoongKetevanPress6.strTitle: Hone in on the problematic angle

ChoongKetevanPress7.strDesc:
"Especially since you were a fancypants academic, pulled himself up by his bootstraps, smartest kid in creche, and she was a dumb-as-rocks tribal gaga for God."

His body jerks, hands flexing, as if compelled to leap up and throttle you to death. The impulse has been carefully trained out of him.

At last he speaks, jaw visibly clenched. "Do you have a point?"

You shake your head. "Stop me if I get one wrong," you say.

ChoongTortureDetails.strDesc:
"Your captors," you say, "who I stress are not me, we're not associated, I'm itinerant. What did they do to you?"

Choong is shocked out of silence. "You want me to explain how I was tortured? Are you fucking kidding?"

"No, no," you say. He's so uncharitable. "I was just curious!"

"If you really are 'just' curious," he says, "I think it shows unbelievably poor taste. And if not, read the fucking manual."

There probably are relevant instructions in the manual.

ChoongReciprocate.strDesc:
"Maybe it would help if I convinced you I'm on the level," you say. "That I am who I say I am."

"I'm listening," he says.

You tell him about K-LEG, the little asteroid in the middle of nowhere. Growing up in the shadow of the shipbreaker's yard, learning from the get-go that your value was pretty much in direct proportion to your facility with your tools. Looking at the dot of Old Earth, another colourful dot in the starry sea, and wondering how clear water could turn it blue.

At some point you lose track of your own story. It becomes a confusing sequence of ships, people, and spacefaring minutiae. "... that's about it." He nods seriously.

"Come on," you say, "would a spy really make up all of that just to appear trustworthy?"

He shakes his head. "It's tautological. A spy would have to make up something to appear trustworthy, such as all that, and more."

"Help me out," you say. "What could I say to get you to trust me?"

"You don't understand," he says. "You truly don't. No matter what you say, I have to distrust it. Even if it sounds true, even if it would be convenient, even if I'd want it to be true very very much, formally speaking, I can't believe anything you say because you have complete control over my perception of reality. Look up the 'Cartesian demon', if you like."

Incredible: he's actually prescribing secondary reading. You can take the man out of the university ... "But I'm not doing that!" you say. "I'm not tricking you."

"And I want that to be true," he says sadly. "I really do. For what it's worth, you've led quite an interesting life. I hope it's turning out how you wanted."

ChoongPlateau3.strDesc: Dr. Choong waits expectantly for your next question.

ChoongInformWar.strTitle: Alert Choong to the stakes viz a viz: war
ChoongInformWar.strDesc:
"You need to know what we're up against," you say. "The Great Powers are on the eve of open warfare."

"No," he says, "the Great Powers would never."

"This is important," you say impatiently. "I'm serious."

"You look serious." He makes a visible effort to tolerate it. "Fine. Say what you have to say."

You give a rundown of the deteriorating situation between Ceres and Jupiter, seasoned with a few personal anecdotes you've experienced along the way. Ceres being overrun with agents of dubious loyalty. Ships disappearing. Military buildups reported around Mars and Saturn.

"Ceres might try to repeat the attack on Ganymede, or worse, an attack on Titan. Titan could demolish Ring Station without a second thought. Xinhua and the US are being drawn into open conflict with one another. It's all bad."

"This is nothing new," says Choong calmly. "In fact, it's right on schedule."

ChoongInformWarDemandExplanation.strTitle: Demand to know what schedule he's referring to
ChoongInformWarDemandExplanation.strDesc: "'On schedule?'" you repeat. "You knew this was coming?" "Yes," he says. "This war in potentia has been modelled in detail since the 50s. It should've happened sooner, but we got lucky." "You can model a war?" Choong raises a hand again, an annoying habit of his. "It's settled, in the academic community, that the System is in decline. Terminal decline. The writing's been on the wall since we lost Earth." A cold chill creeps down the back of your neck. He sounds so confident, so calm, completely at odds with the terrifying sentiment. Haunting his words is a spectre of decades of furious, desperate debate, and all that has been collated, synthesised, and presented as fact. You swallow. "You sound like a doomer on a social feed," you say. They're a dime a dozen. He both nods and shakes his head, a noncommittal back-and-forth. "I'm sure plenty of them are former colleagues. BNW didn't like the idea. If your paper wasn't happy enough they'd blackball you. Then you had plenty of free time to argue with OSINT nutters." "So they're right? What do you mean, decline?" Choong blinks his distinctive both-eyed blink, like a genteel reptilian. "I mean in every field of academic inquiry, in every way we organise our social critique, we see that the building blocks to keep a human alive in space are disappearing." He holds up a hand and checks off his fingers. "Food, water, oxygen. Our breadbaskets aren't producing enough food. Our volatiles aren't processed with enough speed. Medicine, the amount of novel ailments discovered in colonisation aren't even properly categorised, let alone understood. Security, society, all fragmenting. Two superpowers are tooling up to decide who's king of a bunch of rocks. They needn't bother. Famine will do their work all the quicker." "Uh huh," you say, the dutiful skeptic. "So how long have we got? Ten years? Five?" Choong purses his lips. "What's today's date?" You tell him. He does a quick calculation in his head. "Six months." "Six?!" you all-but choke on the word. "Six if we're being optimistic. Our subsistence - excuse me, our means of producing life-sustaining goods - barely contributed to a vast reserve banked from Earth. From the second they went up, to the days they came tumbling down, the Earth elevators worked day and night ferrying us food and water and people and oxygen and, you get the picture, for twenty years. Twenty. Years. It was our cornucopia, our horn of plenty. We were profligate with it. No one expected -" he swallows. He blinks and moves on. "Since then, our consumption has always been a considerable net negative. You can't really expect a handful of Quonset huts on Titan or Mars to provide for all the millions exiled from the garden of Eden. Offworld industries are, always were, paper tigers; propaganda. Once our Earth surplus runs out, well ..." "You, you ..." You struggle for a rejoinder. He waits patiently, a sad little smile on his face. "... you can't be serious." Is that the best you've got? It's the best you've got. "It's like I said," he continues, unperturbed. "We lost Mother Earth." Mother Earth, you note, not Old Earth, like the System brands it. "Oh, the effort out here has been valiant, admirable in its own way - our tangle of outposts, colonies - some of those Martian films weren't half bad - but our number is up."

ChoongInformWarDemandExplanationEnd.strTitle: Ask how the end will come
ChoongInformWarDemandExplanationEnd.strDesc:
"What will happen in six months?" you ask. "When we run out of supplies. We starve?"

"No," he says. "The war will come sooner than that. With it, new emergency powers, reorganisation of the economy. Rationing. They will stretch out the reserves as long as they can. The war will touch everyone, everything, and steadily reduce the scope of the problem - fewer mouths eat less. That will buy another few years for the victor."

Plot_Ceres_Clandestine_Interventions_Dea.strDesc: [us] [records] a debriefing of a successful wet work mission.
[us] [checks] the planter.

You peer into the fronds of the planter, not knowing exactly what you're looking for. Down near the base, half buried in the soil, you see a small folded up piece of paper. You unfold it, and find a typewritten note: 
 
TEMPORARY ASSET AUTHORIZATION GRANTED
VERIFICATION: Follow the evening redness.
UNDERGROUND TARGET AT LARGE ON RING STATION.

LATEST INTERCEPTS INDICATE XINHUA PASS PHRASE: Have you ever grown nightshades? RETURNS: Only in borrowed soil. 

LOCATE TARGET VIA PASS PHRASE AND TAG USING METHOD OF YOUR DISCRETION

There are further instructions below.

More text above a tiny silver capsule taped to the paper. The text reads:

WET WORK DIRECTIVE APPROVED

UPON DISCOVERY OF TARGET, BREAK BETWEEN MOLARS AND BLOW FOR MIN FIVE SECONDS. RETURN VERIFICATION HERE

You stare at the tiny pill, trying not to think about what would happen if you accidentally swallowed it.
You accept the wet work mission.
You deny the wet work mission, for now.

ValkyrieSarcophagus1111.strDesc: spinning spinning spinning you're trapped in the instant eternity of the box again and spinning the wheel is spinning the planets too and there is the Object - COME TO ME, it says, COME TO ME. I did, you say, but I did! BUT THEN YOU LEFT, it says, waspishly. IT'S ALWAYS LIKE THIS WITH YOU. I'M STARTING TO HAVE DOUBTS. This isn't healthy for us, another part of you says. I'm pulling the plug - You jerk awake at a piercing whistle, seated on the platform for a Mojave tram.

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing3.strDesc:
You begin to pass exhibits of the squad's work, pockets of defence neutralised, dead bodies and shell casings drifting slowly to the floor. Occasionally you can hear humming up ahead, automatic weapons riffing in classic call and response.

Passing through the last choke point you find one of your marines leaning against a wall, listlessly spraying coagulating foam across a nasty pattern of holes in the abdomen of his suit. "Go on in," he says, weakly. "CASEVAC's on the way."

You enter a large cavern fifty metres a side: a headquarters at a nexus of tunnels, sporting a barracks and comms equipment and weapons galore. There's easily thirty Xinhua marines here, a whole platoon, moving with purpose to secure enemy territory. A handful are guarding surrendered Confederate resistance fighters, and two are performing enthusiastic but probably doomed paramedicine for a young man on the brink of death.

In the centre of the cavern, in pride of place, is the Colchian Sarcophagus. On top of it, cross-legged, sits Francisco Ortega. He perks up when you enter, with barely concealed eagerness.

"[us-firstname]! Nice of you to join us."

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing4.strDesc: The marines are reluctant to linger near you and Ortega. Whatever you're about to discuss, they don't want to know. That suits you fine. "You better give me some answers, Frank," you say, voice pitched low. "This is a nightmare." "It is," he says solemnly. "But with you here, it's going to be victory, very soon. Okay, answers: here we go." He takes out a slim digital wafer from a pocket and twists it. It cracks satisfyingly, the break planned by the manufacturer. He hands it to you. "I've cleared you for Operation Valkyrie," he says. "Everything I'm about to say will be on that pad, all our intel, analysis, reports. Read it when I'm done. Suffice it to say, if you've talked with Ben, you have some idea of what's at stake, and what's about to happen." "We'll get to that," you say. "First, why me? Why bring me in on the Yangtze?" "I was clutching at straws," he says. "Valkyrie is not the most popular doomsday project ever conceived. There are retrograde elements on our side who want it to fail. Bringing Ben in, there was extreme risk - all-but certain - he would liquidated before he could help us. It was a snap decision on my part, mysteriously fumbling the key piece of the puzzle, but hey." He shrugs, a veteran gambler who bet it all on red and then watched it come up red. "It worked." "That was me walking through customs a couple of hours ago," you say. "If it hadn't worked, if they wised up, I'd be dead." "But they didn't and you're not," he says easily. "It's what we in the intelligence community call a Lord of the Rings play. Y'know, giving the ring to a sneaky hobbit -" "Stop that," you say, as heated as is humanly possible in a team huddle. "Stop the flippant attitude and have some professional courtesy. Everyone here is risking their life on your whim." That sobers him up, slips through a crack in his jaded armour. "You're right," he says. "You're right. I apologise. You came through for me." "Good," you say, mollified. "So. What is Valkyrie?"

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing5.strDesc:
He takes the digital wafer and thumbs it a couple of times. He turns it back to you. It's displaying an internal intelligence document, authored by a working group identified by number alone. "Analysis of the theoretical capabilities of teleportation-assisted weapons," he says. "Valkyrie is the outcome. The quickest, safest way to win the war with Titan is never to have it in the first place."

He taps the screen. Technical specifications, blueprints, a CAD rendering of a device constructed on a nanometre scale. "Dot explosives," he says. "Titan thinks we're going to launch an amphibious assault on Virginia, because they've been dreaming about something like that since they took Omaha beach. Not so. Once we have that man in that box," he jabs decisively at the braincase and the sarcophagus, "we're going to zap a dot explosive into the head of every three star general and above in the Department of Defense."

You digest that. He thinks for a second, adding: "And the President, Vice President, a few key Congresspeople, you get the gist."

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing6.strDesc:
"And then?" you say, feeling faintly queasy.

"What do you mean, 'and then'? Poof! No more military command," he says impatiently. "There's no way around it. We could try and hold them hostage - what then? Resentment festers until they retaliate, and we're back to square one. We need to decapitate it, completely, in one stroke. Let the hydra grow back a head that can conceive of a truce."

"You think this will work," you say. Not really a question.

Ortega fidgets, drumming on the lid of the sarcophagus. "There is no good option," he says. "This is the best we can do. Try asking a Titanian about Hiroshima sometime. They're certain superweapon deterrence worked when they did it."

"I see," you say. "Turnabout is fair play."

Ortega shakes his head. To him this is already a foregone conclusion. The only important actions remaining are those that must occur to bring it to pass. "What would you do? What do you want? The Jovian revolution, everywhere, ships fighting and dying and killing people like us, until there's nothing left to fight over? If you've got doubts, I'll hear 'em, but spare me the equivocation."

The scope of this is too big for one person to process. Certainly, it's past the point where things may be averted. "No matter what I think," you say slowly, "it's out of my hands." You glance at the Xinhua platoon, steadfastly ignoring this exchange of ideas on the other side of the proscenium.

"Yes," says Ortega, with heavy finality. "It is."

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing7.strDesc:
You're left to your own devices for some time. You let Ortega take Ben off your hands.

New arrivals enter the cavern, a second contingent of marines escorting men and women in civilian pressure suits. A mixture of intelligence officers and theoretical physicists, judging by how they separate into camps, delegating members as go-betweens, ants from separate hives convinced to co-operate. They set up equipment - arcane even to your broad fields of expertise, and so probably designed for this task - around the sarcophagus.

You bounce between boredom, fear, elation, shame, guilt, and enough time passes that boredom massively wins out. Where's God in all of this, you wonder, the Colchian's or Ben's or an alien's or yours? If He has any opinion on the proceedings, He's kept it to Himself so far.

Your banzhang, the sergeant you stood up, coughs at your side, jolting you from reverie. "Oh," you say. "Is it over? Did we win?"

Her expression is guarded. "They need you."

"They need me what?"

"They need you in the sarcophagus too."

ValkyrieInterstitialPostCrossing8.strDesc: "My orders are to bring you to the box," she continues, watching as your eyes slide towards the exits: they are all blocked by stone-faced marines. "Preferably conscious."

ChoongFinaleDecideXinhuaWait.strDesc:
He walks away from you. You're left to your own devices for a bit. Choong broods - and broods, and broods, and broods.

At long last he returns to you. "Let's have it your way, then." An ocean of relief washes over you. "But I don't want to see you again," he continues. Any rapport you had has clearly vanished, a small price to pay. "Even if you're right, I don't have to like it, nor you."

"Deal," you say, after a moment long enough to be polite.

ChoongFinaleDecideTitan.strTitle: Convince him to side with Titan
ChoongFinaleDecideTitan.strDesc:
"If Titan get the teleportation tech first, they can destroy Xinhua without firing a single shot."

Choong looks at you like you've grown an extra head. "And?"

"And, they'll win." He's not getting it. "No apocalyptic interplanetary war. You'd be saving millions of lives, even the System itself."

Choong's eyes steadily enlarge, rapidly ascending through degrees of disbelief. "If you think I'm giving the secret of functional omnipotence to the CIA, you're as bugfuck insane as they are."

"Just because we don't hear about them in the news, doesn't mean they're not heroes-"

"I'd rather you put me back in the pain room," he says flatly. "And set it to max."

ChoongFinaleDecideAppealToGod.strTitle: Convince him to ask a deity for help
ChoongFinaleDecideAppealToGod.strDesc: "Something or someone through the sarcophagus can surely help us," you say. "If you go through, you can find an alien who can stop the war. Or save Earth." "It's not a cosmic vending machine," he says. "Doctor Who isn't waiting in the wings to abolish the commodity form." He's talking in academic-ese again. "We don't know that isn't true," you say. "The God of New Colchis seemed benevolent. What would it do if you promised it a few million more followers?" He starts, as if zapped with a mild electric current. A faint sweat breaks out on his forehead. "That's such a ... you actually want to invoke deus ex machina. It's insane." "I don't know what that means," you say. "I'm saying you should ask a God to prevent the apocalypse." "That's exactly what it means!" "Oh," you say. Then what is he so hung up on? "Another concept for me to research." He takes a moment to calm himself, breathing carefully, and continues. "Ethically, you can't magic humanity to become less warlike or more trusting of one another." "I don't see why not, and I really don't care," you say. "The alternative is no more humans. The alternative is you, sitting here, talking to Mr Moretti for the rest of your short life. No disrespect, sir," you say to the old gentleman, who waves the very thought away. "You're still afraid of going into the sarcophagus." "Yes," he says, not bothering to hide it. "It scares me." "You know the end is coming, Dr. Choong," you say. "There's a chance you can change that. Don't make the same mistake again." You see that hit home. From there, the battle is won, and it's a matter of clearing up Dr Choong's remaining objections. He's ready to return.

ChoongFinaleDecideKetevan.strTitle: Convince him to reunite with Ketevan
ChoongFinaleDecideKetevan.strDesc:
"At the end of the day, I'm a romantic, too," you say. "Have you never wanted to be with Ketevan again?"

"Every day for twenty years," he says.

"Good. Me too." You motion at him as if he's a child afraid to enter a dark room. "You can."

"Oh, yes," he says. "Just like that?"

"Yes," you say firmly. "Just like that." It seems he responds best to bold claims substantiated mostly by tone of voice. It's a bit like talking to customer service.

"I don't know where she is," he says petulantly. "Or what she is. Maybe she's nothing. Maybe it was all hallucination. Maybe it's a cosmic prison. She could as easily be in Hell as Heaven."

"From what you told me about Ketevan, I doubt any of that," you say, "and if it is true, I doubt it would slow someone like her down. She's waiting for you. Somewhere out there, amongst the stars."

Choong goes quiet. "Thank you for saying that, [us-firstname]. God knows I want it to be true, too." He rubs the fabric of his shirt between his fingertips. "What else have I to lose?"

ChoongFinaleDecideSelfPreservation.strDesc:
"You wanted a body again," you say. "I think there's a ludicrously small chance of that ever happening."

"Harsh, but true," he says.

"So I think you go hard as you can in the other direction," you say. "Use the sarcophagus. Transcend this mortal coil. Whatever you become on the other side, surely it's better than this."

"And what if it's the exact same situation?" he says. "If there, too, I'm a consciousness dependent on life support and charity, what have I gained?"

"Not to be reductive, but everyone's dependent on life support and charity," you say. "From before we're born, to a considerable time after. I'm happy to keep feeding you like a pet smartfish, but why should you be? You've hit rock bottom. Dig up."

In the end, he's persuaded there may be something better for him. He's loathe to admit it, but you can tell part of him will miss the comfy chair by the fire.

ChoongLeaveAndEnd.strDesc:
Duty calls. You prepare to take off the headset, and deliver the pair of you to your fates. You remember one question.

"You said you were going to tell me what your God told you, right?"

Choong nods, a little embarrassed, as if he was hoping you had forgotten that pinned discussion.

"I did. It ..." He locks eyes with you, daring you to challenge him on his last, and therefore closest kept secret. "It told me to trust whoever would share my burdens," he says. "I thought that was general advice. Basically a platitude. It wasn't until today I considered it relevant, or specific."

He laughs, once, mirthlessly. "I suppose I've never met anyone willing to share my burdens before now."

"You think it foresaw this happening?" you ask.

"God knows all," he says. There isn't much more to say.

ChoongHistory_1.strDesc:
"When we lost contact with Earth, that changed things." He gets a faraway look in his eye, as if he's watching an explosion from a great distance. 

He waves his hands, trying to circumscribe the disaster. "Forgive me for lingering on this point. All our institutions went into survival mode, and never really left. I was an anthropology fellow, and of course there was never any funding, and then it became: gun to your head, justify your entire field. How does studying people - Earthers no less, who are probably all dead - keep us from starvation in the next five years?" The question answers itself: not in any way.

He shrugs and continues. "Luckily I was working on a thesis that the department quite liked, and I actually got funding. I survived the cull. I went to live with Belter communities, to study the strange fringe groups emerging in isolation. I had a camera, some data cards, a couple of PDAs. That's it."

AVClub_The_Return_Cops_MakeBreak_RunAway.strDesc:
You defer to the wisdom of crowds.

Flotilla is a maze, and not one you're familiar with. If anyone has a destination in mind, they don't stop to tell you. You join the mad scramble, pausing occasionally to listen out for the sounds of Ayosec behind you, and at one confusing juncture, in front of you.

The congealed ships echo with gunfire and screams. It's unusual for AyoSec to operate beyond their stomping grounds around Ganymed, but as the well-armed Flotillans know, not unprecedented. You can hear when Ayo hit a pocket of resistance: the fire tempo spikes and the timbre of answering munitions takes on a distinctly illegal tone.

After gaining some distance on the advancing corporate forces, the crowds slow down, and the tone shifts from panicked to wary. People form slower-moving knots, coordinating and keeping lookout and trying desperately to access the wireless mesh.

AVClub_The_Return_Cops_MakeBreak_RunAgai.strDesc:
Trying to slip through the panicky human tide is difficult going. Nobody's prepared for some damn fool running into them, as you are. The next few minutes is kinetic chaos as you alternate between squeaking by on the periphery and shoulder-checking two, three people whenever you need to cross the passage.

The flow against you ceases without warning. Rounding a corner, you face an AyoSec compliance team.

AVClub_The_Return_FinishTape.strDesc:
Smiley's gone from his customary position at the PDA. You hit play, heedless of the confusion around you.

The singing returns in full force, a warm counterpoint to the impending threat. The timeline preview shows the honour guard milling around without change, so you track forward a couple of times, looking for anything that stands out. The singing cuts and chops sharply.

There! A flicker. You scrub back. The audio is overwhelmed with static, and in a heartbeat, the sarcophagus goes from inert to brighter than the sun, whiting out the screen.

"What the fuck!" says someone in the room, either following the video or unprepared for the blinding light, or at a burst of gunfire. 

"This is Ayotimiwa Security," says an amplified voice outside. "This is a routine zoning compliance sweep. Present your identity papers and residential licence. Show us empty hands or be shot on sight."

You scrub to the end of the video. The honour guard cheer, hug each other, weeping for joy.

The sarcophagus is open, and the youth is nowhere to be seen.

AVClub_The_Return_LookEscape.strDesc:
The Flotilla has been the victim of idiosyncratic retrofitting since day one. There's bound to be another way out.

Taking stock of the room, Smiley is nowhere to be found. There's a press at the door as several try to exit at once. Abacho stands nervously against one wall, by one of the interior doors. He waves at you.

You bound across the low common area, almost colliding with Molly Liu as she emerges from the kitchenette with a sawn-off flechette gun. You give her a wide berth. She cocks the gun, mouth set, and heads for the exit too.

You reach Abacho at speed, bouncing off the wall. He catches you. "In here, in here!" he says.

AVClub_The_Return_LookEscape_GoInside.strDesc:
It's a bunkroom, where three others from the club are waiting nervously.

Two walls of the cramped bunkroom are inset bunks, stacked four high. The far wall is festooned in foldout storage blocks, all closed. One is covered by a "Hang In There!" poster, showing a muscly Petware cat doing pullups on an iron bar.

Abacho rips it down to reveal an exposed vent shaft. "There's a safehouse. Go one left, fifty metres. Two rights, then one left. Got that?" There's a harried chorus of assent. "Good enough. Get in!"

The remnants of the AV Club wedge themselves into the vent. When it's your turn, Abacho steps between you and the hole. "One moment. This is important."

AVClub_The_Return_LookEscape_Smoked.strDesc:
He searches your eyes. Unbidden, you stare back into his. Is it your imagination, or are they tinged with flecks of gold?

He nods, satisfied. "I had to know. Smiley vouched for you, but he's gone. He might be a rat, I don't know. But you're good."

"Ayosec is coming for you?"

He shrugs. "It doesn't matter. Sooner or later, something was coming." He lays down on the floor, hands over his head. "Get out of here. I'm the legal resident. They might just let me live."

With one last look at the prostrated man, you climb into the vent.

AVClub_The_Return_LookEscape_DidNotSmoke.strDesc:
Abacho produces the weed pen you rejected earlier.

"We have zero time here, so I'm going to be very clear. Smoke this, right now. Or take your chances outside."

Every ounce of confusion and outrage condenses into a single word: "What?!" But Abacho is unimpressed.

"Smoke it now," he repeats testily. "3, 2, 1, smoke."

AVClub_The_Return_VentEscape.strDesc:
It's slow going. The vent network is almost inhumanly tight, and everyone grows familiar with accidental kicks to the face. Abacho's directions are superfluous, as his route is also the only one you're able to fit through.

In the meantime, you have plenty to listen to. The metal underneath resonates with boots tromping, screams, and sporadic gunfire. Your fingers slip on the surface as your sweat forms a greasy layer across your upper body.

Everyone freezes as you crawl past a dorm room being invaded by Security. You watch the scene unfold through the a vent grille. The officers storm the room, round up the residents, and cable tie their hands. There's little you can do besides wait, desperately afraid to make a sound. One of the younger, sprier captives tries to make a break for it when he sees an opening, but a round catches him in the spine before he makes it to the door. Less-lethal or not, he stops moving.

Then there's a rigamarole of theatre as the individuals have their IDs scanned, which are invariably found wanting, and are packed into cubes aboard the skiff idling in the passageway.

CeresP3Finale1.strDesc: A runner catches up to you, out of breath and sweating with the gravity. "[us-fullname]!" she says in between gasps. "We humbly request your presence aboard the Yangtze-3." The Yangtze is a Xinhua warship that has been docked with Ceres for months, ostensibly conducting wargames and small-unit tactics drills for Coalition marines. "Who are you?" you ask, once the woman has stopped puffing. She's dressed in aggressively smart casual, with buzzed hair and a deceptively muscular build. "Oh," she says. She conspicuously looks around to check no one is listening. "Have you ever grown nightshades?" You look at her. "You have to give me the counter-phrase," she says, much too loudly. "Just take me to your leader," you say wearily.

CeresP3Finale2.strDesc: The clueless marine-cum-field agent trots ahead of you all the way to the restricted docks. There you are handed off to a series of Xinhua Navy crewmen, who each guide you a short distance until they hand you over like a baton: into the Yangtze's bay, into the Yangtze itself, leaving you parked in the Yangtze's mess hall for thirteen minutes. Finally a junior officer asks you to follow her to the wardroom. No-one seems to know what this is about. An officer with three stars on their vac suit admits you both to the wardroom. They make a show of scanning your temporary shipboard ID and comparing it with your face. It's already over capacity, stone-faced Navy men and women waiting with subdued impatience, and you only get in with a lot of silent shuffling. Still, your junior officer as if by magic conjures an empty chair at the central table, and ushers you into it. The others around the table, sitting and standing two deep, spare you only a glance, if that. At the far end of the wardroom, a bulging array of screens like an insectoid eye is awash with information. Every twenty seconds or so, for no reason you can discern and with no pattern, the lights flicker.

CeresP3FinaleScreens.strDesc:
Half the screens show live camera feeds clustered together in one hemisphere. The other half show spectral imaging of the station, accompanied by long text outputs that surely could not be relevant within the limited time available to read them. The long table in front of you is overlaid with a fabric-screen displaying a schematic view of the station and its docked ships, including this one. It's pockmarked by green coloured circles denoting friend, red circles for foe, and grey for unknowns. There are a great deal of unknowns.

You scan the live feeds. It takes a second to comprehend, but they're spy cams from the POV of operatives in situ, half a dozen at least. Occasionally the screen jumps to a new perspective you've not yet seen. It's a dizzying demonstration of clandestine power. One of the camera feeds is from a street food vendor handing out fried scorpion on a stick. Two pose as a couple romantically entwined, faces pixellated to hide their identities. So many eyes here, there, everywhere, you think, palms itching. You'd never know.

CeresP3FinaleListen.strDesc:
A woman in crisp civilian clothes stands to one side of the monitor array, holding the room in rapt attention as she speaks. In the dim LED blue you can just faintly see that she's sporting a shiner of a black eye. There are fresh scrapes medically stapled shut on her hands. "Reminder that while the floor is open to questions, we are approaching zero hour. At zero hour, our analyst pool on the hardline will handle operational affairs, priority one, and the ship will go dark." Her voice is measured, collected. You think if the station's reactor went critical before your eyes, she'd coolly narrate the whole thing.

"The object," says an older man - balding, overweight, the only one in the room sporting a tobacco pipe, and therefore the Captain - "is the informant on the station Concourse. What'd'you call'im? 'Mothman'?"

"Correct," says the woman, whom you dub the Steward. "He poses as a dilletante, a cultural journalist. It's cover for his role as a fence, trading rare earth metals with the opposition, including V-79. There's further background in your briefing packets."

"This is your dog and pony show." The Captain waves the pipe dismissively. "I'm just playing host."
