ChoongKetevan.strDesc:
"Tell me about Ketevan," you say, "the girl who became one with God."

"What about her?" he asks politely.

If there is a reason this man has been tortured to death and back, it is surely this, you reflect. For it is obvious that he is preparing to become evasive, preparing to deceive, even if he has tried and failed time and time before. Though represented by this software-dream projection of his body, he cannot help but send unconscious signals through it.

What a tragedy for Dr. Benjamin Choong, that he be born a terrible liar.

"How did you meet?"

"Probably in a refectory," he says, squinting, "The main social hubs, shared eating spaces, that kind of thing."

"You knew each other."

"Oh, in a sense," he says, "by sight. We saw each other around. You got to know everyone in those tight-knit communities."

"You knew her by sight," you repeat. "So what, you invented the name 'Ketevan'?"

"I knew her name." He stares at the table between you. "I knew everyone's name. I'm good with names."

"An academic, good with names," you say drily. "What's my name, Ben? I told you right after we met."

He opens his mouth. And shuts it again. His gaze is squarely down.

"I'm [us-fullname]. I'm a ship captain from K-LEG. I'm not your jailer."

He chooses not to reply, nor to look up.

ChoongKetevanLying.strTitle: Tell him he's lying about Ketevan
ChoongKetevanLying.strDesc: "I think you're lying to me," you say, "about this woman. I don't know how exactly." "Do your worst," he says. The words are defiant, even though they come from a man who could be reasonably mistaken for a ghost. You stand up and walk to the fire. Stretching your legs helps to think, though of course it also reminds you that your legs are curled beneath you on the floor of your ship. "Is this a lie you've told before?" you ask him. No reply. "I can't imagine I'm the first person to realise that," you say to the fire. A log shifts a little, and it sparks eagerly. "You must have clammed up, and they would have pressured you." The fire is much more interested in your ideas than Ben. "Did you break?" you say to the man, silent and still in his chair. "Have you already broken? How many times? And why try it to keep silent, even now?" He says nothing. "It's -" you catch yourself, a sentence halfway out the door. It's going to be easier if you're honest with me. A cliche straight out of a movie. But that's the difficulty. What can you tell this man? There's no point lying. Look where you are. I'm actually on your side! All these cliches had sounded farcical until this very second, now that they are bizarrely applicable; and cliches are all you have, because you have not the first idea how to talk to a prisoner, how to get them to reveal what they know, how to win their trust. That's the trouble. He expects that you're going to start torturing him yourself, and if he really doesn't believe you, what will you do?

ChoongKetevanPress1.strDesc:
"I want to know more about Ketevan," you say plainly. "Because you don't want to tell me."

He quirks his eyebrows, saying nothing. A mute parry - 'good for you'.

"She's the sole Belter you've named. She must've been important."

No reply.

ChoongKetevanPress3.strDesc:
"Maybe you were in love."

No reply.

ChoongKetevanPress4.strDesc:
"Under the surface, I'll bet you're a romantic at heart."

No reply.

ChoongKetevanPress5.strDesc:
"Are researchers supposed to fall in love with their subjects?"

No reply, but a palpable hit: he's affronted, angry.

Plot_Scholar_Flat_Racks.strDesc: About a dozen containers of various sizes line the walls. Some are embedded in the floor. Where to start?

Plot_Scholar_Racks_North.strDesc: Nothing here but a collection of research tomes. You are impressed by the range of disciplines covered: mathematics, engineering, art, chemistry, and the histories of ancient Earth civilizations.

Plot_Scholar_Racks_East.strDesc: This set, near the workbench, is full of tools and small parts. Some remain neatly organized. Others are knocked to the ground.

Plot_Scholar_Racks_Floor.strDesc: These appear meant for large item storage. Rolls of textile, stacks of thin metal sheeting, measured glassware, some larger tools and ... something behind the soldering iron there? A seam?

Plot_Scholar_Racks_Floor_Seam.strDesc: You move the tools aside and press the seam softly. It releases a spring and pops open a tiny hatch, not much larger than the palm of your hand. Inside you find a tiny black notebook. It is a graphed ledger penned in a neat hand. Names, dates, and a final column, unlabeled at the top, but with entries behind each name. John Wayne (GalCon) Francisco Ortega (Xinhua) Han Xiaoli (GalCon Double) Lawrence Masterson (GalCon) Pan Tao (GalCon) Flipping to the very back page of the notebook, you find two additional lines cw GalGon: Q: Where is true West? A: Follow the evening redness. cw Xinhua: Q: Have you ever grown nightshades? A: Only in borrowed soil.

PLOT_Ceres_Ask_Prove_BCRS.strDesc:
You approach Francisco Ortega. He's looking jumpy as usual. Careful as you can, you ask how someone like you can prove your loyalty to the Xinhua cause.  

"You have a few options,"  Ortega starts.

"First is territory. The whole belt is in open conflict. Might makes right. If you trade for a Xinhua beacon, you can take it out to unclaimed space near some profitable asteroids. Deploy it and we have eyes on those rocks. Keeps our supply lines open."

"Titan's deploying their own beacons, you could neutralize them - so long as you feel safe in enemy territory."

"The cause can always use able pilots. If you're feeling brave, you can sieze or destroy a Titan allied vessel. Demand their surrender, or take them out by force."

"Lastly, mining. The belt is rich. If you find some ore, you can sell it to one of our faction kiosks here. That gets you scrip for more weapons and beacons, and it helps fill our coffers."

"Besides that, you could try and run special ... errands for our mutual friend. Check the coffee machine. It's a dead drop, so we don't have to keep meeting like this."
PLOT_Ceres_Ask_Prove_BCRS.strTooltip: [them-firstname] may have advice for how to prove your loyalty to Xinhua.

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strDesc:
The man is two bites in to a mushroom burger. "Francisco Ortega?" you ask.

"Yes?" he says, digging in a bag for a sauce capsule.

"I'm looking for Benjaming Choong."

Ortega chokes, coughing up crumbs and a single mushy chunk. He whirls about. "Who the hell are you? What outfit are you from?" he hisses. You fold your arms and give him nothing. He scans the crowd anxiously. "I'll get ahold of someone with clearance. The Fountain, half an hour. Be there."

He shoulders past you, eager to pretend you've never met.
PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strTooltip: [them-firstname]'s social profile matches a name on Choong's hidden document. Maybe [them-subj] [knows] something.

ENCFirstDockBCRSLeave.strDesc:
Your encounter with Eleni ends there, on that note, with only the customary sorting of payment and debt to plow through - a neutral and empty space, in contrast to the strangeness of the whole sit-down. She insists on paying. You let her, and promise to get the next one, which is never going to happen.

You amble back to the concourse to bid your final goodbyes. The desperation of the shoppers and the sellers seems muted now, and no more greeters try to inveigle you into their stores, such is the change in your aura.

"Be seeing you," Eleni says. She makes a curious circle gesture with one hand - a goodbye? - and is gone.

What an odd duck.

ENCFirstDockBCRSHmm3.strDesc:
"Scratch that," you say, "don't forget I asked. I want to nail this down, whatever it is."

"Mm?" she says, smiling politely, meaninglessly.

That's it. That's what it is.

"You said," you say slowly. It's as if you're on the cusp of waking. The words are there, but struggling to be said. "You said the Calicoans ..."

"Yes," she says unhappily.

"You said they were taught to worship a way of life that never was ..."

"I did," she says. "I did say that." She scowls. But it's just an expression. There's no feeling behind it.

"A man on K-Leg said something very similar to me before I left," you say.

She waves a hand questioningly.

ENCFirstDockBCRSHmm4.strDesc:
"I'm going to ask again," you say. "Tell me the truth. Do I know you?"

Eleni stops fidgeting with her necklace, and places her hands in her lap. "Well, now. That's one question I can't help you with."

Her eyes, behind her thick glasses, are magnified like a bug's. The overblown pupils reach the hard edges of the frame as they dart around, scanning the room. They recentre, and she fixes you with a strangely steely gaze.

Inside that steel, a trace of gold.

The name comes unbidden to your lips, and once arrived, refuses to leave. It doesn't make sense, and yet out it comes. "... Smiley?"

The question hangs between you like a smart munition searching for a target.

She smiles at you. No more maternal beneficence. It recalls Smiley's fixed, dopey trademark - but with a new element, a wildcard that turns the wide silly expression predatory.

"It's me. In the flesh," she - they? He? - says, and sighs. "The flesh and like a kilo of silicone prosthetics, anyway. Shit. [us-firstname], how've you been?"

"How have I been?" you say hollowly. "Fuck you. Whoever you are, go fuck yourself. What is going on?"

"I'm trying to help you," she says - you settle on she for now, with nothing else to go on. "You wandered away from K-LEG and wound up at Ceres, from the frying pan into the fire, truly. And I suppose I have a soft spot for a fellow AV Clubber."

"I want nothing more to do with you." You stand up. Heads turn your way. You're not bothering to lower your voice.

"Sit down," she says levelly. One of her hands, under the table, seems to be tracking your every movement. 

You ease back into your chair. You've seen people in similar situations, in crowded rooms on K-LEG. You try desperately to remember how they ended.

"Thank you," she says conversationally, as if you had passed her a sauce packet. She runs a tongue along her teeth, then reaches into her mouth. She spits into her hand, and tosses a large set of dentures onto the table. The long white teeth drip, saliva strung between the points.

"That," she says, again running a tongue around her mouth, "was driving me crazy."

ENCFirstDockBCRSHmm2.strDesc: "What happens now?" you ask. "We're just talking," she says. It's surreal: Smiley and Eleni, the thesis and the antithesis, swim together, pooling into something new. "Talking normally, calmly. Let's not put Niko out. I had to learn Greek for this bit, I don't want to burn it." "So you're not Greek." "I am not." "Then what?" "An Episcopalian." She shrugs. "What's it to you?" "You got all your 'friends' on K-Leg killed, or shipped off to Prokofiev," you hiss. "I barely got out. That's what it is to me." "That," she says, appearing a little hurt, "was not my fault. That was quite a setback for me, actually. I'm picking up the pieces." "You think you're a victim in all this?" "I didn't say that," she says, smiling hungrily. "It's that old adage - you know, 'nobody thinks of themselves as a villain'. Right? When an adult says it to a child, they're implying: 'therefore, because it's relative, there's no such thing as a villain!' An early pitfall in your conception of other people, and people shoot right on through to adulthood without revisiting it." You stare across at the table. "What the fuck are you talking about?" "I'm trying to say, a single counterexample torpedoes the whole thing." She points to herself. "And that's me. I'm the counterexample." You don't want to repeat yourself, so you think of the next most pertinent question. "Can I go now?" Smiley, Eleni, whoever she is, edges out of the booth first. "Way ahead of you. It's on my tab." You can see the pistol now. At least you weren't falling for a bluff - that's nice to know. She stows it under her coat. "I really was trying to help," she says. "Be seeing you." She slips out of the cafe. The host looks up at her departure, frowning. You finish your coffee, trying to shake a sudden attack of depersonalisation. The videotape ... not for the first time since K-Leg, you wish you'd never found it.

Braincase1_1.strDesc:
He places you in front of the fire, a cup of coffee before you, and a blanket across your shoulders. "That ought to help," he says. "If not, you can turn off the cold in the settings menu. I wouldn't, though."

You try to stop your teeth from chattering, and to suppress the urge to immediately open the menu and slam that slider to zero. "W-why not?"

He shrugs, taking the armchair opposite you. "I've come to appreciate it. Being cold, and growing warm again." He holds his hands out to the hearth. "Ever warmed yourself by a fire?" A quick runthrough of your entire life: you have not. You raise your hands to the fire as well. It's too hot, and you pull back. He laughs softly. "For our ancestors, this was the cutting edge of entertainment."

ChoongEnvironment_1.strDesc:
"Okay," you say, shoving the unbidden word association aside. "But why?"

"It's one of a handful of presets bundled with oneirotic software. My captors spared every expense," Choong says dismissively, eyeing the bottles of gin and rum on the mantle above the fireplace. "This one was an ad for Moretti coffee." You remember something about that - for a while, all the corps were abuzz over having their own branded dreamscapes, before the tech was overwhelmingly and inextricably associated with porn. "That's Mr. Moretti over there."

You follow where he points, to another chair off to the side. An old Italian man, with a steaming coffee cup and a face like dark leather, nods to you. His face and body settle into a perfect match for the famous Moretti silhouette logo.

ChoongEnvironment_1_1.strDesc: "Can he hear us?" you whisper, startled that you hadn't noticed him before. "I'm minding my business," the old man says, his voice high and thin. Euro accented, tastefully done. Choong makes a quick face at you - eyes wide, grimacing, as if to say, what can you do?

ChoongVideotapesDemo_1.strTitle: Jack out and slot the tapes
ChoongVideotapesDemo_1.strDesc:
You jack out, find the copy you made of Videotape #3, and upload it to the Renbao rig. You jack back in to find Choong staring at the ceiling, literally twiddling his thumbs.

You conjure the video and hit play. Choong leans forward. There's a shock of recognition when he sees the footage. Oddly, he has an even greater shock when it gets to the Lunar portion of the tape. The rest of it doesn't elicit anything, even the very end with the bizarre ritual.

"You've seen this before," you say to him, certain.

"No," he says. "I made this."

ChoongVideotapesDemo_1_1.strDesc:
A-hah. Less a puzzle piece sliding into place, more checking the reference image to confirm you put it in the right spot. "Explain."

"I took it in New Colchis," he says. "This is my footage. Or it used to be. Someone's edited it anachronically, so it appears cryptic." He frowns. "They've even spliced it with my old lecture recordings."

That sparks something. "Did you ever get odd jobs as a videographer, or make an ad for the school?"

"Off and on I would, to make rent." He groans. "And I remember that ad. It took Terry Wu the whole shoot to string one complete sentence together. No wonder he took an axe to the arts program, he was barely literate. Why do you ask?"

"That was on another tape," you say. "With more of your filmography."

"The plot thickens," he says. "Or does it? This still makes zero sense to me. The plot stays thick. The plot is a superdense nugget of," he casts around for a word, "stuff."

ChoongPlateau_1Exit.strDesc:
Choong stretches, and checks his watch, a cheap Renbao tchotchke made and worn as an anachronism.

"Do you want to take a break?" you ask. "Do you feel tired, you know ... here?"

"I'm game if you are," he says. "It's this or the media library." He half-smiles. It's something he's thoroughly sick of by now.

ChoongTakeBreak.strDesc:
"I could use a moment, if I'm honest."

Choong nods. "I'm in no rush. Do what you need to do, and I'll be here when you're ready." He pumps a fist, smiling. "Keep fighting that good fight."

He's in high spirits, all things considered.

ChoongInsistAliens.strDesc:
"But," you say, "they say their God talked to them. They developed a working teleportation device. That's not by random chance. How could an alien not be behind it?"

"An alien could be behind it," he says, and in his voice you can hear the pedagogic gears begin to turn. "It simply doesn't answer anything important, like why it would tell them to do it, or how. We can't see this alien of yours," he says, 'of yours', as if this is your wild fancy. "We can't touch it, hear it, or observe it in any way, and we only know of it through secondhand testimony. I don't know how or why everything has happened the way it did," he says, trying to make it sound like a concession, "but, speaking metaphysically, saying 'an alien did it' is the same conclusion as 'God did it' or 'a wizard did it'. It's not important."

That's you told. You sit back, considering him, rather than his words. The teacher voice he puts on, is that something he brings out whenever he's arguing disingenuously? A persona he adopts to conceal his true feelings? It's a compelling trick, to bog you down in argumentation, but something tells you he didn't experience everything he did and come out the other side without deciding for himself one way or the other.

ChoongInsistAliens2.strDesc:
"You're playing games with me," you say. He looks at you levelly. It's how you might imagine the captain of an enemy ship, as you come about, revealing to their scopes an underbelly bristling with weapons running hot. Contact.

"You said you believe they've discovered a technology that contradicts all of physics," you say, resisting the urge to fidget. "Now you pretend to be disinterested in how they did it."

"Uninterested," he says automatically.

"Whatever!" you snap, wondering how things got to this point. "This phenomenon you claimed to witness, whatever it is, it's obviously supernatural. Why won't you admit that?"

"There's no such thing," he says.

"Excuse me?"

"There's no such thing as the supernatural, by definition," he says. "I don't mean to provoke you, but you have to allow me this point. 'Natural' encompasses all things that exist. 'Supernatural' describes things that do not, cannot, exist. If something exists, it is natural. If something does not exist, it is supernatural. Witnessing something and calling it supernatural is a category error, whether or not you can explain it."

More word games. "Do you believe the New Colchians discovered teleportation by accident," you say carefully, hoping to pin him with a yes-or-no. "Or not?"

He spreads his hands. "I don't know." 

This is as close as you can get to a win: you're sure that he's lying.

ChoongPlateau4.strDesc: Dr. Choong stares, eyes empty of emotion.

ChoongVideotapesDemo.strDesc:
You describe to him your story of finding a videotape in a derelict spaceship, drifting millions of kilometres from anywhere. He listens, nodding, not really understanding.

Finally when it comes to the videos themselves, you have a bright idea.

"Wait here," you say.

"I'm not going anywhere," he says, a shade reproachful.

ChoongAccuseKetevan.strDesc:
"You had an illicit relationship with Ketevan," you say. "That much is clear. But why would you be embarrassed or defensive about it when it happened decades ago? Because that's just a ruse. You must have moved on. She's probably dead, or -" and how to put the alternative? You shrug. "Or an angel or something. No doubt you've tied up your interrogators in knots for years pretending to hold on to that."

He's perfectly still - which is a dead giveaway. He seems to realise it himself after a moment. He takes a deep breath, and resettles in his chair. "I don't see how it concerns you," he says, "or anyone else, for that matter. What do you want, the poetry I wrote her? A knife carving in the hull, 'B+K'?"

"You're doing it again," you say evenly, "pretending it's the love affair you're protecting." He doesn't reply, and the only sound is the howling wind.

ChoongAccuseReligion.strTitle: He's lying about the Colchians' religion
ChoongAccuseReligion.strDesc:
"I don’t believe that you don’t believe in the supernatural," you say. "However you define it. However you rationalise it. I think you know more about the Colchian God, whatever it was."

"Okay, it was an alien. Happy?" He smirks.

"Not really, no." You look in your coffee cup. It’s long been empty. Shouldn’t it refill itself automatically, in a place like this? "Your whole life has been empirical observation. A claim that contradicts physical laws isn’t something you could equivocate about: 'oh, well maybe it’s real and nobody ever figured it out’. Then you dress up the contradiction with meaningless philosophy."

"Sophistry," he supplies the word for you. Then, after a second, "which, um, isn’t something I’m doing."

ChoongAccuseGeneral.strDesc:
"I dunno, man," you say. "You're not being honest somehow. There's a chunk missing from all of this. I can feel it. You know what it is, and you're not talking."

"I'm talking," he says, an edge of desperation to his voice, as if he's mentally preparing himself for more pain. "I'm doing nothing but."

Plot_Ceres_The_AV_Club_Lookup_Watch_Part.strDesc: [them] [uses] [them] to find a constellation of cryptic forum posts that make reference to The Flotilla, gold, something called The Black Sun, and a strange video format you have never heard of called a VHS tape.

InspectVideotape.strDesc:
It's a small black obelisk, unlike anything you've ever seen before.

You wave your PDA at it and wait for the image recognition suite to resolve. It's a 'videotape', says the precis, a kind of early analogue storage medium accessed via a VHS player. It eagerly regurgitates guff about the Format Wars. You swipe it away.

The shell has two clear windows on the front. Through those there are two spools holding a reel of tape. Maybe it's like a laundry back on the station, and you can look inside the player and watch the tape running.

What the hell was it doing out here?
InspectVideotape.strTooltip: Give the box a closer look

TurnTapeOver.strDesc:
You turn the shell over in your hands. The reverse side is covered with colourful stickers.

<mark=#ffd700ff><color="black">               BE KIND, REWIND :)<alpha=#00>a</alpha></color></mark>

<mark=#ff0000ff><color="black">               WARNING: DO NOT COPY.<alpha=#00>a</alpha></color></mark>
<mark=#ff0000ff><color="black">               COPYING TAPES IS A FELONY<alpha=#00>a</alpha></color></mark>

<mark=#ff00ffff><color="green">               NEW RELEASE! ONE NIGHT RENTAL!<alpha=#00>a</alpha></color></mark>

The PDA seems to think they are era-appropriate, which does not help you.

You notice one of the long edges has bright orange tape stuck to it. Thick block letters written with a marker pen read, <mark=#ffa600ff><color="black">    "VOID OPAL INHALANTS #3."     </color></mark> This one, which must be its title, makes even less sense.

Maybe you need to see Inhalants 1 & 2 to get it.

VideotapeOnlineResearch.strDesc: There's no use staring at the tape. The two unblinking windows in its hull aren't going to budge. You've got to ask other people about it, and it's not like you've got any friends - any who know about legacy home media, that is. Why not see what the local station net has to say?
VideotapeOnlineResearch.strTooltip: The internet will know what to do

VideotapeOnlineResearchHub.strDesc: The PDA glows, ready to assist you with your search.

VideotapeOnlineResearchScrollForums.strTitle: Hunt for any discussions of videotapes
VideotapeOnlineResearchScrollForums.strDesc: K-LEG has three main bulletin boards: the Ayotimiwa employee forums, the K-LEG official Subreddit, and Cho-Cho-Cho, the latter of which is by far the most popular, even if most of the features don't work. It's built that way on purpose. A cursory scan of the employee forums turns up nothing, and the subreddit has only a sticky post about how it's evil to pirate media. CCC, on the other hand, has more to say. You read several long chat threads about a 'videotape' and how excited the posters are to see it live. These actually concern an X-pop singer whose new single, videotape, is charting well across the inner system. But soon enough you strike gold. It's a locked thread, and the OP's account has been deleted. What remains are the replies from another concerned user, leaving behind a one sided conversation. >>> Do you mean like box? How big > DELETED >>> Ohh, I get you. no never. But ill keep my eyes peeled. > DELETED >>> Sorry i misunderstood. Sure I can take a look at it. Im at NoodlEgg stand for another 15 if you want to meet. > DELETED >>> hello? :fish_emoji: The timestamps are ten minutes apart between the final few posts. It's unclear if the deleted user showed up.

79AU_Inside2.strDesc:
You lay back in the comfortable sheets and watch the lobby for a while.

Not to put too fine a point on it: nothing happens. No events occur. Nothing transpires. Nothing happens. Nothing happens.

79AU_Inside3.strDesc:
You reach up and give the man behind the desk a wave.

He looks back pleasantly.

When this has gone on long enough that you think he's neither seen nor understood you, one of his hands crests the lip of the front desk and wiggles back at you.

79AU_Inside4.strDesc:
You muster your strength, heave, and fall out of the bed, knocking the wheelchair beyond your reach.

Nothing hurts, but you're stiff. The wheelchair, three feet away, might as well be at 80 AU.

You look to the receptionist. He looks at you.

You crawl toward the chair. At eye level with the wheels, you prop yourself up on one elbow and force the wheel locks on.

Then it's a simple but laborious matter of clambering up the chair without overbalancing it, rotating yourself to the correct orientation, and pulling your nonresponsive legs onto the footrests.

You have unlocked the ability to travel to various locations within the hotel.

79AU_Inside5.strDesc:
You turn the chair 180 degrees and head for the big double doors. Another liveried man is waiting there. As you pass an indeterminate threshold where your motion is read less as curiosity and more a desire to leave, the man opens the door for you.

The door opens on to the void of space. On the other side of that familiar gulf glitters the Milky Way core. From your vantage point, it isn't clear how the pressure imbalance is being maintained. You're not keen to find out.

You wheel the chair back. The doorman holds it until he's certain you won't return, then pulls it shut.

79AU_Inside6.strDesc:
The elevators move up and down the glass shaft, carrying no passengers that you can see.

You press a call button, but it seems to require a key card to pay any attention to you.

79AU_Inside7.strDesc:
You trundle past the common rooms - a restaurant, a bar, a laundry, all empty but for the staff - to the one that first caught your eye, the pool.

At first you think you're sweating. This proves to be a trick of your perception as you adjust to unfamiliar humidity, high enough that you can see the vapour in the air, rising from the twenty five metre swimming pool.

There's a lump in your throat. You've never seen so much water set aside for bathing.

79AU_Inside8.strDesc: You park yourself in front of the receptionist. The default opener, 'where am I?', seems redundant. You know you're in an alien megastructure. 'What is this place, who built it, who are you?' - it's all old hat. You rifle through things to say. Ah: you've got it. A hotel staple. "English?" you say. The receptionist nods. "Yes. It is." He's wearing a gold vest over a black shirt. Defying an expectation you didn't know you held, he's not generically handsome: he's older than the median, cheeks interestingly pocked by old acne scars, an indeterminate Eurasian cant to his features. He has the gravel voice of someone who starts smoking the second their shift ends, every day, for twenty years. It's pleasant. A name bar on his lapel, in a thick serif, says Joakim.

79AU_Inside9.strDesc:
"You're not human," you say.

"No," he agrees, "I am not."

He holds up a finger: wait. He revolves his hand so that the finger points back at his chest.

He reaches his other hand across his breast to his side. He clutches an unseen handhold and pulls open his chest like a stove door. Inside is an engineer's nightmare of clockwork, circuitry, gas valves, and mechanical arms transferring tiny gizmos from buffer to buffer.

He closes the door after you've had a good look. His vest and shirt show no signs of damage, nor of having been parted at all.

Clockwork would have a difficult job carrying out the functions that Joakim can - but that might be impolite to say. And he only showed what was underneath his chest. The tricky components might be elsewhere.

"Thank you for showing me that," you say.

He flaps a hand. "It was no trouble."

79AU_Night11.strDesc:
Opposite you is President Ose, now wearing a striking velvet dinner jacket in a rich burgundy hue. You meet his yellow eyes and find nothing there."

"Players may now select a partner," says Joakim. "Provided the partner is willing."

79AU_Ose12.strTitle: I like the sound of the other guys
79AU_Ose12.strDesc:
"I don't doubt it," Ose says. "It's a seductive idea, moving to and fro without aim, guided by nothing more than desire. Motes floating on the solar winds. Sounds quaint."

"It does."

"I know your kind has that impulse in them. Here and there."

"What impulse?"

"Hedonism. Pleasure as the primary good. Joy as the telos," Ose holds up his empty glass. "Another drink?"

"You sound skeptical," you say.

"Not at all. I'm quite certain, actually."

"Certain of what?"

"That I'd rather be the wind than the mote," Ose replies.

79AU_Ose13.strDesc:
"Yes," Ose says. "Although, no. Not in the pejorative sense. I'm not sure you have a word for it. Imagine a selfishness that expands. Imagine yourself elevated, beyond. Alone, yes. We all are. Surely you've noticed that. But...untethered."

"Is all your kind untethered?"

"We are, in fact. Eventually. We live and learn and when we've matured to a certain age we just ... leave."

79AU_TripOut.strDesc:
The trip is a long one, and you find yourself wishing the days would pass with the familiar monotony of long haul travel. Instead, your sparing moments of consciousness are haunted with regrets about the world you left behind, the one you had some hand in creating. 

A New World Order, forged in the hungry fire of the last. Entire nationstates leveled in an instant. The old masters dead or dying. You consider who the new masters will be, and no matter how you look at it, the truth is inescapable: you helped them level a shotgun at the body politic, and then they blew off a couple limbs.    

You miss Ben. You'd love to talk to him. You can't believe that in these moments of self reflection, you find yourself longing for the practical evaluations he produced so effortlessly. On particularly dark days, you even miss the condescending pedantry. It's that bad.   

Your unconscious moments are even more disturbing, somehow. The dreams, once relegated to sleep, have begun to invade your waking moments. Every time you close your eyes you see the golden idol, a version of the Colchian sarcophagus rendered in massive scale and looming over your ship like an angry god. 

What's more, the moment your mind slips out of thought and into patterns of default, you hear the chorus of church bells, the eerie tintinnabulation giving way to a vision of infinite black expanse punctuated by glowing purple nodes in an ever swelling network, each point in the system expanding in logarithmic fractal patterns so vast as to silence what's left of your rational mind.

After all this, you've become a ragged ghost of your former self. Food and sleep present themselves as foreign concepts, crude sources of a nourishment you find better met by long contemplation of the infinite sparkling network that returns to you in vision.

Staring out at the endless and somehow expanding plane of purple nodes, you're struck by the certainty that time has only ever been a side effect of distance, of the velocities necessary to close said distance, a quaint but useful epiphenomenon that managed to confound your species for far too long. 

After all, the very voyage you're on now would have been unthinkable before the development of the Epstein drive powering your ship. Under previous outmoded technologies of thrust, it would take months, years to travel from where you were only days ago. So what of those years? Gone. Obliterated by speeds that previous generations could have only dreamed of.  

"Here to there," you keep saying, often aloud. "Once here. Now there."

You're shocked when you finally see it. At first it's just a shimmering in the distance, a golden wink brief enough to have been imagined, like sunlight glinting off a shard of glass in the tumbling surf. 

Peering through your scopes, the shimmer takes form: a golden penumbra limning a perfect circle growing as you draw near. The shape comes in flashes now, here and gone in a fraction of a second, each sight somehow freighted with the experience of lifetimes, yours, yes, but also somehow others, past and future generations living and dying in an instant.

79AU_DreamOne.strDesc:
You've never seen a persimmon. In fact, you're only remotely aware of what a persimmon is. But in your dream, the one that comes to you every time you close your eyes, you're certain that's what you're looking at. 

The orange fruit is dangling from a crooked branch on an otherwise barren bush growing atop a hill overlooking miles of scrubland. High morning sunlight warms your body and flashes gold as beams pass through the dew glistening on the flesh of the berry.

You reach for it, and suddenly it shrinks from your view. The entire bush in fact races away, zooms out for miles, hundreds of them, thousands, the fruit now so distant as to be off-world, a far-flung orbiting body, a golden pinprick in the now night sky shining bright as Polaris and radiating just the same significance.

It is a way point. A guiding light. A signal fire lit in an ancient brazier from a torch held by someone you've never met but you're certain you know. 

You stare at the distant gold-winking light in the otherwise black sky and awaken with a cold certainty that you know exactly where it lies: 79au. The object calling to you in your dreams orbits Sol at 79au. And you know you have to find it.

PLOT_79au_StartTrigger_DreamOne.strTitle: Trigger for the 79au Plot Start Beat

79AU_NightOse.strDesc:
"Him," you say, and point towards President Ose in the corner. "Or ... that. I choose that."

A cold silence invades the room. Emerald sinks down into her seat, shoulders slumped, arms limp. Fire slams an open palm onto the table so hard the glassware rattles. 

"Now now. Don't be cross," Ose says, and stands up from the table. "It's just a game, after all."

The VIPs at the wet bar gather themselves and exchange brief goodbyes as they file out of the room. Emerald, Fire and Sanguine move to join them. 

"See you later?" you try. 

Fire looks back at you. "I sincerely hope not," she says, and then leaves the room after the others. 

"Don't worry about her," Ose says, and gives you a wink. "She's very competitive." 

You look around the room, empty now besides you, Joakim and Ose, who has his hand outstretched to admire his perfect manicure. 

"The pair has been chosen," Joakim says. "Who will begin?"

"Me," says Ose, and then claps his hands twice.

You feel a nearly imperceptible rumbling beneath your feet, here for just a moment and then gone. You look to Ose, who shows a fanged grin.    

"Show me out, would you?" Ose says.

You travel with Ose to the elevator, and sit there for what feels like an eternity as the lift reaches your floor. Your companion is far from the curious and seductive conversationalist he was before. In fact, he seems utterly indifferent to your existence.

The elevator dings and Ose steps inside.

"What's next?" you ask him.

"That, you'll find, is entirely up to you." Ose says. The doors close before him, and you're alone again. More alone than you've felt in a very long time. 

You take the elevator down to the lobby and find Joakim, who points you in the direction of your ship. He's very graciously topped off your reactor with enough fuel to make the trip home, a courtesy he informs you is granted to all visitors of the hotel. 
  
Following Joakim's directions, you wheel yourself down a long corridor that seems to grow darker and longer as you travel. The trip is so long that your mind begins to wander after the architecture of this strange place, and just as it does you find yourself in the bridge of your ship, with no recollection of ever traveling through an airlock. 

Finding no real reason to stay, you plug in coordinates towards home, and your ship begins the long return journey.

ChoongPainRoom0.strTitle: Enter the torture device with Choong
ChoongPainRoom0.strDesc:
A door you've not yet noticed in the cabin - because moments ago it was not present - catches your eye. It's a heavy steel plate perfectly set into the wooden logs. Choong opens it. On the other side is a small room perhaps three metres a side, its walls a dull off-white, evenly lit despite the apparent absence of a source.

Choong waits in the doorway, holding it open. "After you," he says.

There's only one way to do this: pretend nothing bad is going to happen in the face of the evidence, and move your arms and legs, which suddenly feel like jelly, in a manner that approximates walking. In this way, your avatar, your digital or spiritual conscious self, moves between places, and you have entered the torture device.

You hear Choong shut the door behind you. Suddenly you can see him, though you haven't moved: your perspective has instantly turned 180 degrees to face him, which disorients you when you realise it. You can't move your arms or legs, either. Choong is standing still opposite you. The door is gone. You experiment, and find you can still speak and move your head.

"What happens now?" you ask.

"The simulation is starting," he says. "Giving us enough time to realise where we are, for cases where we were awakened from sleep, and dread what is to come. We have a few more seconds of relative normalcy."

Dread what is to come, check. It's faintly nauseating, too, being made to stand like this: so strange to feel an alien volition keeping the muscles still. 

You try to move your real arms, your real legs, back on the ship - and find you cannot do so.

ChoongPainRoom.strDesc:
"I can't move," you say to Choong.

"That's part of it," he says reassuringly.

"I can't move in real life," you say, a shot of adrenaline chilling your neck. "I can't move my real body."

"That's part of it too, obviously," says Choong. "Or you'd remove the device."

"What the fuck?" You've never really realised how much you relied on your body to emote. It's tough to freak out while remaining perfectly still. "How can it do that?"

Choong looks as if he doesn't understand you. "Simple. The device reads the signals your brain tries to send to your real body, and it injects countervailing signals of some kind. You're surprised?"

"Ow!" A lance of pain shoots through your head, as if you've suddenly developed a mild headache. That's more or less what it is. "Of course I'm surprised! I've never done this before!"

Choong winces, too. "It begins," he says. "Ah, well. It looks like you're in it for the long haul."

It never occurred to you that you couldn't take it off. You try to summon your admin interface, any of the various navigation tools you used to get here in the first place - nothing. You're completely trapped, thanks to a mesh sock over your head that makes you resemble a petty criminal. This was supposed to show your willingness to take some licks, convince Choong you're legit, and end when it's too much - now you've doomed yourself to God knows what.

Choong really must think you're lying. He's blase because he assumes you have a way of stopping this. He assumes you'll leave when the going gets tough. He doesn't know you might both be about to die.

ChoongPainRoom_1.strDesc:
"Dr. Choong, listen to me," you say urgently, squinting as the headache waxes and wanes behind your eyes. "I don't know what's about to happen. But I'm telling the truth. I can't move, and I have no way to end this now it's started."

"Me neither," he says, glib.

"Listen, you stupid son of a bitch!" you yell. "I'm -" and find you cannot speak.

"Mind your language," he says calmly. "It shuts down your speech centre so you don't waste time cursing the operators. Saves your energy for juicy secrets and begging later. Brace for the next stage."

The headache expands instantly, as though someone has shoved a spike into your skull. How were you supposed to brace for that? You cry out in spite of yourself. So does Choong.

You roll your eyes and head at Choong to try to communicate. He blinks back tears. "When will your speech return? Thirty seconds, give or take."

ChoongPainRoom_1_1.strDesc:
The pain is bad enough to make you want to curl into a ball on the floor and not move, to make no sound but for a whimper. But you're forced to stand and stare straight ahead. It's unfair. On top of everything else, it's unfair.

You look in mute recognition at Choong; he looks at you. You both suffer in silence. Finally your voice returns. "- speak now? Okay," you try to order your thoughts. "Please listen to me. I'm stuck in here, I'm really stuck in here. What happens at the end," you pause to swallow, voice faltering, "what happens at the end of the sim? Is it lethal?"

"It's going to escalate soon, fair warning," he says. "It isn't usually lethal, depending on the presets. It will continue as long as it detects your brain function, or someone outside ends it." He shuts his eyes, and carries on. "Brain function ends with a protective coma, or it dies; or both, one then the other. That's my understanding."

"You're too smart for your own good," you say. No swearing, just pure anger. "If I'm in a coma I can't keep feeding you glucose, can I?"

"Whatever will I do without my precious glucose," he says acidly. Both of you cry out again as the pain ratchets up. "Fuck!" he says. "Fuck, fuck, f-" his mouth stops moving.

ChoongPainRoom_1_1_1.strTitle: Try again to convince him of the danger
ChoongPainRoom_1_1_1.strDesc:
The pain is bad enough that rather than speak, you moan involuntarily. It takes a supreme effort of will to stop yourself. There's no dignity in any of this. It just sucks. You try to think of something, anything else, imagining yourself on a sunny spacewalk or at a busy K-LEG bar, but these phantoms do not satisfy, they are ground down, dispelled, eroded by the base note of pain.

"Please believe me," you say, all of your effort going into concentration. "Nobody's going to end it. Everything I've told you is true."

"'Please believe me'," he says, when his mouth can move again. "I've tried that one before."

"I mean it," you say.

"Tried that one before too."

Your vision doesn't change exactly, but it is difficult to pay attention to it. "There's nothing I can do. I'm going to die."

"That too," he says.

ChoongPainRoom_1_1_1_1.strDesc:
Conversation is not forthcoming. There is nothing to do but stare at each other in mutual agony.

You are drowning. No, really: you are drowning. It is so sudden and all-consuming a sensation that you forget the pain - you cannot breathe, your lungs are full of water, your brain is starving for oxygen, you furiously will your body to inhale but nothing happens - and it goes on and on and on without end -

"I'm drowning," you rasp out the words (where does the air come from?). "Help me."

"I'm drowning too," says Choong. You almost forgot he exists, even though he never left your sight. His voice is small, as he's preoccupied by other matters.

"How," you say. At any moment your mind's eye is going to close, the curtain is going to come down on the show. No more you.

"It tells your brain it's drowning. So you are drowning," he says.

"Oh," you say. Interesting, but hardly relevant: you're about to die. Even the realisation that you are breathing is no help: they're meaningless breaths, fake, the oxygen is being diverted on the way to your brain - and all of this is a virtual dream, anyway, none of it's real - except your impending death, which is the only real thing left -

And it ends. You are not drowning. You're left with the splitting headache, almost a welcome return, comforting: you are not about to die. Not yet.

You gasp, and breathe deep as you can while totally immobilised. Choong does the same. You're crying, and so is he. Sobbing for joy, for pain, for terror, for the momentary abatement.

"It gets worse," he says through the tears, either an apology or a warning.

"It gets worse?" you say. You wish you could wipe your nose, but mucus trickles down your upper lip and into your mouth. You spit, but no liquid is expelled.

"Much worse," he says.

ChoongPainRoom_1_1_1_1_1.strDesc:
A line of white fire traces itself from your sternum down to your navel. The skin retracts perfectly, and your chest splits apart. Your ribs crack one by one, and with each one you feel it snap and give way, a deep wrongness. You scream and shut your eyes. You've seen your own organs, heart and lungs pulsing in a gooey cavity. It's too much to bear.

You're lost to sensation for a moment. Awful, horrible, incandescent things are happening to your insides, but you're not really present: you're a disassembled model tossed to the floor, innumerable separate parts, less than the sum of the whole. Later, when the simulation forces your eyes open and the images to pass in front of you, it's doing it to someone else, you're not seeing them, which is lucky for you and unlucky for them, because they seem to hate it very much.

Returning to yourself is like awakening: with dismal certainty, you are not in a bed, but still in this fucking room, and screaming is coming from your own mouth. An uncertain amount of time has passed. You stop screaming, almost reluctantly, because screaming actually felt like a good escape from the pain.

Your body is whole, healed, and you are unfortunately alive.

ChoongTortureHimSendHim.strTitle: Send Choong to the Pain Room
ChoongTortureHimSendHim.strDesc:
You think of all the poor souls on Mars and Titan, Venus and Ganymede, Luna and Ceres; even the handful of souls worth saving on K-LEG, who must surely exist, even if you never met any.

There's no other choice. One must suffer so the rest might not.

You context-switch Ben Choong from the Moretti Branded Experience to The Pain Room, and in he goes, a portion of water poured from one cup into another.

Nothing changes from the exterior. The brain shell does not move, and the perfusion keeps glugging away. You hear no ghostly cries of anguish.

ChoongEuthaniseOffer.strTitle: Offer to put him out of his misery
ChoongEuthaniseOffer.strDesc:
"After enduring all this," you say carefully, "... I'm sure many people would rather choose death."

"It crossed my mind many times," he says.

"How can I put this ..." You shrug. "Is that something you want?"

"No. God, no!" He looks shocked at the mere suggestion. "Fuck that. I want to live!"

"Oh," you say. You look around at the dreamscape, the log cabin, Mr Moretti smoking quietly in a corner. "Here?"

"Here," Choong says fervently. "Don't kill me on a whim." 

He adds, with an exaggerated and deferential head bob: "Thank you, please."

ChoongAskAboutNext.strTitle: Ask what he'd like to do next
ChoongAskAboutNext.strDesc:
"You probably won’t believe me when I say this," you say, "but you’re a free man."

"Bully for me."

You press on. "What would you like to do? Where would you like to go?"

He grimaces. "I can’t really go anywhere, and it sounds like I’d have precious little time to do anything when I got there, notwithstanding how little I can do for myself."

"There’s bound to be a biomed outfit who would take you," you say steadily. "You could get sensory input routed in here. Eyes, ears, maybe even legs and arms. I don’t know much about the field but there have been other cases of rehabilitation, victims of the triads on Mars. There’s more to it than you think."

He sniffs. "I don’t want to spend the final months of my life as a medical curiosity. Hook me up to a nutrient supply and a power source and leave me be."

On balance, maybe that’s all one can hope for in life.

ChoongAskAboutChangeMind.strTitle: Ask what would change his mind
ChoongAskAboutChangeMind.strDesc:
"You don't trust me. I understand that." He bobs his head, having the grace to look abashed. 

"But ... you have to have some basis for trust, right? There must be something I can do. Whatever it is, I'll do it." He looks at you appraisingly. You raise a hand, palm up. "What? What is it?"

He bites a lip, thinking. 

You frown. "It'd better not be expensive."

ChoongListenToIdea.strDesc:
"Everyone I have met in this place," he begins, "who has run me through the program - and it’s happened more times than I can count - would always run it the same way." He stands up, for the first time in a while, and stretches. He peers out the window at the coruscating snow. "We would meet here. Mostly here. They would talk. I would answer. I would frustrate them. They would put me in the torture room, and that would be that. When I woke up, it would start again."

He lets the silence hang, and you let him let it. The wind soughs in the trees. "But," he says, "without exception, they never entered the room itself." He turns from the window. "They were very careful to avoid it. I think they actually fear it. It is certainly," his head twitches, so subtly you almost dismiss it, "no picnic, once you're in."

"So, what," you say. "You want to do it to me? Retrograde burn?"

"Not exactly." He clasps his hands behind his back. His posture straightens. "We will go together. Both of us, in the same space, subjected to the same sensation. If I can witness it firsthand, I can almost believe it."

"Oh, that's all, then," you say. "I figured you'd be glad for a break."

"If you are who you say you are, it would be the last time I ever do it," he says. "If you're not, I'd call it just desserts."

"I am who I say I am, and it sounds really really bad," you say. "Besides, you're in that big complex brain device. I got my headgear from a Renbao bargain outlet. Will it even run?"

He waves a hand impatiently. "Think about where you are right now."

"Um," you say. "A spaceship. Or an Italian log cabin."

"Wrong. You're in your own head." He starts pacing the hearth, back and forth. "In my head, across the link, the same dream is playing in tandem. We're communicating. The hardware doesn't know what it's doing, it just does it. This will work. If you want me to trust you, you've got to be - " he hesitates, then says it anyway, "stupid enough to agree to this. Right now, so you don't have time to prepare a fake."

It's a hard sell. Are you stupid enough - his words - to agree to it?

ChoongEnterDeviceYourself.strTitle: Enter the torture device with Choong
ChoongEnterDeviceYourself.strDesc: He offers an outstretched hand. After considering it at length, you take it. You clasp hands for one awkward second too long; he reminds you that, as the user with access privileges, you'll need to set it up. You apologise and disengage, and he guides you through the necessary steps of the simulation menu.

CeresP3TitanFinale8.strDesc: 'Jane' has taken to polishing and oiling a pistol, taking it apart to poke it with a pipe cleaner. The small metallic clicks convey her disdain for the whole presentation louder than words would. She speaks up. "You brought a foreigner into our safehouse, why, exactly? To use the overhead projector?" "No," says John. "I needed you to see [us-custom-characterGenderCond|his|her|their] face. You and your team are going to board the Yangtze, liberate Ben Choong from the brig, and deliver him to [us-custom-characterGenderCond|his|her|their] ship. The [us-shipname], unless I'm mistaken." Silence greets his words. It's an impossibly tall task, you think. Boarding an enemy ship, blind, and for what purpose? To aid you? But you realise the commandos' silence isn't dissent. They're studying the warship on the screen. They're considering it.

CeresP3TitanFinale9.strDesc: "That's suicide," you say. All heads turn to you: perhaps that was a little too honest and a little too quick. "It's a suicide mission. Even if you've had months to prepare, unlimited supplies, no way you can just infiltrate and sneak back out from an enemy warship." Blank Ceresian faces watch you. Inscrutable Americans. John claps your shoulder. "[us-firstname], a word in your ear?" He takes you aside. Jane musters the troops, cracking out instructions with the speed of someone used to command. "Yeah, so, that's kind of a selling point for these types," says John, sotto voce. "Don't get me wrong, they're smart, capable warriors and all. But they've been raised on a steady diet of tier one operator myths, Navy SEALS and Army Rangers tearing up Iraq and Venezuela and Vietnam. They don't really like a mission unless there's a chance they get to drape a flag over a coffin, know what I mean?" You look back at the revolutionaries. Not one of them is a day over twenty-five. "That's a bit cynical," you say evenly. "Isn't it?" "When can their glory fade? O the wild charge they made!" he quotes at you. You grit your teeth. "The world's a cynical place, compadre. Always has been. Better get used to it."

CeresP3TitanFinale10.strDesc: You wonder if any of them are going to protest the ludicrous mission parameters, but none do. Instead, the revolutionaries start to break down the problem, occasionally asking a logistical question or two of John. From the capabilities they discuss, it's apparent this assault on the Yangtze has been considered, even planned for, sometime in the near past. No one bats an eye that the objective of the mission has changed to the extraction of a person of interest.

CeresP3TitanFinale11.strDesc:
Clay takes you back the winding ways to the Port. He's chuffed by a fullish stomach, ten dollars in his pocket, and another ten on its way.

"What do you think of them?" you ask him, pausing for a break in a disused vent shaft. "The 'Revolutionaries'."

Clay seems to think about it for a bit. "I'unno," is all he has to say. Maybe you gave him too much credit.

CeresP3TitanFinale12.strDesc: You return to your ship. Fifteen stressful hours pass, watching the Yangtze on your scope and waiting to see any telltale signs of sabotage or alert. The first is an emergency broadcast from Ring Station. "All ships, all ships Ceres-local," says an unusually hurried ATC operator. "Be advised, Yangtze-3 has initiated emergency undock, again, the Yangtze is undocking from the Ring. No flight plan. We do not know the vector. All ships, all ships, sanitise your inbound or outbound vectors. Look out the window if you have to. ATC out." You watch as the massive warship decouples from Ring Station. Ships for hundreds of kilometres around pull back, or break from their plan, no doubt stressing the ATC further. Some docked ships follow the Yangtze's example, deciding that whatever the warship is doing is something they should do too. They all get bespoke emergency warnings. Hard to say what's going on. Perhaps the team boarded through the station and they fear reinforcements. There's another significant possibility - New contacts appear outbound from the Yangtze. Lifeboats, escape pods. The scope's glare protection kicks in as the screen whites out. Something on the Yangtze just went nuclear. "Holy shit," you say. "Holy shit!" When the scopes can see again, the ship is in pieces. Surgically scuttled, it looks like, rather than a critical explosion. The blast originated a few hundred kilometres from the Ring. Whoever was in control of the Yangtze did their best to spare the station, putting as much distance between them as possible. Even so, you watch as the first wave of debris passes through the Ring. The station is hardened against attack. A nuclear fragmentation grenade on their front doorstep is testing that. No doubt people on board will be killed, but the Ring will survive. Even the most hardened revolutionary wouldn't want a space station to shred itself under its own momentum around their planetoid.

CeresP3TitanFinale13.strDesc:
A few minutes later, there's a knock at the door, so to speak. One of the lifeboats comes perilously close to your ship, and won't respond to hails.

You dock with it, although it feels more like catching a ball before it can hit the ground. The interior is obscured by a mist of blood. "Hello?" you say over the intercom. It's ghoulish, but a pertinent question: "Anyone alive in there?"

There's no way around it: you admit the cloud of blood aboard your ship. A body comes with it, staring sightlessly at you through her vac suit: Jane. The blood is hers, pumping freely through holes in her neck and side.

One of her hands has a death grip on a large grey box. There's no sign of her comrades, nor of the man they were sent to retrieve.

ValkyrieBorderIntro.strDesc:
The trip to Mojave would have been short if not for the argument you had with Choong. 

Knowing you'd need some kind of cover story to get through security, you had the brilliant idea to confer with him on the matter. This led to a battery of increasingly maddening clarifying questions from Ben. Then, when you provided answers to those questions, the fastidious scholar produced what felt like dozens of caveats. 

In the end you were able to pin him down with what you actually needed: forged credentials, namely identifying material for yourself and a plausible manifest declaring whatever the hell you can pretend the brain case is. 

Luckily, Ben was able to provide a contact. It was someone he didn't like very much. Someone he called 'sloppy', which was a damning adjective coming from him. 

In any case, the papers came through: a false ID and manifest, along with a convincing enough cover story, all loaded into your PDA. 

With these in hand, the only thing you lack is confidence. But that, too, can be faked.
ValkyrieBorderIntro.strTooltip: PLACEHOLDER: The player sees this by stepping on a zone trigger on BCRS_ROOF. Zone triggers have no strPlot set, so we set it manually.

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strDesc:
Exposed water pipes from the recycling plant run over your head, humming and sloshing. You laugh, inaudible to anyone but you, such is the power of the noise. This is the 'Fountain', a very large section of the ring, and the closest thing to a public space on the station. Benches and standing rocks suggest a landscape garden, along with a few odd planters. The benches are full of couples enjoying discrete conversation. Up the curve of the ring, jogging toward you, there's a squad of Coalition marines on first shift PT.

Your roving gaze lands on someone staring at you. Red cheongsam, Afro-Asian. Their hand falls gracefully, palm out. An invitation.

You fall into step beside them. Sandalwood scent, you think, and self-consciously you try to remember the last time you'd had such a luxury for yourself. They have enough makeup on that maybe they don't have any at all. Maybe they just have a lucky complexion.

"-?" you say, your voice lost to the water overhead. "Did you kill Ben Choong?"

They don't look at you as they reply. "I sincerely hope not," they say. Their accent is, of all things, American, complete with vocal fry. "I'm answering for my employer, right. I was in bed forty minutes ago." 

"You hope not?"

"Lower your voice," they say steadily. "Even here. If you get out of hand, I have to get my security involved, or risk my cover." A smile plays at the corner of their mouth. "Understood?"

With a glance over your shoulder, you get the sense that someone of far greater mass than you is keeping a respectful but fixed distance. 

"Understood, sure," you reply, trying to match their tone. "And you understand this: you tell me what's going on or I'm going to act like an unstable space captain who just did 3 AU for nothing."

They stop to admire a particularly interesting rock on a solid white display plinth. You stare at their profile until they nod, acquiescing. Then you look at the rock too.

"We're clear, Captain. And believe me, I would love to tell you what I know. But first, I have to know where you stand. So?"
PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strTooltip: It's a short walk away. You'll be back before you know it.

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strTitle: Express Loyalty to GalCon and Titan
PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strDesc:
"Well hell yeah. Another soldier for the good guys." 

"Now let's see here," Wayne continues. "I can't really tell if you paint houses. Hard to gather sometimes. But if wetwork ain't your bailiwick we could always use a cracker. But I wouldn't recommend that myself. Xinhua runners don't fuck around. Two steps in and suddenly you'll find yourself with a whole lotta not-so-pretty pictures on a data card you'd swear you wiped ages ago. Happened to a buddy of mine a couple years back and he's still suckin air down Prokofiev way. I should send him a package..."

"Hate to hear it, hombre," Wayne says. "I guess this is sayonara."  

He tips his cap and holds up two more fingers. "Shot for the road?"

He drains the little cup like he's done it a million times before. You eye your own drink with naked suspicion, given the circumstances. 

"More for me then, I guess," he says, and drinks your glass down. He unfolds himself off the stool and saunters out of the bar. 

John Wayne, huh? At least the name won't be hard to remember.

Especially since he left you with the tab.

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strTitle: Express Ambivalence to The Proxy Powers
PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strDesc:
"Playing the field, I see," Wayne says. He winks. "I like someone who keeps their options open. More money in that. Although you might get dead."

Wayne holds up another two fingers without asking if you're drinking. 

"Well," he says. "I ain't gonna help you no more because you don't know who you work for and I sure as shit don't neither."

The shots arrive and he downs both before walking out without so much as an adios. 

John Wayne, huh? An odd presence, to say the least.

He left you with the tab.

"That's reassuring, at least," they say. "If not your...aggressive overtures. But loyalty must be proved, you see. So. A test."

"Let's hear it," you reply.

"There's a coffee kiosk on the main floor of BCRS. Not much to it. Check beneath the discarded pouches, though, and you might find what you're looking for."

"And what's that?"

They bend down to inspect the rock more closely. You wonder, briefly, if a stone could hold the answer to all your questions.

"You know, back on Earth," they begin. "Before the ablation cascade took the whole world from us. Some would say our nation thinks not in decades but in centuries."

They turn and look up at you from below. 

"Such patience might serve you well now, Captain," they say before standing, dusting off their hands, and walking back up the pathway the way they came.

PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strTitle: Express Ambivalence to The Proxy Powers
PLOT_Ceres_The_Scholar_Establish_Contact.strDesc:
"Lukewarm," they say. "Never a good sign. You'll end up spat from God's mouth with an attitude like that."

"Never been a fan of blind loyalty," you reply. 

"It's time you saw, then," they say.

And with that, they continue their walk up the path.

79AU_Approach60.strDesc:
The Object is quite the conversationalist. Silly you, thinking it was mute. You hadn't learned its language. It took a little mental adjustment, a bit like training yourself to speak your native tongue back to front. That hurdle overcome, you find the Object verbally adroit, suave, quick with a joke, and equally content to play the listener.

Would you have ever believed that there are higher orders of physics, natural laws that you're the only human ever to appreciate? The Object would have. Indeed, it helped you find them, even encouraged you to name a few after yourself. Not all of them - future explorers should be allowed to share that honour. 

In hindsight it's hard to understand the furore on Ceres over a cheap party trick like teleportation. The secrets you're privy to would bring nations to their knees, on your personal order, no less. You clear one room of your ship and dedicate it to your studies, conducting experiments and assays into new forms of physicalised thought, splicing axiom and aphorism before ducking behind a mental blast shield in case they explode, as they occasionally do, into real flames.

The Object is your capable assistant throughout, studiously copying your dictations to paper on its clipboard. It's not so deft with a stylus, however, because when you find the things it has written - it's always leaving them lying around when you're not looking - they contain none of your most penetrating insights, the thoughts you knew must be saved at all costs. 

It's no matter. Each day leaves you so much further ahead intellectually that it would have been embarrassing, even misleading, to reread your old notes. The Object's negligence is revealed as wisdom. It's saving you from yourself. You know there's no need to thank it. You're colleagues in a shared scholarly tradition. This is what it is to have a peer.

79AU_Approach78.strDesc:
The Object leaves you as the torch drive goes cold.

It's been days since you've spoken aloud to it, or it to you. Your thoughts have been intertwined, a single shared monologue, since approximately last Thrwensday when the hull antennae glitched and you saw no point in rebooting them.

It's a shock to feel it leaving, to feel your thoughts regress into your own. Your last words sound plaintive to your ears.

"Please, don't go," you say.

"I'm not going anywhere," it says, with its ready good humour. "I'm right outside."

The blinkers over your mind recede. You're in the airlock, spacesuit donned and ready for EVA. You're going through the procedure for exiting the ship.

79AU_ApproachDock.strDesc:
You return to the ship and march to the NAV console. You point the torch drive at Sol and the nose toward the object.

You set it to maximum Gs.

You're crushed into your seat; then you're crushed against nothing; then you're crushed against the back wall of the bridge. You did not engage the seat's safety webbing. Your bones were not made to bend this way, nor your blood to pool in the chambers of your heart and brain like it has.

You black out.

79AU_ApproachDock1.strDesc: your vision is dark and blurry and half a dozen alarms whistle against one another and an incredibly rare feature on the NAV Station is active and repeating in a deep male monotone, "Terrain, Terrain, Terrain -"

79AU_Inside1.strDesc:
It's been quite a few days.

Your memories of the journey to 79AU are all there, but they feel more like a recollection of a movie, or an anecdote someone else has told, rather than things you did or things that happened to you.

You remember the crash. Your body remembers the crash. Your broken leg has been set, correctly, and is several weeks further mended than it should be; subjectively it was only broken within the hour. A thick plaster cast encases most of the leg.

Otherwise you're as close to factory defaults as you get, overlooking the curious way you receive and process information. The station's interior is a hotel. You flew your spaceship here. Those are two facts that you add to your collection.

A wheelchair waits at your bedside.

CruzCall2.strDesc: Isamard snaps into existence on the screen. She's in a recording booth of her own, but whether that's next door or on another planet is impossible to know. "Hello, young [us-custom-characterGenderCond|man|lady|... person]. It is me: Isambard Cruz! We met not long ago. Did not talk much, but sometimes, is how strong bonds are forged." She has storage bricks piled nearby, all set to travel mode. Her cat is in a pet carrier atop the pile. "And you showed polite interest in Jomari. That counts a lot." She sniffs. "I watched the tape you found. Perhaps I am a hypocrite. Don't care. Not important. The tape, it worries me. Abacho and friends are in danger. With the law and ... with others. Avoid them. Or," she shrugs with a quirk of her mouth, "go see them. Is your funeral." Not the best timing. Would it have killed her to call when you were both on station? ... Did she think it would?

CruzCall3.strDesc:
Isambard continues after a moment, developing a cryptic little grin. "I have a clue for you, if you avoid funeral. I recognise a man in the video. The student in the classroom, put camera up his nose. He work for me many years ago. He was older - he is older now too - but is him, I am certain. Benjamin Choong," she says, enunciating clearly, and repeats it for emphasis. "With two o's.

"He lives on Ring Station at Ceres, in the old hub. He won't return my message ... I have address. Take your ship, fly to Ceres, go to his apartment. Maybe he tell you why his private video was on mysterious VHS. And you do wellness check. Leave reply for me with ZaraFone, please."

She reaches without looking and rubs her cat - Jomari? - Jomari's head through the carrier bars. "I would go, but I fear the danger will come for me too. Instead I go where no one will look. Therefore I need itinerant ship detective - and here you are! Too perfect arrangement not to ask."

She smiles ruefully. "Having watched this message, you are plus two hundred thousand US dollars. Use it to get to Ceres - any remainder, you keep. If you take the money but don't go, you are bad person, and will meet a sticky end. All right. Good luck. Good bye now." She hits a button, and the video ends. Not one for ceremony.

CruzCall4.strDesc:
You check your account. As promised it's healthier by two hundred grand. And all it cost was the threat of a curse from an old Filipina.

As leads go, it's slim. As incentives go, it's weak. But it's all you've got. If you want to find out who made that tape, it looks like you've got to get your ass to Ceres.

ENCFirstDockBCERCalico.strDesc:
You spend some time watching the city at work, from a vantage point at the terminal overlook. You grip a yellow and black striped safety railing for security - it's the only such safety device you can see. The Ceresians seem very comfortable floating themselves from building to building, sailing through unmarked volumes that they somehow know are for public transit, without ever once colliding. A helpful plaque advises that visitors and non-residents use software assistance to travel these arteries.

Before too long, as you follow the luminous floating arrows overlaid in your PDA's viewfinder, you have your first collision. There are two types of traveling Ceresians: single, harried looking salarymen, and gaggles of youths bantering in American drawls. It's the latter that you hit, though you could've sworn you were following your arrow correctly. Somehow a limb gets hooked and then you smack through the middle of them like a bowling ball.

Their voices turn from loud and happy to shrill and angry. A tall boy in a polo shirt emblazoned with a scowling Vegeta disentangles himself from his friends. He floats toward you, stopping gracefully with a blast from his wrist jets. "Hey, Offworld," he says, and it's clearly meant as a disparaging form of address. "You made a mistake just now. You mind apologising to my friends here?"

His right hand crosses to his left hip. A twitch of his fingers pulls his shirt back just enough to reveal the distinctive wooden grip of a Colt 1911 poking out the waistband of his jeans.

ENCFirstDockBCERCalicoApologise.strDesc:
"It was totally my fault," you say. "I don't know how to get around yet. I hope nobody was hurt."

"Mm," he says, considering. "That dog ain't gonna hunt." His friends, now reformed as a group of eager spectators, giggle and snicker.

"Someone oughta teach you how to apologise properly, Offworld," he says, gripping the pistol butt in hand. "Someone like me."

"Sure, if you're good at apologising, you can give me some pointers," you say. The laughter from his friends stops. Uh-oh. It turns out their brains are developed enough to detect irony.

He draws the gun. His followers sigh happily. His hand is down for now, but his eyes - his eyes are pinpricks of rage. What the hell is this kid's problem?

"Beg, Offworld," he says. "Beg for your life."
